items.title: What do the VIPs buy?
items.body:
## What it is
Now compare **what each segment buys**. Join the segment label back onto the orders, then break sales down by segment and category with a `pivot_table`.

## Why it matters
If VIPs over-index on Technology while Regulars buy Office Supplies, that changes what you stock, bundle, and promote *to grow your best customers*. A retention strategy that ignores what VIPs actually purchase is guesswork; this breakdown makes it evidence-based.

## The technique
You computed `segment` on the per-customer `clv` table, but buying data lives on the per-order `df`. So you **merge the label back** onto every order (join on `Customer Name`), then pivot sales by `Category` x `segment`. This is Week 2's merge + pivot working together on a real decision — exactly how techniques compound once you have them.

items.title: Pandas pivot_table for a two-way breakdown
items.why: pivot_table to cross segment and category. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Bring the segment onto each order, then pivot
```python
df = df.merge(clv["segment"], on="Customer Name", how="left")

pivot = df.pivot_table(index="Category", columns="segment",
                       values="Sales", aggfunc="sum")
print(pivot.round(0))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
segment          Regular     VIP
Category
Furniture        148000.0  + 89000.0
Office Supplies  151000.0  + 95000.0
Technology       121000.0  +186000.0
```

## Read it
Scan the VIP column against Regular: **VIPs spend far more on Technology** than Regulars do, even though there are 4x fewer of them. That's the actionable nugget — your best customers are tech buyers, so a VIP program built around technology (early access, bundles) targets profit where it already concentrates.
```python
# VIPs' top sub-categories
vip = df[df["segment"] == "VIP"]
print(vip.groupby("Sub-Category")["Sales"].sum().sort_values(ascending=False).head(3))
```
```
Sub-Category
Phones      82000.0
Machines    61000.0
Copiers     58000.0
```

cards.whenRight: Right — the label becomes a dimension to break sales down by.
cards.whenWrong: It does — once labelled, pivot by category x segment to compare.

cards.whenWrong: It's very useful — it tells you what to promote to your best customers.

days.title: Do your best customers come back?
days.summary: Concept, then the repeat-rate output. Retention is the engine behind CLV.

items.title: Do your best customers come back?
items.body:
## What it is
High CLV usually comes from **coming back**, not one giant order. The **repeat-buyer rate** is the share of customers who placed more than one distinct order — the simplest, sharpest retention metric.

## Why it matters
It changes the whole strategy. If your VIPs are *repeat* buyers, a retention program protects most of your profit — keep them happy and the value keeps flowing. If they're one-time *whales*, you instead need a re-engagement or acquisition strategy. You cannot choose the right play until you know whether value comes from loyalty or from luck.

## The one-line trick
Count distinct orders per customer (`nunique`), test `> 1`, and take the **mean of that boolean Series** — because `True`/`False` average to a proportion (True=1, False=0). So `(orders_per_cust > 1).mean()` *is* the repeat rate. Then split it by segment to see if VIPs are more loyal than Regulars (they almost always are).

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Compute the repeat-buyer rate
```python
orders_per_cust = df.groupby("Customer Name")["Order ID"].nunique()

repeat_rate = (orders_per_cust > 1).mean()
print(f"{repeat_rate:.0%} of customers ordered more than once")
```
```
71% of customers ordered more than once
```

## Boolean .mean() is a proportion — see why
```python
print((orders_per_cust > 1).head())
print("mean ->", (orders_per_cust > 1).mean().round(2))
```
```
Customer Name
Aaron Bergman     True
Aaron Hawkins     True
Aaron Smayling    True
Adam Bellavance   True
Adam Hart         True
Name: Order ID, dtype: bool
mean -> 0.71
```
True counts as 1, False as 0, so the average is the share that are True.

## Retention by segment
```python
clv["repeat"] = orders_per_cust > 1
print(clv.groupby("segment")["repeat"].mean().round(2))
```
```
segment
Regular    0.62
VIP        0.96
```
**96% of VIPs are repeat buyers vs 62% of Regulars** — your profit is loyalty-driven, so a retention program is the right lever.

cards.prompt: Repeat-buyer rate is the share of customers who placed more than one distinct order.
cards.whenRight: Right — count distinct orders, then the fraction with >1.
cards.whenWrong: It is — the proportion of customers with more than one order.

cards.prompt: Taking `.mean()` of a True/False Series gives the proportion that are True.
cards.whenRight: Right — True=1, False=0, so the mean is the share of Trues.
cards.whenWrong: It does — booleans average to a proportion.

items.title: Update the memo (v3)
items.body:
## What it is
Same memo discipline (**headline → evidence → recommendation**, one page), new finding. The CLV story is about *people*, so the recommendation must be a customer action — not a metric restated.

## Why it matters
"The top 20% drive 79% of profit" is interesting. "Launch a VIP loyalty program to protect the 79% of profit concentrated in our top 20% — who are 96% repeat buyers and skew to Technology" is *useful*: it names who, why, and what to do. The recommendation is the entire reason you did the week's work; a memo that stops at the number wastes it.

## What to include
Lead with the 80/20 headline. Back it with three evidence bullets (profit share, VIP buying mix, retention gap). Close with one concrete action and a next step (a pilot).

resources.label: How to compute churn rate properly - 10 min (top YouTube result)

exercises: Build a churn definition: customers with no order in 6+ months
Find the 5 customers who lost you the most money
Plot order count distribution — is it heavily skewed?
questions: Why is CLV not the same as 'lifetime sales'?
What's a cohort analysis?
Why does retention drop sharply from 1st to 2nd order in most businesses?
How would you use this analysis for a marketing budget?
mastery_questions: Aggregate the data to the customer level: for each Customer ID, compute total Sales, total Profit, order count, and average discount. Paste the first 5 rows and the row count. Now rank customers by total Profit descending and assign segments: VIP (top 10%), High Value (next 20%), Medium (next 40%), Low (bottom 30%). Use PERCENTRANK or NTILE logic. Paste the segment count and aggregate profit for each segment.

Compute the Pareto curve. Sort customers by total profit descending. Add a cumulative profit column (running sum). Add a cumulative percentage of total profit column (cumulative / grand total). Add a cumulative percentage of customers column (row number / total customers). Find the row where cumulative profit percentage first exceeds 80%. Paste that row. What percentage of customers does it represent? Is it above or below 80/20?

Build the segment profile table: for each segment, compute average order count, average order value (Sales / order count), average discount received, and Category mix (percentage of orders in each Category). Paste the table. Write two sentences comparing VIPs to Low Value customers on at least two dimensions -- specifically, do VIPs receive lower or higher average discounts? This connection between segmentation and discount policy is the finding that ties weeks 3 and 4 together.

Build the Pareto chart: a combination chart with cumulative customer percentage on the x-axis, a bar chart showing each customer's profit contribution, and a line showing the cumulative profit percentage. The 80% line on the y-axis is the key visual reference. Paste the chart. A reader should be able to identify the 80/20 point from the chart without reading the underlying table.

Write the memo update: one new paragraph stating the three specific characteristics that distinguish VIP customers from Low Value customers, with numbers for each. Do not write "VIPs spend more" -- write "VIP customers place an average of 14 orders per year versus 2 for Low Value customers, at an average order value of $847 versus $312, and receive an average discount of 8% versus 24%." Paste the paragraph.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to write the SUMIF formula for aggregating order-level data to the customer level. It is a multi-column SUMIF with customer ID as the criteria and multiple columns to aggregate -- mechanical but error-prone to write manually. Verify the output for 3 spot-check customers. Do NOT ask Claude to write the memo paragraph comparing VIPs to Low Value customers -- that comparison requires reading the actual numbers from your segment table, not generating plausible-sounding ones.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Your audience for the CLV analysis is the marketing team. They want to know: 'Who do we send the next campaign to?' Lead your memo update with 3 specific named customer segments and the action for each.
weeks.pre_flight: Before building the segmentation, compute the total number of unique customers in the dataset and the total profit. Then estimate: if the 80/20 rule holds exactly, how many customers are in the top 20% and what is their aggregate profit? Write those two numbers down. The comparison between your estimate and the actual Pareto calculation is informative -- most datasets are more unequal than 80/20, and a few are less.
common_mistakes: Computing customer total profit at the order level instead of the customer level. A customer with 20 orders appears 20 times in the raw data -- aggregate to the customer level first with a SUMIF or groupby before segmenting.

Using revenue instead of profit for CLV segmentation in a dataset where margins vary widely. A customer who buys heavily discounted Furniture may have high revenue and negative profit contribution. Profit-based segmentation gives a more accurate picture of true customer value.

Assigning segment labels that overlap (top 10%, top 20%, etc.) instead of non-overlapping ranges (top 10%, 10-30%, 30-70%, 70-100%). Double-check that every customer appears in exactly one segment and the segment percentages sum to 100%.

Charting the Pareto curve with profit on the x-axis instead of cumulative customer count. The convention is customers on the x-axis, cumulative profit on the y-axis -- the curve bends toward the top-left, showing that the left portion of customers drives a disproportionate share of profit.

Ignoring the Low Value segment in the analysis. The finding about VIPs is interesting. The finding about the Low Value segment -- specifically whether they are loss-making at high discounts -- is actionable.
weeks.debug_help: The PERCENTRANK-based segmentation fails if you are using PERCENTRANK on the profit column directly, because PERCENTRANK assigns the same rank to ties. For customer segmentation, you want RANK.EQ or RANK.AVG on the sorted profit column, then divide by total customers. The cleaner Excel approach: sort by profit descending, add a rank column (=ROW()-1, adjusted for header), then use IF nested on the rank fraction. In Python: df['percentile'] = df['profit'].rank(pct=True) and cut into segments with pd.qcut or pd.cut.
stretch: Compute the retention rate by segment: of customers who placed an order in 2016, what percentage placed at least one order in 2017? Compute separately for VIPs and Low Value customers. The retention rate difference by segment is one of the strongest arguments for differential treatment of customer groups.

Map the VIP customers by State using a geographic pivot table. Are the VIP customers concentrated in specific states? If so, does the regional concentration match the high-performing regions from week 1? Connecting the customer analysis to the geographic analysis is the kind of multi-dimensional insight that distinguishes a senior analyst's work.

Compute RFM scores (Recency, Frequency, Monetary) for the customer base as an alternative segmentation approach. Score each customer 1-5 on each dimension, then combine the scores. Compare the RFM segments to the profit-based segments. Where do they agree and where do they disagree? The disagreements are the most instructive cases.

weeks.title: Superstore v0.4: SQL version
weeks.context:
You have done the Superstore analysis twice: once in Excel, once in Python. This week you do it in SQL -- the language that runs every serious data organisation's analytical infrastructure. Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, and every other data warehouse accepts SQL as input. Pandas is useful when you can fit the data in memory on your laptop. SQL is what you use when the data lives somewhere else and you cannot.

The SQL version of the Superstore analysis has a specific goal: every pivot table and calculated metric from weeks 1 through 4 should be expressible as a SQL query that you can run against a database. You will load the Superstore CSV into a local SQLite database and write queries.sql with at least eight queries -- one for each of the main analytical questions. The queries should be readable: comments above each one, clear aliases, formatted with line breaks.

CTEs (Common Table Expressions, the WITH ... AS clause) are the SQL equivalent of naming an intermediate result in Excel. Instead of a formula that references a formula that references another formula, you name each step: WITH customer_totals AS (...), then segment_ranks AS (...), then SELECT FROM segment_ranks. CTEs make complex SQL readable and debuggable, and they are the standard pattern in every modern analytics SQL style guide.

Self-joins are how you compute year-over-year comparisons in SQL. You join the orders table to itself, matching on Category and the year, and compute the ratio between the two year's values. It is not intuitive until you see it once, and once you see it it is the natural way to express "compare this year to last year."

By Sunday: queries.sql committed to the Superstore repo with at least eight queries, every query producing a result that matches the corresponding Excel or Python output, and a brief comment above each query explaining what question it answers.

days.title: SELECT — read columns from a table
days.summary: The language every warehouse runs on. Concept, video, then real queries with output.

items.title: SELECT — read columns from a table
items.body:
## What it is
**SQL** is how you ask a database for data. The core statement names the columns you want and the table to take them from: `SELECT columns FROM table`. `*` means every column; `LIMIT` returns just a few rows for a quick peek.

## Why it matters
You've done Superstore in Excel and pandas; SQL is the third tool, and the one every serious data organisation runs on — BigQuery, Snowflake, Redshift, and Databricks all speak SQL. The reason is scale: pandas works while the data fits in your laptop's memory; SQL runs the same logic against billions of rows that live on a server you'll never download. Same questions, vastly bigger data.

## The mental bridge from pandas
`SELECT col FROM t` is `df[["col"]]`. `WHERE` is your boolean mask. `GROUP BY` is `groupby`. You already *know* the analysis from Weeks 2-4 — this week you're learning a second way to *say* it. That's why you'll re-answer the exact same Superstore questions: so the SQL is recognition, not new analysis.

## Setup (free, in-browser)
Go to **sqliteonline.com**, click *Import*, upload your Superstore CSV, and name the table `superstore`. No install, no account.

days.title: WHERE — filter rows
days.summary: Concept, video, then filtered queries with output. SQL's boolean mask.

items.title: WHERE — filter rows
items.body:
## What it is
`WHERE` keeps only the rows that match a condition — the exact pandas boolean mask, written in words. Pair it with `ORDER BY` to sort and `LIMIT` to cap.

## Why it matters
Analysis is filtering to the rows that answer the question: the loss-making orders, one region, the biggest losses. In pandas you wrote `df[df["profit"] < 0]`; in SQL it's `WHERE profit < 0`. Same idea, and recognising that mapping means you're not learning analysis again — just new syntax for logic you own.

## The gotcha to internalise now
Combine conditions with the **words** `AND` / `OR` (not pandas' `&` / `|`), and you don't need the extra parentheses pandas forced on you. `WHERE region = 'East' AND sales > 500`. Text values go in single quotes; numbers don't. Get that and WHERE is effortless.

items.title: SQL intro: SELECT, FROM & WHERE
items.why: WHERE filtering in context. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Filter to loss-making orders
```sql
SELECT order_id, sub_category, profit
FROM superstore
WHERE profit < 0
LIMIT 3;
```
```
order_id        sub_category  profit
US-2016-108966  Tables       -383.03
CA-2017-118983  Tables       -129.44
US-2015-150630  Binders      -123.86
```

## Combine conditions with AND
```sql
SELECT order_id, region, sales
FROM superstore
WHERE region = 'East' AND sales > 500
LIMIT 3;
```
```
order_id        region  sales
CA-2017-152156  East    731.94
CA-2016-138688  East    957.58
...
```

## The 10 biggest losses: filter + sort + cap
```sql
SELECT sub_category, profit
FROM superstore
WHERE profit < 0
ORDER BY profit ASC
LIMIT 5;
```
```
sub_category  profit
Machines     -3839.99
Binders      -3701.89
Tables       -3399.98
Bookcases    -1665.05
Tables       -1359.99
```
`ORDER BY profit ASC` puts the most negative (biggest losses) first.

cards.prompt: `WHERE profit < 0` keeps only rows where profit is negative — SQL's boolean mask.
cards.whenRight: Right — WHERE is the SQL filter.
cards.whenWrong: It does — WHERE is exactly a boolean mask in words.

cards.prompt: In SQL you combine two conditions with the words AND / OR.
cards.whenRight: Right — AND/OR words (pandas used & and |).
cards.whenWrong: It does — SQL uses AND/OR, no & or |.

cards.prompt: `ORDER BY profit ASC` sorts largest profit first.
cards.whenRight: Correct — ASC is ascending (smallest/most-negative first); use DESC for largest.
cards.whenWrong: Backwards — ASC is smallest-first; that's why it surfaces biggest losses.

days.title: GROUP BY — summarise into groups
days.summary: Concept, video, then grouped queries with output. The pivot table of SQL.

items.title: GROUP BY — summarise into groups
items.body:
## What it is
`GROUP BY` collapses rows into one row per group, paired with an **aggregate** (`SUM`, `AVG`, `COUNT`). It is the SQL pivot table — and the same split-apply-combine as pandas `groupby`.

## Why it matters
Every "per X" question — profit per sub-category, sales per region — is a GROUP BY. It's the workhorse of analytical SQL, and re-deriving your Week 1 margin finding with it proves the analysis transfers across tools (which is what makes you genuinely fluent rather than dependent on one).

## WHERE vs HAVING — the classic confusion
`WHERE` filters **rows before** grouping; `HAVING` filters **groups after** aggregating. "Orders over $500" is a WHERE; "sub-categories whose *total* profit is negative" is a HAVING (it tests an aggregate). And every column you SELECT must be either in the GROUP BY or wrapped in an aggregate — otherwise SQL doesn't know which row's value to show.

items.title: SQL aggregate functions, GROUP BY & HAVING
items.why: GROUP BY + aggregates explained clearly. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Q1 (margin leaders) in SQL
```sql
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY sub_category
ORDER BY total_profit DESC
LIMIT 5;
```
```
sub_category  total_profit
Copiers        55617.8
Phones         44515.7
Accessories    41936.6
Paper          34053.6
Binders        30221.8
```

## The loss-makers — HAVING filters the GROUPS
```sql
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY sub_category
HAVING SUM(profit) < 0
ORDER BY total_profit ASC;
```
```
sub_category  total_profit
Tables        -17725.5
Bookcases      -3472.6
Supplies       -1189.1
```
Three sub-categories lose money overall — the same answer Excel and pandas gave, now in SQL. `HAVING` (not `WHERE`) because it tests the aggregated `SUM(profit)`.

cards.prompt: `GROUP BY sub_category` with `SUM(profit)` returns one total-profit row per sub-category.
cards.whenRight: Right — group, aggregate, one row per group. The SQL pivot.
cards.whenWrong: It does — GROUP BY + aggregate = one summarised row per group.

cards.prompt: `HAVING` filters groups after aggregation, while `WHERE` filters rows before it.
cards.whenRight: Right — WHERE pre-aggregation (rows), HAVING post-aggregation (groups).
cards.whenWrong: Correct — WHERE filters rows first, HAVING filters grouped results.

cards.prompt: You can SELECT a raw column that's neither grouped nor aggregated.
cards.whenRight: Correct — every selected column must be in GROUP BY or inside an aggregate.
cards.whenWrong: Not allowed — non-grouped, non-aggregated columns error out.
cards.sim: GROUP BY category; SELECT sub_category -> error

days.title: Aggregate over time (year-over-year)
days.summary: Concept, video, then the yearly trend query with output.

items.title: Aggregate over time (year-over-year)
items.body:
## What it is
To see a trend you group by a **slice of the date**. In SQLite, `strftime('%Y', order_date)` extracts the year as text, and you GROUP BY that to get one total per year.

## Why it matters
"Is the business growing?" is a time question, and time questions are answered by grouping on a date part — year, quarter, month. It turns a pile of dated orders into a trend line: the Q2 year-over-year answer you computed in pandas, now in SQL. Grouping by a *derived* value (not a raw column) is also a small but important leap — it shows GROUP BY works on expressions, not just columns.

## How to read YoY
Once you have revenue per year, year-over-year growth is just each year compared to the one above it. Even reading the rows top to bottom tells you the direction; the exact % is the next refinement.

items.title: SQL aggregate functions & GROUP BY
items.why: The grouping concept, applied to a time slice. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Revenue and profit per year
```sql
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS yr,
       SUM(sales)  AS revenue,
       SUM(profit) AS profit
FROM superstore
GROUP BY yr
ORDER BY yr;
```
```
yr     revenue    profit
2014   484247.5   49544.0
2015   470532.5   61618.6
2016   609205.6   81795.2
2017   733215.3  ...
```
Read it top to bottom: revenue dips slightly in 2015, then climbs strongly through 2016-2017 — a growing business. Grouping by the *extracted year* (an expression, not a stored column) is the key move.

cards.prompt: Grouping by the year extracted from a date gives one total per year — a trend.
cards.whenRight: Right — extract the year, GROUP BY it, one row per year.
cards.whenWrong: It does — grouping on the extracted year yields a per-year trend.

cards.prompt: `GROUP BY` only works on stored text columns, never on a value derived from a date.
cards.whenRight: Correct — you can GROUP BY any expression, like strftime('%Y', order_date).
cards.whenWrong: Not true — GROUP BY works on derived expressions too.

days.title: Top customers (CLV in SQL)
days.summary: Concept, video, then the CLV leaderboard query with output.

items.title: Top customers (CLV in SQL)
items.body:
## What it is
The CLV you computed in pandas last week is a single SQL query: group by the customer, sum their profit, sort, and cap with LIMIT.

## Why it matters
This is the payoff of learning one idea in two tools. When you see that `df.groupby("Customer Name")["Profit"].sum()` and `GROUP BY customer_name ... SUM(profit)` produce the *identical* leaderboard, the concept detaches from the syntax — and that transfer is exactly what makes a hire valuable. You can drop into any stack and express the analysis.

## The pattern
`GROUP BY customer + SUM(profit) + ORDER BY DESC + LIMIT 10` is a reusable shape: "top N things by some total". You'll use it for top products, top regions, top anything.

items.title: SQL GROUP BY & aggregates
items.why: The grouping concept behind the CLV query. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Top 10 customers by lifetime profit
```sql
SELECT customer_name,
       SUM(profit) AS clv,
       COUNT(DISTINCT order_id) AS orders
FROM superstore
GROUP BY customer_name
ORDER BY clv DESC
LIMIT 5;
```
```
customer_name    clv      orders
Tamara Chand     8981.3   5
Raymond Buch     6976.1   6
Sanjit Chand     5757.4   9
Hunter Lopez     5622.4   6
Adrian Barton    5444.8   10
```
This is the **same leaderboard** your pandas CLV table produced in Week 4 — identical names, identical numbers. Same data, same logic, different language. `COUNT(DISTINCT order_id)` is the SQL of `nunique()` — real orders, not line-items.

cards.prompt: Top-10 customers = GROUP BY customer, SUM(profit), ORDER BY DESC, LIMIT 10.
cards.whenRight: Right — group, sum, sort, cap: the whole leaderboard.
cards.whenWrong: It is — that one query is CLV plus a ranking.
cards.sim: GROUP BY customer_name ORDER BY clv DESC LIMIT 10

cards.prompt: pandas `groupby` and SQL `GROUP BY` express the same underlying idea.
cards.whenRight: Right — split-apply-combine in both; only syntax differs.
cards.whenWrong: They do — both are split-apply-combine; identical logic.

[WRITE] One sentence: does this match your pandas CLV top-10 from Week 4?

days.title: Save your queries

items.title: Save your queries
items.body:
## What it is
Collect every query you wrote this week into one file, `queries.sql`, each with a one-line comment saying what it answers.

## Why it matters
A saved, commented `.sql` file is a **deliverable**, not a throwaway: anyone (including future-you) can rerun it against the data and reproduce every answer. Reproducibility is the line between real analysis and ad-hoc poking — and in a job, the queries you can hand over are worth far more than the ones you typed and lost.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## queries.sql — your reusable analysis
```sql
-- Q1: Margin leaders and laggards
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore GROUP BY sub_category ORDER BY total_profit DESC;

-- Q2: Year-over-year revenue and profit
SELECT strftime('%Y', order_date) AS yr, SUM(sales) AS revenue, SUM(profit) AS profit
FROM superstore GROUP BY yr ORDER BY yr;

-- Q3: Top 10 customers by lifetime profit (CLV)
SELECT customer_name, SUM(profit) AS clv
FROM superstore GROUP BY customer_name ORDER BY clv DESC LIMIT 10;
```
Re-run each in sqliteonline to confirm they still work end to end.

cards.prompt: A commented .sql file makes your analysis reproducible and reviewable by others.
cards.whenRight: Right — anyone can rerun it and get the same answers.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a commented query file is a reproducible deliverable.

mastery_questions: Write Query 1: total Sales, Profit, and Profit Margin by Category. Use a CTE to compute the aggregates first: WITH cat_totals AS (SELECT Category, SUM(Sales) as total_sales, SUM(Profit) as total_profit FROM superstore GROUP BY Category) SELECT *, ROUND(total_profit * 1.0 / total_sales, 4) as margin FROM cat_totals ORDER BY margin DESC. Paste the result. Does it match the week-1 Excel pivot? If not, write which cells differ and why.

Write Query 2: annual revenue with year-over-year growth using a self-join. WITH annual AS (SELECT strftime('%Y', "Order Date") as year, SUM(Sales) as revenue FROM superstore GROUP BY 1) SELECT a.year, a.revenue, ROUND((a.revenue - b.revenue) * 1.0 / b.revenue, 4) as yoy_growth FROM annual a LEFT JOIN annual b ON CAST(a.year AS INT) = CAST(b.year AS INT) + 1 ORDER BY a.year. Paste the result. Does the YoY growth match weeks 1 and 2? Write one sentence about what the LEFT JOIN handles that an INNER JOIN would not.

Write Query 3: customer lifetime value -- total Profit, order count, and average order value per customer, sorted by total Profit descending, with LIMIT 10. Paste the top 10 customers and confirm the top customer's profit matches the week-4 customer aggregation. Now write Query 4: the segment distribution using a CASE statement to assign VIP/High/Medium/Low based on the NTILE(10) window function. Paste the query and the segment counts.

Write Query 5: the discount bucket analysis using a CASE statement equivalent to the nested IF from week 3. Add a GROUP BY on the bucket and Category. Paste the result confirming the margin at each discount bucket matches the week-3 analysis. Write one sentence about when you would use a CASE statement versus a lookup table join for binning a continuous variable.

Add a validation query for each of the four main queries: a simpler aggregation that checks the grand total. For example: SELECT SUM(total_profit) FROM (your margin query) should equal SELECT SUM(Profit) FROM superstore. Write and run all four validation queries. Paste their output. Validation queries are the SQL equivalent of the manual spot-check you did in week 1 -- every analyst who works in SQL should have this as a reflex.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the self-join year-over-year query -- the syntax for joining a table to itself with a year offset is mechanical and Claude writes it correctly. Verify the output against weeks 1 and 2. Do NOT use Claude to debug wrong query results. Debugging SQL requires understanding what data each clause produces -- use SELECT to inspect intermediate CTEs one at a time.
weeks.pre_flight: Install DB Browser for SQLite (free, cross-platform) and import the Superstore CSV into a new SQLite database. Run SELECT * FROM superstore LIMIT 5 and paste the output. Confirm the column names match what you expect from the CSV. If the column names have spaces (they do -- "Order Date", "Customer Name"), you will need to quote them with backticks or brackets in every query. Write that reminder at the top of queries.sql.
common_mistakes: Using integer division in SQLite. In SQLite, 1/3 returns 0, not 0.333. Always cast at least one operand to float: 1.0/3 or CAST(numerator AS REAL) / denominator. The most common manifestation: computing margin as Profit/Sales returns 0 for all rows because both are stored as integers.

Forgetting to quote column names with spaces. "Order Date" without quotes fails with "no such column: Order". Use backticks in SQLite: `Order Date`. Include a comment at the top of queries.sql reminding yourself of this -- it will save 20 minutes of debugging when you return to the file.

Writing SELECT * in production-style queries. SELECT * is fine for exploration, but every query in queries.sql should name its output columns explicitly. A query that returns unknown columns is a query that breaks silently when the source schema changes.

Not testing each query result against the corresponding Excel or Python output. The point of the SQL version is reproducibility -- if the numbers differ, you have a bug in one of the three versions and you need to find it.

Using subqueries where CTEs would be clearer. A query with three levels of nested subqueries is correct but unreadable. Refactor to CTEs before committing. Code that nobody can read in six months -- including you -- is technical debt.
weeks.debug_help: If a query returns unexpected results, use SELECT COUNT(*) to check row counts at each intermediate step. If a JOIN produces more rows than you expect, you probably have a many-to-many join -- check that the join key is unique on at least one side. If a GROUP BY returns fewer rows than you expect, you might have NULLs in the group column -- SQLite groups NULLs together as a single group, which can surprise you. Run SELECT "column_name", COUNT(*) FROM superstore GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 2 for any suspicious column and check whether NULL appears in the output.
stretch: Translate the queries to BigQuery SQL syntax (free tier available). The main differences: backtick quoting is the same, but date functions use DATE_TRUNC instead of strftime, and CAST uses a different syntax. Running the same queries in BigQuery proves they work against a production-grade engine.

Write a query that identifies customers who placed orders in 2016 but not in 2017 (churned customers) using a NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE IS NULL pattern. Churn identification in SQL is a standard analyst skill and this dataset is a clean example.

Write one stored view: CREATE VIEW customer_segments AS (your segment query). Then write a query on top of the view: SELECT * FROM customer_segments WHERE segment = 'VIP'. Views are the SQL equivalent of a named range in Excel -- they hide complexity and make downstream queries readable.

weeks.title: Statistical thinking for analysts
weeks.context:
Everything you found in weeks 1 through 5 is a pattern. Patterns are not findings. A finding is a pattern with evidence that it is real and not noise. "Furniture margins are lower than Technology margins" is a pattern. "Furniture margins are 7.2 percentage points lower than Technology margins (95% CI: 5.8 to 8.6 pp, p < 0.001)" is a finding you can defend.

Most business analysts never learn this distinction formally, which means most business analyses are underpowered. Someone presents "the West region grew 4% faster than the East" without asking whether 4% is a real difference or whether it would disappear with a different time window. Statisticians call this the file-drawer problem -- the analyses that do not show a significant result get quietly put away, and the ones that show a positive result get presented, regardless of how noisy the signal is.

This week you upgrade every finding from weeks 1 through 5 with appropriate statistical support. Confidence intervals around mean profit margin by Category. A t-test comparing VIP customer order values to Low Value customer order values. The Pearson correlation between Discount and Profit with a p-value. And a check for Simpson's paradox -- whether an aggregate finding reverses when you break it down by a subgroup.

Simpson's paradox is worth a specific example. If Technology has the best overall margin but the worst margin in the West region, the aggregate finding is misleading for the West region sales team. Any recommendation based on "Technology is our best category" could lead the West team to push the exact subcategory where they are losing money. Checking for reversal is not optional when regional or segment breakdowns exist.

By Sunday: every key finding in the Superstore analysis upgraded with a confidence interval or p-value, Simpson's paradox check documented for at least one finding, and the analyst memo updated to reflect the statistical framing.

days.title: Samples and selection bias
days.summary: A pattern in a biased sample is not a finding. Concept, then how it bites your Superstore data.

items.title: Samples and selection bias
items.body:
## What it is
Your data is almost always a **sample**, not the whole population. **Selection bias** is when that sample isn't representative — so a pattern in it may say more about *who got into the data* than about reality.

## Why it matters
"Patterns are not findings." A finding is a pattern with evidence it's real *and* generalisable. If the sample is skewed, even a strong, statistically clean pattern can be an artefact. Three common forms quietly distort analysis:

- **Survivorship bias** — you see the customers who checked out, not the carts abandoned. Conclusions about "what customers want" miss everyone who left.
- **Self-selection** — people who leave reviews are systematically happier or angrier than the silent majority.
- **Coverage** — Superstore is *one* retailer's orders. Patterns here ("Tables lose money") may not hold for retail in general.

## The habit
Before trusting any pattern, ask: *who or what is missing from this data, and would including them change the story?* This question costs ten seconds and saves you from confidently shipping a conclusion your sample never supported.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Interrogate what the sample actually covers
```python
print(df["order_date"].min(), "->", df["order_date"].max())
print(df["region"].value_counts())
```
```
2014-01-03 -> 2017-12-30
West       3203
East       2848
Central    2323
South      1620
```
Read it as a *coverage check*, not a result: this is **4 years, one company, US-only, South under-represented**. So any claim you make is really "for this retailer, 2014-17, mostly West/East." That scoping isn't pedantry — it's the difference between an honest finding and an overclaim. Bias isn't fixed by more rows; it's fixed by representativeness, which a count like this helps you see.

cards.prompt: A strong pattern in a biased sample may not hold in the wider population.
cards.whenRight: Right — bias can manufacture or hide patterns.
cards.whenWrong: It can mislead — a biased sample's pattern needn't generalise.
cards.sim: sample: only checkouts -> 'everyone buys!' (abandoned carts unseen)

cards.prompt: Collecting more data automatically removes selection bias.
cards.whenRight: Correct — more biased data is just more bias; representativeness is the fix.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — volume doesn't fix bias; a bigger skewed sample is still skewed.

days.title: Confidence intervals
days.summary: Concept, video, then a real CI computed and printed. Report a range, not false precision.

items.title: Confidence intervals
items.body:
## What it is
A single number — "average margin = 7.2%" — hides uncertainty. A **confidence interval (CI)** gives a *range* that probably contains the true value (95% is the usual level). The less data you have, the wider that range.

## Why it matters
"Margins are 7.2% lower" sounds exact and authoritative. "7.2% lower, 95% CI [3.1%, 11.3%]" is *honest* — and far more useful, because it tells the reader how much to trust the estimate. The killer application: if you're comparing two groups and the CI of their *difference* crosses zero, you cannot claim there's a real difference at all. CIs are how you avoid betting the business on noise.

## The intuition
A CI is built from the **standard error** — roughly, how much your sample average would wobble if you'd drawn a different sample. More data shrinks the standard error, so the interval tightens. A wide CI is the data honestly telling you "I'm not sure".

items.title: Interpreting confidence intervals (with examples)
items.why: What a CI does and doesn't mean. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Compute a 95% CI for a sub-category's profit
```python
import numpy as np
x = df.loc[df["Sub-Category"] == "Tables", "Profit"]

mean = x.mean()
se   = x.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(x))      # standard error
lo, hi = mean - 1.96*se, mean + 1.96*se
print(f"n={len(x)}  mean={mean:.1f}  95% CI = [{lo:.1f}, {hi:.1f}]")
```
Output (illustrative):
```
n=319  mean=-55.6  95% CI = [-76.2, -35.0]
```
Read it: Tables average a **loss** of ~$56/order, and the whole interval is **below zero** — so "Tables are unprofitable on average" is a claim the data genuinely supports, not noise. If the interval had been, say, [-20, +15], you couldn't say that.
```python
# A wider interval from a tiny group honestly says 'not sure'
small = df[df["Sub-Category"]=="Copiers"]["Profit"]
print(len(small))   # ~68 -> wider CI than Tables
```

cards.prompt: A 95% CI is a range that likely contains the true value — not a guarantee it does.
cards.whenRight: Right — it quantifies uncertainty, it isn't a promise.
cards.whenWrong: Close — it's a likely range, not a certainty.

cards.prompt: If a difference's 95% CI is [-2%, +9%], the difference is definitely positive.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it crosses zero, so 'no difference' is still plausible.
cards.whenWrong: Not definite — a CI spanning zero is inconclusive.

cards.prompt: A bigger sample makes the confidence interval narrower.
cards.whenRight: Right — more data shrinks the standard error.
cards.whenWrong: It does — larger n tightens the interval.

days.title: Correlation
days.summary: Concept, then df.corr() printed. Put a number on a relationship instead of eyeballing.

items.title: Correlation
items.body:
## What it is
**Correlation (r)** measures how strongly two numeric variables move together, on a fixed scale from **-1 to +1**: +1 a perfect upward line, -1 a perfect downward line, 0 no linear relationship. The **sign** is the direction; the **magnitude** is the strength.

## Why it matters
In Week 3 you *eyeballed* discount vs profit on a scatter. Correlation replaces "they look related" with "r = -0.22, a weak-to-moderate negative relationship" — a single, comparable, defensible number. You can compute it across many pairs at once to see which relationships are worth investigating, turning a wall of columns into a ranked shortlist.

## How to read |r|
Roughly: |r| above ~0.7 is strong, ~0.3-0.7 moderate, below ~0.3 weak. But always pair r with a scatter — r only captures *linear* relationships, so a strong curved relationship can show a near-zero r. The number and the picture together tell the truth; either alone can fool you.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## One pair, then a matrix
```python
print(df["Discount"].corr(df["Profit"]))
```
```
-0.219
```
A **negative** r: as discount rises, profit tends to fall — backing the Week 3 scatter — but only *weakly* linearly, which is itself a clue (the real effect is concentrated at high discounts, not a smooth line).
```python
print(df[["Discount","Profit","Sales","Quantity"]].corr().round(2))
```
```
          Discount  Profit  Sales  Quantity
Discount      1.00   -0.22  -0.03      0.01
Profit       -0.22    1.00   0.48      0.07
Sales        -0.03    0.48   1.00      0.20
Quantity      0.01    0.07   0.20      1.00
```
Read the matrix: Profit's strongest partner is **Sales (0.48)** — bigger orders, bigger profit — while Discount's link is weak-negative. Each cell is the r for that pair; the diagonal is 1.0 (everything correlates perfectly with itself).

cards.prompt: Correlation r runs from -1 to +1, and a value near 0 means little LINEAR relationship.
cards.whenRight: Right — sign is direction, magnitude is strength; ~0 means weak/none.
cards.whenWrong: It does — r is bounded -1..+1; near 0 means almost no linear link.

cards.prompt: A near-zero r guarantees the two variables have no relationship at all.
cards.whenRight: Correct — r only sees LINEAR links; a strong curve can give r near 0. Always plot too.
cards.whenWrong: Not guaranteed — r misses curved relationships; pair it with a scatter.
cards.sim: U-shaped relationship -> r near 0 but clearly related

cards.prompt: A high correlation proves one variable causes the other.
cards.whenRight: Correct — correlation is association only; causation needs more (next lesson).
cards.whenWrong: Careful — high r is association, not proof of cause.

days.title: Correlation is not causation
days.summary: Concept, video, then a confounder worked through. Always ask 'what else explains this?'

items.title: Correlation is not causation
items.body:
## What it is
Two variables moving together doesn't mean one **causes** the other. Very often a hidden third variable — a **confounder** — drives both, manufacturing a correlation between things that have no direct link.

## Why it matters
Your Week 3 finding ("high discounts -> losses") is *correlational*. Two stories fit the same data: (a) discounts directly cause losses, or (b) clearance items that were *already* low-margin happen to get the deepest discounts — so the low margin causes both the discount *and* the loss. Same correlation, completely different action: (a) says "cap discounts"; (b) says "stop stocking those items". Asking "what else could explain this?" is the single habit that separates an analyst from a chart-generator.

## The classic to remember
Ice-cream sales correlate with shark attacks. Neither causes the other; the confounder is **summer** (hot weather drives both). Whenever you see a striking correlation, hunt for the summer.

items.title: Correlation vs causation — simple examples
items.why: Why patterns can mislead. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Test for a confounder, don't just assert the cause
Suspicion: maybe deep discounts land on already-unprofitable sub-categories. Check whether discount depth itself differs by sub-category:
```python
print(df.groupby("Sub-Category")["Discount"].mean().sort_values(ascending=False).head(5))
```
```
Sub-Category
Binders     0.372
Machines    0.306
Tables      0.261
Bookcases   0.211
Appliances  0.166
```
The loss-leaders (Binders, Machines, Tables) also carry the **deepest average discounts** — so discount and "troubled sub-category" are tangled together. That doesn't kill your finding, but it means the honest claim is "discounts are *associated* with losses" until you isolate the effect (e.g. compare profit at the same discount level *within* one sub-category). Stating it as "discounts *cause* losses" would be overreach — and a sharp stakeholder would catch it.

cards.prompt: Correlation between two variables alone proves one causes the other.
cards.whenRight: Correct — association is not causation; a confounder can drive both.
cards.whenWrong: It doesn't — correlation never proves cause on its own.

cards.prompt: A confounder is a hidden variable that influences both correlated variables.
cards.whenRight: Right — it creates the correlation without either causing the other.
cards.whenWrong: It is — a confounder drives both, faking a direct link.
cards.sim: summer -> ice cream AND beach crowds -> attacks

days.title: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)
days.summary: Concept, then a t-test printed. A p-value separates signal from noise.

items.title: Is the difference real? (hypothesis testing)
items.body:
## What it is
"Furniture margin < Technology margin" — real difference, or just random wobble in this sample? A **hypothesis test** (here a t-test) returns a **p-value**: the probability of seeing a gap *this big* if there were truly *no* difference between the groups.

## Why it matters
Without it, you over-read every wiggle. A small p-value (commonly < 0.05) means "this gap would be rare if nothing were going on" — so it's likely real and worth acting on. A large p-value means you simply don't have enough evidence yet. This is the tool that stops you from building a recommendation on a difference that's actually noise — exactly the credibility a stakeholder is paying for.

## The one misreading to avoid
A big p-value does **not** prove "no difference" — it proves "insufficient evidence to claim one". Absence of proof isn't proof of absence. And a tiny p-value on a tiny, meaningless difference is statistically significant but practically irrelevant — always check the *size* of the effect too, not just the p-value.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## t-test: Furniture vs Technology profit
```python
from scipy import stats
furn = df.loc[df["Category"]=="Furniture",  "Profit"]
tech = df.loc[df["Category"]=="Technology", "Profit"]

t, p = stats.ttest_ind(furn, tech, equal_var=False)
print(f"Furniture mean={furn.mean():.1f}, Technology mean={tech.mean():.1f}")
print(f"t={t:.2f}, p={p:.4f}")
```
Output (illustrative):
```
Furniture mean=8.7, Technology mean=78.8
t=-7.31, p=0.0000
```
Read it: Technology orders are far more profitable on average, and **p < 0.0001** says a gap that large would essentially never happen by chance — so the difference is real, not noise. Now you can write "Technology is significantly more profitable than Furniture (p<0.001)" and defend it. Had p been 0.4, the honest statement would be "no significant difference detected".

cards.prompt: A small p-value (e.g. < 0.05) suggests the observed difference is unlikely to be just noise.
cards.whenRight: Right — low p = the gap would be rare if there were truly no difference.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a small p-value is evidence the difference is real.
cards.sim: p=0.0000 -> difference is real, not chance

cards.prompt: A p-value above 0.05 proves there is no difference between the groups.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it means insufficient evidence, not proof of 'no difference'.
cards.whenWrong: Not proof — high p means you can't conclude a difference, not that none exists.

days.title: Simpson's paradox
days.summary: Concept, video, then the reversal shown in code. Always check the subgroups.

items.title: Simpson's paradox
items.body:
## What it is
**Simpson's paradox**: a trend that appears in aggregated data can **disappear or reverse** when you split into subgroups (and vice versa). The whole tells one story; the parts tell the opposite.

## Why it matters
It's not a curiosity — it's a trap you can fall into every week. "Discounts barely dent profit on average" can be flatly wrong once you split by category, exactly as you saw in Week 3 Day 4: the blended average looked survivable while Furniture was haemorrhaging money and Technology shrugged it off. The aggregate *lied*; the subgroups told the truth. This is the deep reason you always break down before you conclude — and why an aggregate number should make you ask "is this hiding opposite subgroups?"

## How to defend against it
Whenever you report an aggregate, split it by the most relevant dimension (category, region, segment) and check the trend still holds. If a subgroup reverses it, the subgroup is usually the real story.

items.title: Simpson's paradox explained in one minute
items.why: The reversal in 60 seconds. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## The aggregate vs the subgroups
```python
# Aggregate: average profit by discount band (looks merely 'soft')
print(df.groupby("disc_band")["Profit"].mean().round(1))
```
```
disc_band
0-10%      66.9
20-30%    -46.7
50%+     -216.8
```
```python
# Split by category: the picture fractures
print(df.pivot_table(index="disc_band", columns="Category",
                     values="Profit", aggfunc="mean").round(1))
```
```
Category   Furniture  Office Supplies  Technology
disc_band
0-10%          41.2             55.0       128.4
30-40%        -82.9             -9.3        41.0
50%+         -210.7           -118.0       -33.5
```
At the 30-40% band the *aggregate* is negative, but **Technology is still +41** while **Furniture is -83**. A blanket "discounts hurt" both overstates the damage to Technology and understates it for Furniture. The subgroup view is the actionable truth; the aggregate alone would have mislead the recommendation.

cards.prompt: A trend in aggregated data can reverse when you split into subgroups.
cards.whenRight: Right — that reversal is Simpson's paradox.
cards.whenWrong: It can — combining groups can flip or hide the within-group trend.

cards.prompt: Routinely checking subgroups protects you from Simpson's paradox.
cards.whenRight: Right — breaking down by the relevant dimension is the standard guard.
cards.whenWrong: It does — subgroup checks catch a misleading aggregate.

days.title: Ship: stats-aware

items.title: Ship: stats-aware
items.body:
## What it is
Re-read your Superstore memo and upgrade each claim from a **pattern** to a **finding** — pair it with a number, a confidence interval, a significance test, or a subgroup check.

## Why it matters
"Furniture is less profitable" is a hunch anyone could voice. "Furniture profit averages -$56/order (95% CI [-76, -35]; t-test vs Technology p<0.001), and the gap widens past 20% discount" is a finding a CFO can act on — because every part of it is defended against the question "are you sure, or is that noise?". That ability to *quantify your own confidence* is the entire difference between an analyst people trust and one they double-check.

cards.prompt: A finding is a pattern PLUS evidence that it's real and not just noise.
cards.whenRight: Right — pattern + (number/CI/significance/subgroup) = finding.
cards.whenWrong: It is — the evidence is what turns a pattern into a defensible finding.

mastery_questions: Compute a 95% confidence interval for the mean Profit Margin by Category. In Excel: =CONFIDENCE.T(0.05, STDEV(profit_margins), COUNT(profit_margins)) gives the margin of error; the CI is mean ± that value. Paste the CI for each Category. Write one sentence about whether the CIs for Technology and Furniture overlap -- if they do, the difference in sample means may not be statistically reliable.

Run a two-sample t-test comparing order profit between VIP customers and Low Value customers. In Excel: =T.TEST(vip_profits, low_profits, 2, 3) (two-tailed, two-sample unequal variance). Paste the p-value. Is p < 0.05? Write one sentence interpreting the result in plain English: not "p < 0.05 so it is significant" but "there is less than a 5% probability of observing a difference this large if VIPs and Low Value customers had identical average order profits."

Compute the Pearson correlation between Discount and Profit, and its p-value, using Excel's =CORREL() and =PEARSON(). For the p-value: =T.DIST.2T(r*SQRT(n-2)/SQRT(1-r^2), n-2) where r is the correlation and n is the count. Paste r and p. Is the correlation statistically significant? Write one sentence about practical versus statistical significance -- a significant correlation of -0.12 means discounts reliably decrease profit, but the effect explains only 1.4% of the variance.

Check for Simpson's paradox in the Discount-Margin relationship. Overall, higher discounts correlate with lower margins. Now compute the correlation separately for each Category. Is the direction consistent across all three? Write the three category-specific correlations. If one category has a positive correlation (more discount = better margin, perhaps because high-discount orders in that category are large bulk orders with better per-unit economics), that is Simpson's paradox and it changes the policy recommendation.

Update the analyst memo to add statistical framing to every key number. Replace "Furniture margins are lower" with "Furniture margins are 7.2 pp lower (95% CI: 5.8 to 8.6 pp)." Replace "VIP customers order more often" with "VIP customers place 14.2 orders per year versus 2.1 for Low Value customers (t=8.4, p<0.001)." Paste three revised sentences. A memo that says "significantly lower" without a number is a memo that has borrowed statistical authority it has not earned.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to write the p-value formula for a Pearson correlation in Excel -- it is derived from the t-distribution and is not built in as a single function. Paste the formula, verify it produces a plausible p-value (should be very small for a correlation of -0.4 with 5000 observations), and document it in queries.sql as a comment. Do NOT ask Claude whether a finding is statistically significant. That determination requires the actual data and the actual test result, not a language model's assessment.
weeks.pre_flight: For each of the three main findings from weeks 1-3, write down your confidence in the finding on a scale of 1-5 before running any statistical tests. After running the tests, update the scores. The gap between your prior confidence and the statistical evidence is calibration -- the analysts who are well-calibrated are the ones who can be trusted to say "I am not sure" when they are not sure.
common_mistakes: Reporting p < 0.05 without reporting the effect size. A tiny effect can be statistically significant with enough data. A large effect can be statistically insignificant with too little data. Always report both: the correlation and the p-value, or the mean difference and the confidence interval.

Interpreting a confidence interval as "the true value is definitely in this range." A 95% CI means that if you ran this analysis 100 times with different random samples, 95 of the resulting CIs would contain the true value. The one CI you computed may be one of the 5 that does not.

Reporting "correlation = 0.35 (p < 0.05)" without noting that r² = 0.12 -- discounts explain only 12% of the variance in profit. The percentage of variance explained is the most intuitive measure of practical importance for a correlation.

Not checking assumptions before running a t-test. The two-sample t-test assumes approximately normal distributions in each group. For profit data with extreme values (the $400K fare equivalent in retail is a very large bulk order), the normality assumption is violated. Note this as a limitation if sample sizes are small.

Using the same data to discover a finding and to test it. If you found the Furniture-margin pattern by exploring the data, testing it on the same data produces an inflated p-value. Ideally, you would reserve a holdout portion of the data for confirmatory testing. Acknowledging this limitation in the memo is the honest thing to do.
weeks.debug_help: Excel's T.TEST function arguments are easy to confuse: the third argument is tails (1 = one-tailed, 2 = two-tailed) and the fourth is type (1 = paired, 2 = two-sample equal variance, 3 = two-sample unequal variance). For comparing VIP and Low Value profits, use type=3 (Welch's t-test) because the variances are likely different. Using type=2 when variances differ produces an inflated p-value. Check: if the standard deviations of the two groups differ by more than a factor of 2, use type=3.
stretch: Run a one-way ANOVA to test whether mean Profit Margin differs significantly across the four Regions. Excel's Data Analysis ToolPak has a built-in ANOVA function. Report the F-statistic and p-value. If significant, run Tukey post-hoc tests to identify which specific pairs of regions differ significantly.

Compute the Spearman rank correlation between Discount and Profit as a robustness check on the Pearson correlation. If Spearman and Pearson give very different results, the outliers in the data are driving the Pearson correlation and the Spearman result is more reliable.

Read "Statistics Done Wrong" by Alex Reinhart (free online, 3 hours). Chapter 4 on p-values and Chapter 5 on data snooping are the two most relevant to business analysis. The book makes the case that most published statistics are overstated, and the reasons are exactly the errors listed in common mistakes above.

weeks.title: AI-Augmented analyst + Prompt Engineering
weeks.context:
Every analyst you will compete with for jobs has access to Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot. The ones who use AI well will be more productive. The ones who use it carelessly will produce confident-sounding wrong answers that are embarrassing to defend. This week you learn to be the first kind.

The discipline is verification. AI is genuinely excellent at generating SQL, writing formula syntax, drafting memo templates, and suggesting chart types. It is unreliable at interpreting data it cannot see, making business judgements that require domain knowledge, and catching subtle errors in analysis. Knowing which tasks to outsource and which to keep is the skill -- and it is a skill you practise by deliberately testing AI outputs against your own analysis this week.

The specific workflows you will build: a schema-aware SQL prompt (you paste the CREATE TABLE statement plus a question, AI generates the query, you run it and verify the output), a memo draft-and-critique loop (you paste your findings in bullet points, AI drafts a memo, you edit for accuracy and voice), and a formula generation prompt (you describe the logic in plain English, AI generates the Excel formula, you verify with spot checks).

The prompts.md file is the deliverable. Not the analysis -- you have already done the analysis. The deliverable is a documented set of prompts that work reliably for your analytical workflow, with notes on what each prompt is good for and where it fails. This is your personal AI cheatsheet, and it compounds over time: the better you get at prompting for analysis tasks, the more you can outsource the mechanical parts and spend your time on the parts that require actual thinking.

By Sunday: prompts.md committed to the Superstore repo with at least five working prompts, each with a "use for / not for" annotation, and one documented example where AI produced a wrong answer and you caught it.

days.title: AI accelerates, you stay accountable
days.summary: The one rule: AI drafts, you verify. Concept, then the right vs wrong workflow.

items.title: AI accelerates, you stay accountable
items.body:
## What it is
Every analyst you'll compete with has Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot. The edge isn't *using* AI — it's using it **well**: let it draft, then **you verify against the data**, and you remain accountable for every number you ship.

## Why it matters
AI is fluent, and fluency reads as confidence — but fluency is not accuracy. It will write a plausible SQL query against columns that don't exist, or invent a statistic, in the same self-assured tone it uses when it's right. Ship that unchecked and you'll be humiliated defending a wrong number in a meeting. Used with verification, the same tool makes you 2-3x faster with *no* loss of trust. The whole skill this week is building the verify-reflex so AI's speed never becomes AI's risk.

## The contract
AI supplies *drafts and syntax*; you supply *the data, the judgement, and the final sign-off*. It never gets to be the source of a number — only a faster way to produce something you then check.

items.title: See it in practice (with output)
items.body:
## Same tool, two outcomes
```text
BAD (no verification):
  You: "What % of Superstore losses come from discounts?"
  AI:  "Approximately 30% of losses stem from excessive discounting."
  -> a confident number with NO basis. You can't defend it. Don't ship it.

GOOD (AI drafts, you verify):
  You: "Write pandas to sum Profit for orders with Discount > 0.3."
  AI:  df.loc[df["Discount"] > 0.3, "Profit"].sum()
  You RUN it:
```
```python
print(df.loc[df["Discount"] > 0.3, "Profit"].sum())
```
```
-94157.3
```
```text
  -> now you have a REAL number you computed and can explain. That's the workflow.
```
The difference isn't the tool — it's that you executed and checked. AI proposed; you verified.

cards.prompt: AI can produce confident-sounding but wrong answers, so you must verify against the data.
cards.whenRight: Right — fluency is not accuracy; verification is non-negotiable.
cards.whenWrong: It can — AI sounds sure even when wrong, so always verify.

cards.prompt: If the AI's answer sounds detailed and confident, you can trust it without checking.
cards.whenRight: Correct — confidence is not evidence; run it and check against the data.
cards.whenWrong: No — tone is not proof; verify against the actual data every time.

items.body:
[WRITE] Two places AI could genuinely speed up your Superstore workflow.
[WRITE] Two places AI is risky (a confident-but-wrong answer would bite you), and exactly how you'd verify each.

days.title: Schema-aware prompts for SQL
days.summary: Concept, then a weak vs strong prompt and the verified result.

items.title: Schema-aware prompts for SQL
items.body:
## What it is
AI writes SQL fast — but only well if you hand it the **table schema** (columns + types) and a **precise question**. A vague prompt yields a confident, plausible, *wrong* query (joining columns that don't exist, mislabelling aggregates).

## Why it matters
You already wrote these exact queries by hand in Week 5, which makes this the perfect, safe place to learn prompting: you can *verify* the AI against an answer you trust. The lesson generalises — on real jobs you'll prompt against schemas you know, paste the result, and check it. Schema-aware prompting is the difference between AI as a force-multiplier and AI as a generator of subtle bugs.

## The pattern
Always give it: the table name, the columns (with types if it matters), and the exact output you want. Then **run** the SQL it returns and compare to a known result before you trust it.

items.title: See it in practice (with output)
items.body:
## Weak vs strong prompt
```text
WEAK:   "write SQL to find my best products"
        -> AI guesses column names; likely wrong.

STRONG: "Table superstore(order_id, sub_category, category, sales, profit,
         discount, order_date, customer_name). Write SQLite returning each
         sub_category's total profit, highest first."
```
AI returns:
```sql
SELECT sub_category, SUM(profit) AS total_profit
FROM superstore GROUP BY sub_category ORDER BY total_profit DESC;
```
Now **verify** — run it and compare to your Week 5 hand-written answer:
```
sub_category  total_profit
Copiers        55617.8
Phones         44515.7
Accessories    41936.6
```
Matches Week 5 exactly -> trust it. If it hadn't matched, the prompt or the query was wrong, and you'd have caught it *because you checked*.

cards.prompt: Giving the AI your exact table schema makes its SQL far more likely to be correct.
cards.whenRight: Right — column names + types remove the guessing that causes wrong queries.
cards.whenWrong: It does — schema-aware prompts cut wrong-column errors sharply.

cards.prompt: AI-generated SQL can be trusted and shipped without running it.
cards.whenRight: Correct — always run it and check against a known answer.
cards.whenWrong: Never ship unrun — execute and verify against trusted data.
cards.sim: AI SQL -> RUN -> compare to Week 5 -> then trust

days.title: AI as a memo drafter
days.summary: Concept, then a prompt that drafts from YOUR numbers — which you then edit.

items.title: AI as a memo drafter
items.body:
## What it is
Hand the AI **your** findings (the real numbers) plus the audience, and it drafts the memo prose in seconds. You then edit for accuracy, voice, and truth.

## Why it matters
Writing is the slow part of analysis; drafting from known points is where AI genuinely shines. But there's a hard rule: it must build *only* from numbers you supply. The instant you let it invent a figure to make a sentence flow, you've planted a landmine — invented numbers are how analysts get fired. So you feed it facts, it returns phrasing, and you delete anything you can't trace back to your own analysis.

## The pattern
Give it: the audience (and their technical level), your bullet findings *with numbers*, and the structure you want (headline -> evidence -> recommendation, word limit). Then edit ruthlessly — for your voice and to strip any claim the data doesn't back.

items.title: See it in practice (with output)
items.body:
## A drafting prompt
```text
PROMPT:
"Audience: a non-technical sales director. Draft a 150-word memo with
 headline / evidence / recommendation from these findings:
 - discounts above ~20% turn the average order unprofitable
 - 24% of orders exceed that
 - Furniture is hit first (negative from 20-30%), Technology resilient
 Recommend a discount cap. Plain language, no jargon."
```
AI returns a clean draft. **Your job now:** read every sentence and (1) confirm each number is one you computed, (2) cut anything invented, (3) make it sound like you.
```text
EDIT LOG (what you should do):
- AI wrote "discounts have devastated margins for years" -> DELETE (no time-series claim in your data)
- AI wrote "~20% cap" -> KEEP (matches your tipping point)
- tighten tone to your voice
```
The draft saved you 20 minutes; the edit kept you honest.

cards.prompt: AI should draft the memo from YOUR numbers — it must not invent figures of its own.
cards.whenRight: Right — you supply the facts, AI supplies the phrasing; verify nothing was fabricated.
cards.whenWrong: Exactly — AI phrases your facts; invented numbers are a firing offence.
cards.sim: you: the numbers | AI: the wording

items.title: Your turn — draft then edit
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Give an AI your real discount + CLV findings; ask for a 150-word director memo (headline/evidence/recommendation).
[WRITE] Edit it. Note two changes you made (a fabricated/overstated claim removed; a voice fix).

days.title: Make AI critique your memo
days.summary: Concept, then a 'skeptical reviewer' prompt that surfaces your blind spots.

items.title: Make AI critique your memo
items.body:
## What it is
Flip the tool from author to adversary: paste your finished memo and ask the AI to **attack it** — find unsupported claims, missing caveats, and alternative explanations a sharp reader would raise.

## Why it matters
You are blind to your own gaps because you know the context the reader doesn't. An adversarial pass *before* your boss sees it catches the embarrassing holes while they're still cheap to fix — the correlation-stated-as-causation, the claim with no number, the recommendation with no cost. It's like having a skeptical senior analyst on call, for free, who never gets tired or political. You stay in control: you decide which critiques are fair and act on those.

## The pattern
Cast the AI in a demanding role ("skeptical data director"), ask for a *specific* number of weaknesses and the questions you'd get grilled on. Specific roles and counts produce sharper critique than "what do you think?".

items.title: See it in practice (with output)
items.body:
## A critique prompt
```text
PROMPT:
"You are a skeptical data director. Find the 3 weakest claims in this memo
 and the exact questions I'd be grilled on in the meeting. Be specific."
[paste your memo]
```
AI returns, for example:
```text
1. "Discounts CAUSE losses" — you've shown correlation, not causation.
   Grill: "How do you rule out that low-margin items just get discounted more?"
   -> Fix: soften to "associated with", or add the within-category check.
2. The recommendation has no cost/risk. Grill: "What revenue do we lose by capping?"
   -> Fix: acknowledge the revenue trade-off.
3. "24% of orders" — over what period? Grill: "Is that 2017 or all 4 years?"
   -> Fix: state the timeframe.
```
You now fix the two fair ones before anyone else reads it. Cheap insurance.

cards.prompt: Asking AI to critique your own work surfaces gaps and weak claims you're blind to.
cards.whenRight: Right — an adversarial pass is one of AI's highest-value uses.
cards.whenWrong: It does — AI as a skeptic catches holes before your audience does.
cards.sim: AI: 'claim 1 is correlation, not causation -> soften'

items.title: Your turn — get grilled (safely)
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Ask an AI to act as a skeptical director and list the 3 weakest claims in your memo + the questions you'd be asked.
[WRITE] Address at least two (add a caveat, soften a claim, or add evidence).

days.title: AI for slide content
days.summary: Concept, then a prompt that turns your memo into lean slides + speaker notes.

items.title: AI for slide content
items.body:
## What it is
Give the AI your memo and ask for **slide bullets and speaker notes**. It compresses prose into talking points so you can *present*, not read aloud.

## Why it matters
Executives get a deck, not a notebook, and the hardest part of a deck is brutal compression — saying the finding in five words on the slide and two sentences out loud. AI is fast at that first pass; your job is to cut further, because the failure mode of AI slides is *too many* words. A lean slide with strong speaker notes is how a finding actually lands in the room, and AI gets you to a draft deck in a minute instead of an hour.

## The pattern
Ask for a fixed, small structure: N slides, each with a short title, ≤3 brief bullets, and 2 sentences of speaker notes. Then trim every bullet that isn't essential — slides are signposts, the notes carry the detail.

items.title: See it in practice (with output)
items.body:
## A deck prompt
```text
PROMPT:
"From this memo, draft 3 slides. For each: a <=5-word title, up to 3 bullets
 (<=8 words each), and 2 sentences of speaker notes I can say aloud."
[paste memo]
```
AI returns, e.g.:
```text
Slide 1 — "Discounts are eroding profit"
  - Avg order unprofitable above ~20% discount
  - 24% of orders exceed that line
  - Furniture hit first and hardest
  Notes: "A quarter of our orders are discounted into the red. Furniture
          turns unprofitable at just 20% off."
```
Now **trim**: if a bullet isn't essential to the recommendation, delete it. The deck is signposts; your voice (and the notes) carry the rest.

cards.prompt: AI can turn your memo into per-slide bullets and speaker notes you then refine.
cards.whenRight: Right — it compresses prose to talking points; you keep it lean.
cards.whenWrong: It can — AI drafts slide content fast; your job is to trim it.

items.title: Your turn — deck-ify it
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Ask AI to convert your memo into 3 slides (short title + <=3 bullets + 2 sentences of notes each).
[WRITE] Trim the result: delete any bullet not essential to the recommendation.

days.title: AI for tricky formulas and code
days.summary: Concept, then a prompt for a fiddly formula — verified on a known case.

items.title: AI for tricky formulas and code
items.body:
## What it is
Stuck on a gnarly Excel formula or a pandas one-liner? Describe what you want in plain English; the AI writes it. Then **test it on a case where you already know the answer**.

## Why it matters
This removes the syntax bottleneck — the 20 minutes lost to "how do I do a year-over-year % in pandas again?" — and lets you stay in the flow of the analysis. But an unverified formula silently produces a wrong column that poisons everything downstream, and you won't see the error because the code *ran*. The verify-on-a-known-case habit is the cheap insurance that keeps AI's speed from quietly corrupting your results.

## The pattern
Describe the calculation and the columns; get the formula; apply it; then hand-check one row you can compute yourself. If that row matches, trust it across the data. If it doesn't, you caught a bug for the price of one mental subtraction.

items.title: See it in practice (with output)
items.body:
## Prompt, apply, verify
```text
PROMPT: "pandas: add a year-over-year % growth column to yearly_sales
         (columns: year, revenue), sorted by year."
```
AI returns:
```python
yearly = yearly.sort_values("year")
yearly["yoy_pct"] = yearly["revenue"].pct_change() * 100
print(yearly)
```
```
   year   revenue  yoy_pct
0  2014  484247.5      NaN
1  2015  470532.5    -2.83
2  2016  609205.6    29.47
3  2017  733215.3    20.36
```
**Verify one row by hand:** 2016 vs 2015 = (609205.6 - 470532.5) / 470532.5 = +29.47%. Matches. Now you trust the column. (2014 is NaN because there's no prior year — correct, not a bug.)

cards.prompt: You should always test an AI-generated formula on a case where you already know the answer.
cards.whenRight: Right — a known-answer check is the cheapest guard against a silently-wrong formula.
cards.whenWrong: Always — verify on a known case before trusting an AI formula across the data.
cards.sim: AI formula -> check 1 known row -> then apply

items.title: Your turn — generate and verify
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Ask AI for a formula/snippet you find fiddly (YoY % growth, a running total, a rank).
[CODE] Apply it, then hand-verify the result on one row you can compute yourself.

days.title: Ship: AI-aware (prompts.md)
days.summary: Save your best prompts as reusable assets and tag AI-aware.

items.title: Ship: AI-aware (prompts.md)
items.body:
## What it is
Collect the prompts that actually worked this week into a `prompts.md` file — your reusable toolkit — and tag the project `AI-aware`.

## Why it matters
Good prompts are *assets*, not one-offs. The schema-aware SQL prompt and the skeptical-reviewer prompt will earn their keep on every future project; saving them means you stop reinventing them. Just as important, documenting that you *verify* AI output signals deliberate, professional AI use — which is now something employers actively screen for. "I use AI and check it" is a hireable sentence; "I pasted whatever ChatGPT said" is not.

cards.prompt: Saving your effective prompts in a file turns them into reusable assets for future projects.
cards.whenRight: Right — a prompt library compounds; you stop reinventing them.
cards.whenWrong: It does — saved prompts are reusable tools, not one-offs.
cards.sim: prompts.md -> reuse schema + critique prompts everywhere
