questions: When does AI confidently produce wrong SQL?
What's the 'verify before trust' rule for an analyst?
Will AI replace junior analysts? When?
mastery_questions: Write a schema-aware SQL prompt: paste your Superstore table schema (the column names and types) followed by the question "write a query that shows monthly revenue and profit for 2017, with year-over-year growth versus 2016." Paste the AI-generated query. Run it. Does it produce the correct numbers? If not, paste the error or the discrepancy. Write one sentence about what the AI got wrong and what you had to fix.

Write a memo draft prompt: paste your three main Superstore findings as bullet points with specific numbers. Ask the AI to "draft a one-page analyst memo to the Superstore CEO with these findings, using a headline-first structure, no jargon, and a specific recommendation for each finding." Paste the draft. Now compare it to your own week-1 memo. Which sentences would you keep? Which would you rewrite? Make at least five edits and paste the edited version.

Write a formula generation prompt: "In Google Sheets, write a formula that returns 'VIP' if the value in column B is in the top 10% of all values in column B:B, 'High' if it is in the 10-30th percentile, 'Medium' if 30-70th, and 'Low' otherwise." Paste the AI formula. Test it on 5 rows against the segment logic you built in week 4. Does it match? If not, identify the error.

Find one case where AI produces a wrong answer. Strategies: ask it to calculate the year-over-year growth rate using a prompt that does not include the actual numbers, then paste the result and compare to your known-correct answer. Or ask it to "interpret what the Superstore Furniture margin trend means" without pasting the actual data -- note where it invents plausible-sounding but unverifiable claims. Paste the wrong output and your correction.

Write the prompts.md file. Five prompts minimum. For each: the prompt text, what it is good for (specific use cases), what it is not good for (failure modes you found), and one example output with a verification note. Paste the file. The "not good for" section is the most valuable part -- it is the information that prevents the dangerous use of AI (confident wrong answers without verification).
weeks.ai_assist: This week the entire content is about AI assistance, so the ai_assist field applies differently: use this week's work as the opportunity to calibrate your trust. For any analytical result from weeks 1-5, ask Claude to produce it using only a description of the question (no pasting your answer). Compare the result to your known-correct answer. The tasks where Claude matches your answer are good AI candidates. The tasks where it diverges are tasks to keep doing yourself.
weeks.pre_flight: Choose three analysis tasks from weeks 1-5 that you found tedious. Write them down. These are your first three AI outsourcing candidates. Then write down one task from those weeks where you are certain the answer is correct and the reasoning is clear. That task is your verification anchor -- you will use it to check whether AI produces the correct analysis.
common_mistakes: Accepting AI-generated SQL without running it. SQL that looks correct can be subtly wrong -- wrong join condition, wrong date function, wrong aggregation level. Always run the query and check the output against a known-correct number before using it in a deliverable.

Using AI to interpret data the AI cannot see. "What does a 12% profit margin tell us about Superstore?" asked without the actual data produces a plausible-sounding generic answer. The interpretation requires the actual numbers in context, which the AI does not have.

Not documenting prompts that work. A prompt that generates a correct SUMIFS formula for a complex condition is worth writing down. Prompts are reusable; rediscovering an effective prompt every time is waste.

Over-editing the AI memo draft until it sounds like you wrote it from scratch. The value of the AI draft is the structure and the first pass. Over-editing it costs more time than writing it yourself. The right ratio: AI for the first 60%, you for the last 40%.

Not testing the formula generation output on edge cases. AI-generated formulas often handle the typical case correctly and fail on edge cases (empty cells, negative values, ties). Always test with at least one edge case from each direction.
weeks.debug_help: When AI generates a SQL query that fails, paste the exact error message back to AI along with the query: "This query produced the following error: [error]. Fix it." AI is very good at debugging its own output given the error message. But verify the fix -- sometimes the fix introduces a new error. If you are on a third round of fixes, step back and write the query yourself using the week-5 patterns as a template. The AI is not always the faster path.
stretch: Build a two-turn prompt loop for memo critique: first turn generates the draft, second turn critiques it ("identify any claims in this memo that are not supported by the numbers provided"). The second turn often catches overstatements that the first turn confidently wrote.

Test whether AI can identify Simpson's paradox from a description. Describe a scenario where the overall correlation reverses within subgroups, without calling it Simpson's paradox. Ask AI to diagnose the pattern. Note whether it correctly identifies the reversal and uses the correct terminology.

Write a "verification checklist" prompt: "Given this analyst memo, list five specific claims that should be verified against the underlying data." Use it on a memo you wrote. Does it surface the claims you would have flagged yourself? Add the useful items to prompts.md.

weeks.title: Superstore v0.5: Executive deck
weeks.context:
You have five weeks of Superstore analysis. Now you compress it into five slides that a CEO can read in 10 minutes and act on. That compression is harder than the analysis.

The instinct when building an executive deck is to show everything you found, arranged roughly in the order you found it. This instinct produces a 20-slide deck where the recommendation is on slide 19. By slide 15, the CEO has moved on to email. An executive deck starts with the answer, then uses the subsequent slides as evidence. This is the Pyramid Principle: conclusion first, then the three or four arguments that support it, then the data that supports each argument.

Each slide has one headline. Not a title that says what the slide is about ("Profitability Analysis"), but a headline that states the finding ("Furniture margins are 7.2 pp below Technology, driven by discounts above 20%"). The difference matters because the title deck requires the reader to derive the insight from the chart; the headline deck gives them the insight and uses the chart as proof. Senior audiences -- the kind who review 15 decks a week -- always prefer the headline deck.

The five slides are: (1) the overall situation and recommendation, (2) the profitability finding, (3) the discount finding, (4) the customer segmentation finding, (5) the three specific recommended actions with estimated impact. Slide 5 is the most important slide in the deck. A deck that ends on "here are the findings" is an analysis report dressed as a deck. A deck that ends on "here are three specific actions and here is what they will change" is a business case.

By Sunday: a five-slide deck in Google Slides or PowerPoint, exported as PDF and committed to the repo, and a rehearsed two-minute version you can deliver from memory.

days.title: The deck is an argument, not a dump
days.summary: Compress five weeks into five slides a CEO acts on in ten minutes. Concept, video, worked structure.

items.title: The deck is an argument, not a dump
items.body:
## What it is
An executive deck is not your notebook with borders. It is a **10-minute argument** aimed at a busy decision-maker: lead with the answer, make one point per slide, and end on an action they can approve.

## Why it matters
The instinct after five weeks of work is to *show the work* — every chart, every caveat. That instinct buries the point and exhausts the reader. Executives reward **clarity, not completeness**: they will act on five slides they understood and ignore twenty they didn't. Compression is genuinely harder than the analysis — it forces you to decide what actually matters — which is exactly why it's the skill that separates analysts who influence decisions from those who just produce reports nobody reads.

## The shape of a winning deck
Five slides: (1) headline + recommendation, (2-4) one finding each with its single best chart, (5) the recommendation with expected impact and next step. Everything that doesn't serve the decision gets cut, not shrunk. The deck is a spine; your voice carries the rest.

items.title: Tips for presenting data at work
items.why: Practical data-presentation habits before you build. Optional.

items.title: See it worked (good vs bad)
items.body:
## The same week, two decks
```text
BAD deck (a data dump):
  20 slides titled "Superstore Analysis"
  - every chart you made, in the order you made it
  - methodology before findings
  - reader is lost by slide 6, decision not made

GOOD deck (an argument):
  Slide 1  HEADLINE: "Cap discounts at 30% to recover ~$62k profit/yr"
  Slide 2  FINDING: "Profit turns negative above 30% discount"  [band chart]
  Slide 3  FINDING: "Furniture is hit first, at 20%"           [pivot chart]
  Slide 4  FINDING: "24% of orders already exceed the cap"     [one number]
  Slide 5  RECOMMENDATION: cap + expected impact + pilot next step
```
Read the good one: a stranger gets the entire decision from the five titles alone. That's the test — if your slide *titles*, read top to bottom, tell the story, the deck works.

cards.prompt: An executive deck should compress to the few slides that drive a decision, not show all your work.
cards.whenRight: Right — it's an argument for a decision, not an archive of effort.
cards.whenWrong: It should — compression to the decision-relevant few is the whole skill.

cards.prompt: More slides means more thorough, which means a better executive deck.
cards.whenRight: Correct — more slides usually buries the point; cut to the decision.
cards.whenWrong: Backwards — extra slides hide the message; executives want the essence.

items.title: Your turn — define the argument
items.body:
[WRITE] Name your audience (CEO / sales director) and the one thing they care about.
[WRITE] State the single decision this deck must drive, and draft your five slide *titles* so that, read alone, they tell the whole story.

days.title: Slide 1 — the headline (BLUF)
days.summary: Bottom line up front: state the conclusion and recommendation in one sentence. Concept + worked example.

items.title: Slide 1 — the headline (BLUF)
items.body:
## What it is
**BLUF — Bottom Line Up Front.** Slide 1 states your single most important conclusion *and* the recommended action, in one sentence, *before* any evidence.

## Why it matters
Assume the reader sees only slide 1 — because often they will, or they'll decide in the first 20 seconds whether to keep paying attention. If the conclusion is buried on slide 12, you've lost. Leading with the answer also disciplines *you*: if you can't state the recommendation in one sentence with a number, you don't yet know what you're recommending. The headline is both the reader's shortcut and your own clarity test.

## What makes a strong headline
It's a *claim with a number and an implied action*, not a topic label. "Superstore Discount Analysis" is a filing-cabinet label. "Capping discounts at 30% would recover ~$62k in annual profit" tells the reader the stakes, the action, and the size — in nine words.

items.title: See it worked (weak vs strong)
items.body:
## Rewrite the title until it's a decision
```text
WEAK (topics — make the reader dig):
  "Superstore Discount Analysis"
  "Q2 Findings"
  "Profitability Review"

STRONG (claim + number + implied action):
  "Capping discounts at 30% would recover ~$62k in annual profit."
  "A quarter of our orders are discounted into a loss."
  "Furniture loses money at half the discount Technology can absorb."
```
Each strong version passes the test: a reader who sees nothing else still knows what you found and what you want them to do. Put your single best one on slide 1, sized with a real number from your analysis.

cards.prompt: The title slide should state the conclusion and recommendation, not just name the topic.
cards.whenRight: Right — BLUF: lead with the answer, not the subject line.
cards.whenWrong: It should — a headline states the conclusion; 'Analysis' is just a topic.

items.title: Your turn — write the headline
items.body: [PRODUCE] Write slide 1: a one-sentence headline stating your main recommendation and its expected impact, with a real number from your analysis. Reject any version that's just a topic label.

days.title: Slides 2-4 — one finding per slide
days.summary: Each slide makes exactly one point: claim as the title, one chart, one takeaway. Concept + worked example.

items.title: Slides 2-4 — one finding per slide
items.body:
## What it is
Your three evidence slides each carry **one** finding: the **claim as the slide title** (a full sentence), **one chart** that proves it, and **one line** of takeaway. One idea per slide, full stop.

## Why it matters
A slide with three ideas communicates none — the audience reads ahead, half-listens, and remembers nothing. Forcing one claim per slide does two things: it makes *you* decide what the finding actually is (a sentence, not a chart), and it lets the audience follow your argument one clean step at a time. The title carrying the claim is the trick most analysts miss: a title like "Discounts" makes the reader work out the point; "Discounts above 30% turn orders unprofitable" hands it to them.

## The discipline
Title = the claim. Body = the *single* best chart that proves it (not three related ones). Footer = one sentence of "so what". If you have a second chart you love, it goes in an appendix, not the slide.

items.title: See it worked (one slide)
items.body:
## Anatomy of a finding slide
```text
TITLE (the claim):   "Discounts above 30% turn the average order unprofitable"
BODY  (one chart):    avg-profit-by-discount-band bar chart
                      (bars green above 0, red below; the cliff after 30% is obvious)
TAKEAWAY (one line):  "61% of orders sit in safe bands; the loss is concentrated past 30%."
```
Contrast with the failure mode:
```text
BAD: title "Discounts"; body = scatter + band chart + category pivot all crammed;
     no takeaway line. Reader sees three things, absorbs zero.
```
One claim, one chart, one takeaway — repeated three times — is the entire middle of your deck.

cards.prompt: Each slide should make exactly one point, stated as a sentence in its title.
cards.whenRight: Right — one claim, one chart, one takeaway per slide.
cards.whenWrong: It should — one point per slide, with the claim in the title.

cards.prompt: To save slides, cram several related charts onto one slide.
cards.whenRight: Correct — multiple charts split attention and kill the single message.
cards.whenWrong: Avoid it — many charts per slide dilute the one point.

items.title: Your turn — three finding slides
items.body: [PRODUCE] Build slides 2-4. Each: a claim-as-title (full sentence), exactly one chart that proves it, and a one-line takeaway. Use your real findings (discounts, CLV, etc.).

days.title: Slide 5 — the recommendation
days.summary: End on the action: what to do, expected impact, next step. Concept + worked example.

items.title: Slide 5 — the recommendation
items.body:
## What it is
The final slide answers the only question the executive truly has: **"so what do we do?"** — a concrete action, its expected impact, and the immediate next step.

## Why it matters
Findings without a recommendation make the audience do *your* job — and they won't; they'll table it. The recommendation is the entire reason the analysis existed, and it's what gets remembered and acted on after everyone leaves the room. A vague "we should consider optimising discounts" wastes the build-up; a specific, quantified, time-bound action ("cap at 30%, ~$62k upside, pilot one region next quarter") is something a leader can say yes to on the spot.

## What it must contain
Three things: the **action** (specific enough to execute), the **expected impact** (a number — the prize), and the **next step** (a small, low-risk move like a pilot). Specific, quantified, actionable — never hedged.

items.title: See it worked (vague vs sharp)
items.body:
## The closing slide, two ways
```text
VAGUE (wastes the whole deck):
  "Recommendations: We should consider reviewing our discounting strategy
   and optimising for profitability going forward."

SHARP (a leader can approve it):
  Recommendation
  - Cap discounts at 30% overall, 20% for Furniture.
  - Expected impact: ~$62k profit recovered annually.
  - Next step: pilot the cap in one region next quarter; measure profit lift.
```
The sharp version names the action, sizes the prize, and de-risks it with a pilot. That's a slide that ends a meeting with a decision instead of a "let's circle back".

cards.prompt: The deck should end on a concrete recommendation with expected impact, not just findings.
cards.whenRight: Right — action + impact + next step is the payoff slide.
cards.whenWrong: It should — close with what to do and what it's worth.

items.title: Your turn — the recommendation slide
items.body: [PRODUCE] Build slide 5: a specific recommendation, its expected impact (a number), and a concrete next step (a pilot or small first move).

days.title: Design pass — make it credible
days.summary: Consistency and decluttering. Concept + a concrete checklist.

items.title: Design pass — make it credible
items.body:
## What it is
A pass purely for **visual consistency** and **decluttering**: identical title styling on every slide, one colour per category used everywhere, aligned elements, labelled axes — and ruthless removal of "chartjunk" (3D effects, gradients, gridlines and borders that carry no information).

## Why it matters
Design is a credibility signal whether you like it or not. If the deck looks sloppy — mismatched fonts, a category that's blue here and orange there, an unlabelled axis — the audience quietly distrusts the *analysis* behind it, even if the numbers are flawless. Clean, consistent design borrows trust for your conclusions; messy design taxes them. It's the cheapest credibility you'll ever buy, and most analysts skip it.

## The standard
Pick one rule per element and apply it everywhere. Same title font and size. Furniture is *always* the same colour. Every axis labelled. Every chart has a takeaway. Nothing on a slide that doesn't earn its place.

items.title: See it worked (the checklist)
items.body:
## Run this checklist over every slide
```text
[ ] Titles: same font, size, position on all slides
[ ] Colour: each category ONE consistent colour across every chart
[ ] Axes: labelled, with units; no mystery numbers
[ ] Clutter: no 3D, no gradients, no decorative gridlines/borders
[ ] Numbers: rounded sensibly (62k, not 61,847.39)
[ ] One takeaway line per chart slide
[ ] Alignment: titles and charts line up slide to slide
```
Before vs after this pass is the difference between "a student made this" and "I trust this person with a decision".

cards.prompt: Visual consistency and removing clutter make a deck more credible, not just prettier.
cards.whenRight: Right — clean design signals rigor; chartjunk signals carelessness.
cards.whenWrong: It does — consistency and less clutter make the analysis read as trustworthy.

items.title: Your turn — design pass
items.body: [PRODUCE] Run the checklist over your deck: unify titles, one colour per category across all charts, label axes, round numbers, and delete every non-informative element.

days.title: Rehearse the 5-minute pitch
days.summary: Delivery sells the analysis. Concept + a self-review rubric.

items.title: Rehearse the 5-minute pitch
items.body:
## What it is
Practise delivering the deck in **5 minutes** — headline, three findings, recommendation — and **record yourself once**, then watch it back.

## Why it matters
The best analysis in the world loses the room if the delivery is shaky, rushed, or hedged. Recording is uncomfortable and exactly why it works: it surfaces the filler words, the slides you can't actually explain, and the moments you go over time — all while it's still cheap to fix, in private, instead of in front of your boss. Five minutes is a deliberate constraint; if you can't make the case in five, you haven't found the core yet.

## What to watch for
Filler ("um", "kind of", "I think maybe") that signals low confidence; any slide you couldn't explain in one breath (it's too complex — simplify it); and overruns (the fix is to *cut content*, never to talk faster).

items.title: See it worked (the rubric)
items.body:
## Watch your recording against this
```text
TIME:    did you finish in <= 5:00? If not, which slide to cut?
FILLER:  count the "um / like / kind of" — aim to halve it next pass
CLARITY: any slide you couldn't explain in one breath? -> simplify it
CONFIDENCE: did you state findings as facts, or hedge everything?
OPENING: did you lead with the recommendation in the first 15 seconds?
```
Two passes against this rubric will do more for how your work is received than another hour of analysis.

cards.prompt: Recording your pitch surfaces filler words and weak spots before the real meeting.
cards.whenRight: Right — you can't fix what you can't see; the recording shows it.
cards.whenWrong: It does — watching yourself reveals the hedging and gaps to fix.
cards.sim: record -> spot 'um', hedging, the slide you can't explain

items.title: Your turn — record the pitch
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Record a 5-minute walkthrough of your deck.
[WRITE] Score yourself on the rubric and note two specific things to improve (a slide to cut, filler to drop, a claim to state more confidently).

days.title: Ship v0.5
days.summary: Export the 5-slide deck to PDF, commit, tag v0.5.

items.title: Ship v0.5
items.body:
## What it is
Export the finished, design-passed, rehearsed deck to PDF and ship it as `v0.5`, alongside the notebook and memo.

## Why it matters
A tight five-slide executive deck is a portfolio centrepiece precisely because it proves the rarest analyst skill: turning analysis into a *decision*. Plenty of people can make charts; far fewer can stand in front of leadership and drive an action in five slides. Shipping this is evidence you can.

cards.prompt: A tight 5-slide deck is a stronger deliverable than 20 slides showing everything.
cards.whenRight: Right — decision-makers reward the distilled argument, not the volume.
cards.whenWrong: It is — five sharp slides communicate more than twenty exhaustive ones.

items.title: Acceptance — v0.5 is done when
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Deck is exactly 5 slides (headline / three one-point findings / recommendation), design-consistent, exported to PDF.
[CODE] Commit and tag:
```
git add .
git commit -m "Superstore v0.5: 5-slide executive deck"
git tag v0.5
git push --tags
```
[WRITE] Drop your repo link in the dashboard check-in.

tasks: Build 3 finding slides (1 chart + 1 takeaway each)
weeks.project: Superstore v0.5 — 5-slide executive deck with specific recommendations. Practiced and exported as PDF.

resources.label: Cole Knaflic on Data Storytelling - 18 min TED
resources.note: 18 min. The most-referenced data viz talk ever. Watch with a notepad.

resources.label: Pyramid Principle in 5 minutes - McKinsey-style (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 5 min. Headline first, support second. How consultants structure every memo. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: One Big Number slides in 4 minutes (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 4 min. Why one giant number beats a chart 80% of the time. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Steve Jobs presentation tactics - 5 min
resources.note: 5 min. The 3-act pitch structure. Steal it for every deck.

exercises: Rebuild the deck without ANY chart — only big numbers and text. Compare effectiveness.
Make a 'CFO-version' that's all about money saved
Make an 'ops-version' that's all about discount caps
questions: Why do executives consume slides not memos?
Why is one-idea-per-slide a rule?
What's the difference between a chart label and a chart title?
mastery_questions: Write all five slide headlines as complete sentences. Paste them. Each headline should contain at least one number ("7.2 pp lower," "top 20% of customers drive 78% of profit"). Headlines that contain words like "significant," "major," or "notable" without a number are placeholder headlines -- replace the qualitative word with the number it is hedging around.

Build Slide 2 (the profitability finding). One chart (the Category margin bar chart from week 1, or the Sub-Category margin chart). The chart title IS the headline. One call-out box flagging the most important data point. No more than three words of body text. Paste a description of the slide layout or the slide itself as an image. If you needed more than 30 seconds to locate the most important number, the chart is too complex.

Build Slide 5 (the three recommended actions). Format: each recommendation is one bullet. Each bullet has three parts: Action (what to do), Metric (what changes), and Estimate (by how much). Example: "Cap Furniture discounts at 20% | Metric: Furniture profit margin | Estimate: +4-6 pp improvement based on orders currently above the cap." Paste all three bullets. A recommendation without an estimate of impact is a wish, not a recommendation.

Practice the two-minute deck walkthrough out loud. Start with Slide 1 (situation and recommendation), move through the evidence slides quickly, land on Slide 5 (actions). Time yourself. If it takes more than 2.5 minutes, cut content from the evidence slides -- they exist to support the recommendation, not to demonstrate effort. Paste the spoken script for Slide 1 (one to two sentences).

Get feedback from one person who has not seen the Superstore analysis. Share the PDF and ask them to read it alone for 5 minutes, then tell you what the three recommended actions are. If they cannot name all three without looking at the deck, the deck is not clear enough. Write what feedback you received and one change you made based on it.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to write the speaker notes for each slide. Paste the slide headline and the one chart description, and ask "write two to three sentences of speaker notes for a CEO audience, using plain language and referencing the specific numbers." Review each set of notes for accuracy against your actual numbers. Speaker notes that reference correct numbers are reusable; speaker notes that say "approximately" or "around" are hedging and need to be fixed with the actual value.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Your audience is a busy CEO with 5 minutes. They want the recommendation FIRST, the supporting data second. Practice answering 'so what?' to every chart out loud. If you can't answer, the chart does not belong on the slide.
weeks.pre_flight: Write the five slide headlines before opening Slides or PowerPoint. A headline should be a full sentence stating a specific finding or recommendation with a number. If you cannot write the headline as a full sentence with a number, the finding is not sharp enough yet. Revise the finding until the headline writes itself.
common_mistakes: Slide titles that describe what the chart shows instead of what it means. "Profit Margin by Category" is a description. "Furniture Margins Are Structurally Below Technology and Office Supplies" is a finding.

Charts with more than five data series. A bar chart with 17 Sub-Categories is a data table dressed as a chart. If you need to show Sub-Category detail, use a sorted bar chart with the top and bottom three highlighted, not all 17.

Putting the recommendation on slide 5 without any estimate of impact. "Cap discounts at 20%" tells the CEO what to do but not why it is worth doing. The estimate of impact ("+$X in annual profit based on current order distribution") is what converts a suggestion into a decision.

Reading from the slides during the presentation. The slides are for the audience. The script is in your head. If you need to read the slide, the slide has too many words. Reduce the text until you can speak the slide without looking at it.

Not exporting to PDF before committing. A .pptx file requires the audience to have PowerPoint and to open it. A PDF requires nothing and looks identical on every device. Always export and commit the PDF alongside the source file.
weeks.debug_help: The most common deck feedback is "it is too long" and the second most common is "the recommendation is unclear." Both have the same fix: start with the recommendation on slide 1, cut slides 2-4 to one chart each, and make slide 5 the most detailed slide in the deck. If you cut the deck from 10 to 5 slides and the recommendation is clearer, you have done it correctly. If the CEO cannot act on your recommendation without seeing the slides you cut, those slides were necessary and you need to make your recommendation more specific.
stretch: Add an appendix slide with the full Sub-Category margin table, the customer segment profile, and the discount bucket analysis. Appendix slides exist for the detailed follow-up questions. Separating them from the main deck keeps the main deck clean while making the detail available.

Record a 2-minute Loom video walkthrough of the deck. Watch it back and identify one slide where your verbal explanation added information that is not on the slide -- that information probably belongs on the slide.

Read "Slide:ology" by Nancy Duarte or watch her 18-minute TED talk "The Secret Structure of Great Talks." The Pyramid Principle and the headline-first structure are the two most transferable concepts for analyst-to-stakeholder communication.

weeks.title: Superstore v1.0: Ship + retro
weeks.context:
The Superstore project has been running for eight weeks. The memo is two pages, the deck is five slides, the dashboard is one sheet, queries.sql has eight queries, monthly_report.py runs in five minutes, and the GitHub repo has everything committed. This week you finish it -- properly.

"Properly" means three things. First, you get one outside reader to look at the memo or the deck and tell you what confused them. Not a friend who will tell you it looks great -- someone who will actually use it. Second, you write a project retrospective. Third, you anonymise the data for sharing and update the repo README to reflect the final state.

The outside reader is not optional. The analyst's curse is that you know what every chart means because you built it. A reader who did not build it will find the one label you forgot, the one chart that has no axis title, and the one recommendation that is not specific enough. Every team you will join as a working analyst has a "two-eyes" rule for deliverables: no analysis leaves the team without another pair of eyes. You are practising that discipline now.

The retrospective is a one-page honest document, not a celebration. Three questions: what took longer than you expected, what would you do differently if you started over, and what is the single most useful thing you learned. The answers to these questions are the learning you take into Project 2. Skipping the retrospective means carrying the same blind spots into the next project.

The Superstore dataset is fictional and does not require anonymisation, but the practice of scrubbing a dataset before sharing is good professional hygiene. Replace "Customer Name" with "Customer ID" (it already exists), confirm no personal information made it into the analysis files, and note the data source and licence in the README.

By Sunday: outside reader feedback documented in the repo, RETRO.md committed, dataset anonymisation confirmed, and the README updated to reflect the final project state with links to all four deliverables.

days.title: Find the rough edges
days.summary: Before v1.0, audit everything for what's half-done, inconsistent, or confusing. Concept + worked audit.

items.title: Find the rough edges
items.body:
## What it is
Before the final ship, audit every artefact — notebook, memo, deck, dashboard, `queries.sql`, repo README — and write down every **rough edge**: half-finished bits, inconsistencies, broken links, unclear labels, numbers that disagree across documents.

## Why it matters
"Shipping" means *finishing*, not *abandoning*, and "it's basically done" is where most portfolio projects quietly die at 80%. A written rough-edge list converts that vague feeling into a concrete, completable punch list — and the act of hunting for edges always finds the embarrassing one (the figure that's $62k in the memo and $61k on the deck) that would have cost you credibility. You can't fix what you haven't named.

## How to audit
Open each artefact as if you were a stranger reviewing it for a job. Note everything that's wrong, unclear, or inconsistent — don't fix yet, just list. A good audit usually finds 5-10 items you'd otherwise have shipped.

items.title: See it worked (a real audit list)
items.body:
## What a rough-edge list looks like
```text
NOTEBOOK
  - cell 12 errors on "Restart & Run All"
  - two cells compute total loss with different filters -> different numbers
MEMO
  - says $62k recovery; deck slide 5 says $61k  (reconcile!)
  - "tipping point" used but never defined
DECK
  - slide 3 y-axis unlabeled
  - Furniture is blue on slide 2, orange on slide 3
REPO
  - README missing a "how to run" section
  - data/ committed by accident (should be gitignored)
```
Specific, checkable items — not "make it better". That's a finishable list.

cards.prompt: Writing a rough-edge list before the final ship prevents shipping half-done work.
cards.whenRight: Right — a concrete punch list turns 'basically done' into actually done.
cards.whenWrong: It does — listing gaps turns a vague feeling into finishable tasks.

items.title: Your turn — audit
items.body: [WRITE] Review every artefact as a stranger would and list every rough edge across notebook, memo, deck, dashboard, queries.sql, and README. Be specific; don't fix yet.

days.title: Fix the rough edges
days.summary: Work the list. Small fixes compound into a professional impression. Concept + the finishing checklist.

items.title: Fix the rough edges
items.body:
## What it is
Work straight down your punch list: restart-and-run-all the notebook, reconcile every number so one figure is canonical everywhere, fix labels and broken links, tidy the README.

## Why it matters
Polish is invisible item-by-item but unmistakable in aggregate — it's the entire difference between "a student made this" and "I'd hire this person". A reviewer can't always name *why* one project feels professional and another feels like a draft, but they feel it, and it's the accumulation of small fixes: the notebook that runs clean, the numbers that agree, the axes that are labelled. This is the cheapest possible credibility, and skipping it wastes all the analysis underneath.

## The standard for 'done'
Restart kernel, Run All -> zero errors. Every number appears identically wherever it's cited. Every chart axis labelled. Every link clicks through. README tells a stranger how to run it.

items.title: See it worked (the finishing checklist)
items.body:
## Drive every item to green
```text
[ ] Notebook: Restart & Run All -> executes top to bottom, no errors
[ ] One canonical value per number, repeated identically everywhere
[ ] Every chart axis labelled, every chart has a takeaway
[ ] All links (repo, notebook, data source) click through
[ ] README: what it is + how to run, in 5 lines
[ ] No stray files committed (data/, .ipynb_checkpoints, keys)
```
When every box is checked, you've crossed from "draft" to "portfolio-grade".

cards.prompt: Polishing the small inconsistencies is what separates a portfolio piece from a draft.
cards.whenRight: Right — reviewers feel the difference even when they can't name it.
cards.whenWrong: It does — the accumulation of small fixes is what reads as 'finished'.
cards.sim: many small fixes -> 'this person is careful'

items.title: Your turn — fix them
items.body: [PRODUCE] Work through your rough-edge list. Restart-and-run-all the notebook to confirm it's clean end to end, and reconcile every number to one canonical value.

days.title: Reformat the memo as a polished doc
days.summary: Move from raw markdown to a formatted document. Concept + the formatting spec.

items.title: Reformat the memo as a polished doc
items.body:
## What it is
Move the memo out of raw markdown into a properly formatted document — clear heading hierarchy, one readable body font, embedded charts at sensible sizes, page numbers, maybe a simple header with your name and date.

## Why it matters
A non-technical reader judges credibility partly by *format*, before they read a word. The identical content reads as more authoritative in a clean PDF than in a plain `.md` file — fair or not, that's how decision-makers respond. On real jobs the deliverable is almost always a polished doc or slides, never a markdown file, so building the habit now matters. Format is the wrapper that makes good content get taken seriously.

## The spec
H1 title, H2 section headings (Headline / Evidence / Recommendation), one body font, charts embedded inline with captions, page numbers, your name + date. One page if you can.

items.title: See it worked (the format spec)
items.body:
## From .md to a doc that gets read
```text
RAW (what you have):           POLISHED (what you ship):
  # Memo                         - H1 title, H2 sections
  some text...                   - one clean body font, real margins
  ![chart](a.png)                - charts embedded, sized, CAPTIONED
  more text                      - page numbers + name/date header
                                 - exported to PDF
```
Same words, completely different reception. Build it in Word or Google Docs, export a PDF, and commit that PDF next to the markdown source.

cards.prompt: A cleanly formatted memo doc reads as more credible to a non-technical reader than raw markdown.
cards.whenRight: Right — format is a credibility signal for that audience.
cards.whenWrong: It does — presentation affects how seriously the content is taken.
cards.sim: raw .md -> formatted PDF with headings + captions

items.title: Your turn — polished memo
items.body: [PRODUCE] Reformat your memo as a clean Word/Google Doc (heading hierarchy, embedded captioned charts, page numbers) and export a PDF committed beside the source.

days.title: Make a public-safe version
days.summary: An anonymized, secret-free version for your public portfolio. Concept + the safety checklist.

items.title: Make a public-safe version
items.body:
## What it is
Create a version you can show the world. Superstore is a public sample dataset, so confirm there's nothing private (no real PII, no credentials, no internal-only commentary) before it goes on your public GitHub and portfolio.

## Why it matters
You *want* recruiters to find and read this — that's the point of a portfolio. A public-safe pass lets you share freely without ever leaking something you shouldn't, and it builds the exact habit that matters far more on real company projects later, where an accidental key or customer record in a public repo is a fireable, sometimes legal, problem. Practising "scrub before public" on safe data now means you won't slip on dangerous data later.

## The checklist
Confirm the dataset is the public sample; remove internal TODOs and private notes from the notebook; ensure no API keys, credentials, or absolute file paths are committed; gitignore the raw data if licensing requires it.

items.title: See it worked (the safety checklist)
items.body:
## Scrub before it goes public
```text
[ ] Dataset is the public Superstore sample (no proprietary data)
[ ] No credentials / API keys / tokens in any file or commit history
[ ] No real PII (names here are sample data — confirm)
[ ] No internal TODOs or private commentary in the notebook
[ ] No absolute local paths ("C:/Users/you/...") -> use relative paths
[ ] .gitignore covers data/, checkpoints, env files
```
Run `git log -p | grep -i "key\|password\|token"` as a quick secrets sweep before you make the repo public.

cards.prompt: A public portfolio version should have sensitive data, credentials, and private notes removed.
cards.whenRight: Right — share the work, never the secrets. Build the habit now.
cards.whenWrong: It should — strip PII, credentials, and internal notes before going public.
cards.sim: remove: keys, PII, internal TODOs, local paths

items.title: Your turn — public-safe pass
items.body: [PRODUCE] Run the safety checklist: confirm no credentials, no private notes, only the public dataset, relative paths. Make the repo portfolio-ready and public.

days.title: Get one real reader
days.summary: Hand it to a stranger and watch where they get confused. Concept + the reader test.

items.title: Get one real reader
items.body:
## What it is
Give your memo or deck to **one person who hasn't seen the project** and watch (or ask) where they slow down, re-read, or get confused.

## Why it matters
You are constitutionally blind to your own clarity gaps — you know too much, so the jargon, the unexplained jump, and the chart with no takeaway are invisible to *you* but obvious to a fresh reader. This is the single cheapest, highest-impact quality boost available: five minutes with one outsider finds more real problems than an hour of you re-reading your own work, because you'll only ever read it as the person who already understands it.

## The killer test
Ask them: "Read this, then tell me in one sentence what I'm recommending and why." If they can't, your headline and structure aren't doing their job — and you've found that out for free, before it mattered.

items.title: See it worked (run the test)
items.body:
## The one-question reader test
```text
YOU:    "Read this memo, then tell me in one sentence what I'm recommending
         and why."
READER: "Um... that discounts are bad? And maybe cap them somewhere?"
        ^ if this is vague, your headline failed -> fix slide 1 / the headline

WATCH FOR (note every one):
  - where they re-read a sentence (it's unclear)
  - a term they pause on (undefined jargon)
  - a chart they skip (no takeaway, or too busy)
  - "wait, which number?" (inconsistent figures)
```
Their confusion is your punch list for tomorrow.

cards.prompt: A fresh reader reveals confusion you can't see in your own work.
cards.whenRight: Right — you know too much to spot your own gaps; they don't.
cards.whenWrong: It does — an outside reader surfaces the jargon and jumps you're blind to.
cards.sim: they can't restate your point -> structure needs work

items.title: Your turn — reader test
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Have one person who doesn't know the project read your memo/deck and do the one-sentence test.
[WRITE] Note every spot where they hesitated, asked a question, or misread something.

days.title: Fix what confused them
days.summary: Reader confusion is data. Fix the work, don't defend it. Concept + worked fixes.

items.title: Fix what confused them
items.body:
## What it is
Turn your reader's confusion into a fix list and apply it: define the jargon, add the missing context, label the chart, tighten the headline, reconcile the number.

## Why it matters
The instinct is to *explain* — "well, what they didn't understand is..." — and you must kill it, because in the real meeting you won't be standing next to every reader to clarify. If one fresh reader was confused, the artefact is unclear, and the next reader (your boss, a recruiter) will be confused too, except they won't tell you — they'll just move on. Treating confusion as a defect in the *work* rather than the *reader* is the mindset that produces things people actually understand. Clarity beats cleverness every time.

## The rule
Every point of confusion becomes a concrete edit. You don't have to act on *opinions* ("I'd use a different colour"), but you must act on *confusion* ("I didn't get what this chart shows").

items.title: See it worked (confusion -> fix)
items.body:
## Translate each reaction into an edit
```text
READER said                          ->  YOU fix
"I didn't get 'tipping point'"       ->  define it on first use, one line
"Which number is the recommendation?"->  bold it / move it to the headline
"This chart — what am I looking at?" ->  add a one-line takeaway + axis labels
"$62k or $61k?"                      ->  reconcile to one canonical figure
"Got bored halfway"                  ->  cut a slide / tighten the memo
```
Notice you're fixing the *work*, never arguing with the reader. That's the whole discipline.

cards.prompt: Reader confusion is information to act on — fix the work rather than defend it.
cards.whenRight: Right — in the room they won't have you to explain; the artefact must stand alone.
cards.whenWrong: It is — treat confusion as a defect to fix, not a reader error to argue with.
cards.sim: 'they misread it' -> no: make it un-misreadable

items.title: Your turn — apply the feedback
items.body: [PRODUCE] Convert every point of confusion into a concrete edit and apply it. Re-check that your one-sentence recommendation is now unmissable.

days.title: Ship v1.0 + retro
days.summary: Tag v1.0, then a short retro. Project 1 DONE. Concept + the retro template.

items.title: Ship v1.0 + retro
items.body:
## What it is
Tag the project `v1.0` — it's genuinely done — then write a short **retro**: what worked, what was hard, and what you'd do differently next time.

## Why it matters
`v1.0` is your first complete, portfolio-grade analytics project: the same questions answered in Excel, pandas, and SQL; a polished memo; a five-slide deck; stats-backed, significance-tested findings; AI-assisted and verified; reader-tested and public-safe. That's a genuine portfolio centrepiece. The retro is what converts the *experience* into reusable lessons — reflection is the step that makes the next project faster and better, and it's the habit that compounds a career instead of just finishing a task. Doing the work teaches you a little; reflecting on it is where most of the learning actually lands.

items.title: See it worked (the retro template)
items.body:
## A retro that compounds your skill
```text
## Project 1 Retro — Superstore
What worked:
  - leading the memo with the recommendation; readers 'got it' instantly
  - re-doing the analysis in SQL cemented groupby for good
What was hard:
  - reconciling numbers across memo/deck (fix: single source next time)
  - keeping the deck to 5 slides (compression is the real skill)
What I'd do differently:
  - write the hypothesis on Day 1 of every project, not midway
  - build the 'final' notebook from the start, not stitch it at the end
```
Three honest bullets each. This is what turns one finished project into a better next one.

cards.prompt: A short retro (what worked / what was hard / what's next) turns a finished project into a reusable lesson.
cards.whenRight: Right — reflection is how one project makes you better at the next.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a retro converts experience into lessons you carry forward.

[WRITE] A short retro in the README: what worked, what was hard, what you'd do differently.
[CODE] Tag and push:
```

git commit -m "Superstore v1.0: final, reader-tested, portfolio-ready"
git tag v1.0
git push --tags
```

exercises: Make a 2-minute Loom video walkthrough of the dashboard
Post a screenshot on LinkedIn
Add the repo to your GitHub pinned repos
questions: What's the smallest unit of analyst polish that makes a real difference?
How does anonymization change trust?
What feedback hurt the most?
mastery_questions: Share the memo PDF with one person who has not seen this project. Ask them to read it alone for 5 minutes, then answer: "What are the three things the Superstore business should do based on this memo?" Write down their three answers. Compare to your three recommendations. If there is a mismatch, update the memo to close the gap. Paste the change you made.

Write RETRO.md. Three required sections: What took longer than expected (be specific -- "writing the memo took 4 hours, not 1, because finding the right numbers for each finding required going back to the pivot tables"), What you would do differently (specific, not generic -- "I would write the slide headlines before building any charts"), What you learned that you will use in Project 2 (the single most transferable insight). Paste the file.

Run monthly_report.py on a fresh Python environment (a new virtual environment with only the packages in requirements.txt). Confirm it runs without error. Paste the last 5 lines of output. If it fails, you have an undocumented dependency -- add it to requirements.txt and re-run. A script that only works in your environment is not a reproducible deliverable.

Review the repo for any files that should not be public: any file with real personal data (the Superstore CSV is fictional, but check for any real data you added during analysis), any credentials or API keys, any large binary files that do not need version control. Paste the output of git ls-files showing what is in the repo. Remove anything that should not be there.

Update the README to its final state. Required: project description in two sentences, the three specific findings with numbers, links to all four deliverables (dashboard PDF, memo PDF, deck PDF, queries.sql), instructions for running monthly_report.py, and the data source with licence. Paste the final README. A README that a stranger can read in 2 minutes and fully understand the project is the correct level.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to review the README for completeness. Paste the README and ask "what information is missing that a stranger would need to understand what this project found and how to run it?" The gaps it identifies are worth fixing. Do NOT use Claude to write the retrospective. The retro is honest self-assessment -- a generated retro sounds like a generated retro and helps no one.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Imagine your CEO reads your memo on her phone in a 2-minute Uber ride. Does the headline give her the answer? Does the recommendation come BEFORE the methodology? If she stops reading after sentence 1, did she still get the most important thing?
weeks.pre_flight: Open the Superstore repo and read the README as a stranger. Does it state what the project found? Does it link to the dashboard, memo, and deck PDFs? Does it say what data was used and where it came from? If any of those are missing, fix them before writing any new content this week.
common_mistakes: Treating the outside reader feedback as optional because "I know it is already clear." The whole point of outside review is that you cannot reliably assess your own clarity on work you built. If the reader was confused about anything, fix it regardless of whether you think the confusion was their fault.

Writing a retro that only covers what went well. The useful information is in what was hard. "The analysis went smoothly" is not a retro entry. "I spent 6 hours on a SUMIFS formula that should have taken 20 minutes because I did not check the date format first" is.

Committing large PNG or PDF files without checking file size. GitHub has a 100MB file limit and repos with many large files are slow to clone. Compress PDFs before committing. Chart PNGs should be under 200KB.
Leaving the README un-updated after all the week-8 changes. The README should describe the current state of the project, not the state it was in when you first wrote it.
Not including a requirements.txt. A repo without requirements.txt requires the reader to guess which Python packages monthly_report.py needs. Run pip freeze > requirements.txt and commit it.
weeks.debug_help: If monthly_report.py fails in a fresh environment, the most common reason is a pandas version incompatibility -- pandas 2.x changed several API behaviours from pandas 1.x. Run pip install pandas==1.5.3 in the fresh environment and retry. If that fixes it, update requirements.txt to pin the pandas version. If it fails for a different reason, read the full traceback -- the last line is almost always the actual error, and it is almost always a missing package or a hardcoded path.
stretch: Add a GitHub Actions workflow that runs monthly_report.py on every push and confirms it exits with status 0. A one-minute CI check that catches broken scripts before they are committed is the minimum viable quality gate for a data project.

Write a one-paragraph "project summary" card that you could post on LinkedIn. It should state the question, the dataset, the finding, and what someone viewing the repo can expect to find. Under 150 words. This is the LinkedIn post version of the project, and it is also the cover letter paragraph for any role where this project is relevant.

Prepare a 90-second verbal pitch for the Superstore project. Record yourself and listen back. If you run past 90 seconds, cut the methodology section and lead with the finding. The methodology is "I analysed the Sample Superstore dataset using Excel, Python, and SQL." That is one sentence. The finding deserves the other 75 seconds.

weeks.title: Project 2 — HR Attrition v0.1
weeks.context:
The Superstore project was a retailer. This week you start a very different domain: human resources. The IBM HR Analytics dataset contains 1,470 employees with 35 columns covering age, gender, department, job role, salary, overtime hours, tenure, satisfaction scores, and most importantly a binary column called Attrition (Yes/No) indicating whether each employee left the company.

Employee attrition costs money. A mid-level engineer who leaves costs roughly 150% of their annual salary to replace -- recruiting fees, onboarding time, lost productivity during the vacancy. For a department with 200 engineers where 15% leave per year, that is $4.5 million annually assuming $200K salaries. An analysis that identifies which employees are at highest risk of leaving -- and what predictors are associated with that risk -- can prioritise interventions that cost a fraction of that.

Your job this week is not to build a prediction model. It is to build four pivot tables, each answering a specific question about which sub-population has the highest attrition rate. The four questions: which departments have the highest attrition rates, which job roles have the highest rates, which salary bands have the highest rates, and how does overtime status interact with attrition? The answers will be specific numbers, not observations about "elevated risk."

Attrition rate is computed as: (employees who left) / (total employees in that group). In the dataset, this means counting the "Yes" values in the Attrition column divided by the total count for each group. COUNTIFS handles this directly. The denominator is total employees in the group, not total employees in the company.

By Sunday: a new GitHub repo named hr-attrition-analysis with the IBM dataset, four pivot tables with attrition rates computed correctly, and a README stating the two highest-risk combinations you found.

days.title: Why people analytics
days.summary: A new domain: HR. Concept of attrition, then compute the base rate on real data.

items.title: Why people analytics
items.body:
## What it is
Last project you analysed a retailer; now you turn the same rigour on **people**. **Attrition** is employees leaving the company, and **people analytics** is using data to understand who leaves and why — instead of guessing.

## Why it matters
Attrition is brutally expensive: replacing an employee costs roughly **50-200% of their annual salary** (recruiting, onboarding, lost productivity). HR decisions are too often made on gut feel — "people leave for money" — when the data frequently says something else entirely (overtime, no promotion, a specific role). Finding the *real* drivers lets a company spend its retention budget where it actually moves the needle. This is exactly the analytical thinking from Project 1, applied to a domain where one good finding can save millions.

## The dataset
The **IBM HR Analytics** dataset: 1,470 employees, 35 columns (age, department, job role, monthly income, overtime, years at company, years since promotion…). The target column is **Attrition** (`Yes`/`No`) — whether each employee left. Everything this week predicts or explains that one column.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Load and find the base rate
The first question in any attrition study: what fraction actually left?
```python
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("HR-Employee-Attrition.csv")
print(df.shape)
print(df["Attrition"].value_counts())
print(df["Attrition"].value_counts(normalize=True).round(3))
```
Output:
```
(1470, 35)
No     1233
Yes     237
Name: Attrition, dtype: int64
No     0.839
Yes    0.161
Name: Attrition, dtype: float64
```
Read it: **16.1% of employees left** — that's your *base rate*, the number every group you analyse this week gets compared against. A department at 25% is a problem; one at 8% is a model. Note too that the classes are **imbalanced** (most stayed) — important to remember so you don't over-read small groups.

cards.prompt: The attrition rate is the share of employees whose Attrition is 'Yes' — a boolean mean.
cards.whenRight: Right — (Attrition=='Yes').mean() gives the rate, like the repeat-rate trick.
cards.whenWrong: It is — it's the proportion of 'Yes', exactly a boolean mean.

cards.prompt: Every department will have the same attrition rate as the 16% overall.
cards.whenRight: Correct — the whole project is finding which groups deviate from that base rate.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — groups vary widely; finding the deviations is the point.

items.title: Your turn — frame the project

days.title: Load and inspect
days.summary: Inspect first, always. Concept, video, then the structure + target balance.

items.title: Load and inspect
items.body:
## What it is
Same discipline as every dataset: before analysing, **look**. `head`, `info`, `describe`, and the target's balance. With 35 columns you especially need to know what's numeric, what's categorical, and whether anything's missing.

## Why it matters
You can't analyse drivers of attrition until you know which columns *are* drivers (numeric like MonthlyIncome, categorical like Department) and that the data is clean. Inspecting also re-surfaces the **class imbalance** (only 16% left) — which matters because a group with just 10 employees can show a wild attrition rate that's pure noise. Knowing your column types now also tells you which technique each driver needs: `groupby` for categoricals, `pd.cut` then groupby for numerics.

## What to check
Column count and types (`info`), missing values (the IBM set is clean — confirm it), the spread of key numerics (`describe`), and the target balance again so it's front of mind.

items.title: Inspect a DataFrame: head(), info(), describe()
items.why: The four inspection commands, reused on the HR data. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Inspect the structure
```python
print(df.info())
print(df.isna().sum().sum())     # total missing values
```
```
RangeIndex: 1470 entries, 0 to 1469
Columns: 35 ...
 #  Column            Non-Null Count  Dtype
 0  Age               1470 non-null   int64
 1  Attrition         1470 non-null   object
 4  Department        1470 non-null   object
 18 MonthlyIncome     1470 non-null   int64
 22 OverTime          1470 non-null   object
 ...
0      <- no missing values, the set is clean
```

## A reusable helper: encode the target as 0/1
```python
df["left"] = (df["Attrition"] == "Yes").astype(int)
print(df["left"].mean().round(3))
```
```
0.161
```
Turning `Attrition` into a 0/1 `left` column is the key move: now `groupby(...)["left"].mean()` gives the **attrition rate** of any group directly. You'll use this every day this week.

cards.prompt: Encoding Attrition as a 0/1 'left' column lets groupby().mean() return the attrition RATE per group.
cards.whenRight: Right — the mean of a 0/1 column is the proportion of 1s = the rate.
cards.whenWrong: It does — mean of 0/1 is the share that left, per group.

cards.prompt: A group of only 10 employees gives an attrition rate as trustworthy as one of 500.
cards.whenRight: Correct — tiny groups give noisy rates; always check the group size (count).
cards.whenWrong: Not equally — small groups are noisy; check counts before trusting a rate.

days.title: Attrition by department
days.summary: The core move: a rate per group. Concept, video, then department rates vs the base.

items.title: Attrition by department
items.body:
## What it is
The workhorse question: **which departments lose the most people?** Group by `Department`, take the mean of your 0/1 `left` column, and you get each department's attrition rate — directly comparable to the 16.1% base rate.

## Why it matters
"We have a turnover problem" is useless to act on; "Sales runs 20.6% attrition vs 13.8% in R&D" tells leadership exactly where to focus. Comparing each group to the base rate is the move that turns a single company-wide number into a *map* of where the problem actually lives. This is the same split-apply-combine you've used since Week 2 — now answering an expensive HR question.

## The pattern
`groupby` the category, `.mean()` the 0/1 target for the rate, and `.count()` (or size) alongside so you know each group is big enough to trust. Always sort, and always compare to the base rate.

items.title: Pandas pivot_table / grouping for a breakdown
items.why: Grouping a category to summarise, reused on attrition. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate per department
```python
dept = df.groupby("Department").agg(
    attrition_rate=("left", "mean"),
    employees=("left", "count"),
).sort_values("attrition_rate", ascending=False)
print(dept.round(3))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
                        attrition_rate  employees
Department
Sales                            0.206        446
Human Resources                  0.190         63
Research & Development           0.138        961
```
Read it against the 16.1% base: **Sales (20.6%) is well above** average and is the biggest group, so it's the priority. HR is high too but only 63 people, so treat that rate with some caution. R&D is below base — relatively healthy. One groupby just turned "we have turnover" into "Sales is the problem".

cards.prompt: Comparing each group's rate to the overall base rate is how you find where the problem lives.
cards.whenRight: Right — deviation from the 16.1% base is the signal.
cards.whenWrong: It is — the gap from the base rate tells you which groups matter.

cards.prompt: Reporting the employee COUNT next to each rate matters for trusting it.
cards.whenRight: Right — a high rate on 63 people is shakier than on 446.
cards.whenWrong: It does — counts tell you whether a rate rests on enough people.

items.body:

[WRITE] One sentence: which department is the priority (high rate AND large enough to matter), vs the base rate?

days.title: Attrition by job role
days.summary: Drill deeper than department. Concept, video, then role-level hotspots.

items.title: Attrition by job role
items.body:
## What it is
Department is coarse. Drill into **JobRole** — the same rate-per-group move, one level finer — to find the specific roles bleeding talent.

## Why it matters
A department average can hide a disaster in one role (a near-Simpson's effect you met in the stats week). Sales overall is 20.6%, but that blends calm roles with one that's on fire. Pinpointing the *role* lets HR target a fix — a specific role's pay, workload, or career path — instead of a vague "fix Sales". The finer the actionable unit, the more useful the finding.

## The pattern
Identical to yesterday, just group by `JobRole`. Sort, keep counts, and look for roles far above the base rate — those are your hotspots.

items.title: Aggregation with groupby() & agg()
items.why: groupby + agg, reused to break attrition down by role. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate per job role
```python
role = df.groupby("JobRole").agg(
    attrition_rate=("left", "mean"),
    employees=("left", "count"),
).sort_values("attrition_rate", ascending=False)
print(role.round(3).head(5))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
                          attrition_rate  employees
JobRole
Sales Representative               0.398         83
Laboratory Technician              0.239        259
Human Resources                    0.231         52
Sales Executive                    0.175        326
Research Scientist                 0.161        292
```
The headline: **Sales Representatives churn at 39.8% — nearly 2.5x the company base rate.** That single role is the hotspot the department average (20.6%) was hiding. *This* is what HR should fix first — and you couldn't see it until you went one level deeper than department.

cards.prompt: Breaking attrition down by role can reveal a hotspot that the department average hides.
cards.whenRight: Right — Sales Reps at 39.8% hid inside Sales' 20.6%.
cards.whenWrong: It does — the finer cut exposes the role driving a department's average.

cards.prompt: Once you know the department, drilling into role adds no value.
cards.whenRight: Correct — the role view found the 39.8% hotspot the department blended away.
cards.whenWrong: Not true — role-level detail pinpoints the actual problem to fix.
cards.sim: dept hides the on-fire role inside its average

items.title: Your turn — role hotspots
items.body:
[CODE] Compute attrition rate + count per `JobRole`, sorted; print the top 5.
[WRITE] One sentence naming the worst role and how its rate compares to the 16.1% base.

days.title: Does pay drive leaving?
days.summary: Bin a numeric driver, then rate per band. Concept, video, then the salary effect.

items.title: Does pay drive leaving?
items.body:
## What it is
Now a *numeric* driver: `MonthlyIncome`. You can't group by a continuous salary directly, so **bin it** with `pd.cut` into bands, then compute the attrition rate per band — exactly the cut-then-groupby move from the discount week.

## Why it matters
"People leave for money" is the most common HR assumption, and data lets you test it instead of repeating it. If attrition falls steeply as pay rises, comp is a real lever; if it's flat, the money story is a myth and you should look elsewhere (overtime, promotion). Either way you've replaced a belief with evidence — and possibly saved the company from throwing raises at a problem raises won't fix.

## The pattern
`pd.cut(MonthlyIncome, bins)` to create salary bands, then `groupby(band)["left"].mean()`. Watch the trend across bands top to bottom.

items.title: Binning with pandas pd.cut()
items.why: pd.cut to bucket a numeric driver, reused for salary. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate by salary band
```python
df["income_band"] = pd.cut(df["MonthlyIncome"],
    bins=[0, 3000, 6000, 10000, 20000],
    labels=["<3k", "3-6k", "6-10k", "10k+"])
print(df.groupby("income_band")["left"].mean().round(3))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
income_band
<3k      0.295
3-6k     0.146
6-10k    0.092
10k+     0.077
Name: left, dtype: float64
```
Read the trend: attrition **falls steeply with pay** — 29.5% in the lowest band vs 7.7% in the top. So for this company the "money matters" story holds, *at the low end especially*: the cheapest-paid third is where the bleeding is. That's an actionable, evidence-backed lever (review pay floors) — not a guess.

cards.prompt: To study a numeric driver like salary, you bin it with pd.cut then take the rate per band.
cards.whenRight: Right — cut to bands, groupby band, mean the 0/1 target.
cards.whenWrong: It is — bin the continuous driver, then rate per band.

cards.prompt: You can groupby a continuous salary column directly to see its effect.
cards.whenRight: Correct — too many unique values; you must bin it into bands first.
cards.whenWrong: Not directly — bin it first; raw continuous values don't group usefully.

items.title: Your turn — the salary effect
items.body:
[CODE] Bin `MonthlyIncome` into bands and compute attrition rate per band.
[WRITE] One sentence: does attrition fall with pay, and where is it worst?

days.title: The overtime effect
days.summary: A binary driver, compared directly. Concept, video, then the single biggest factor.

items.title: The overtime effect
items.body:
## What it is
`OverTime` is a simple `Yes`/`No` column — so no binning needed, just compare the attrition rate for those who work overtime vs those who don't.

## Why it matters
Simple often wins. In the IBM data, overtime turns out to be one of the **single strongest** predictors of leaving — frequently a bigger effect than pay or role. That's a hugely actionable finding because overtime is a *managed* variable: a company can change workload policy far faster than it can restructure salaries. It's also a lesson in analytical humility — the most powerful driver is sometimes the plainest column, which you'd miss if you only chased the fancy ones.

## The pattern
A direct `groupby("OverTime")["left"].mean()`. Then quantify the gap (a ratio) — "overtime workers leave at Nx the rate" is the kind of crisp line that lands in a memo.

mastery_questions: Compute the attrition rate by Department using COUNTIFS: =COUNTIFS(Department_col, department, Attrition_col, "Yes") / COUNTIFS(Department_col, department, Attrition_col, "*"). Paste the table: Department, Total Employees, Attrition Count, Attrition Rate. Which department has the highest rate? Is it more than 1.5x the company average? Write one sentence about whether that gap is operationally significant.

Build the Job Role attrition table. Paste all 9 job roles ranked by attrition rate. Write one sentence about the two job roles at the top and what they have in common (compensation level, manager-to-IC ratio, career ceiling). The most common finding in HR attrition data: roles with limited promotion paths have higher attrition than those with clear advancement trajectories.

Bucket MonthlyIncome into salary bands ($0-3K, $3K-6K, $6K-9K, $9K+) using nested IF. Compute attrition rate by band. Paste the table. Does attrition decrease monotonically with salary? If not -- if there is a band where high-salary employees also have elevated attrition -- write one sentence about what might explain it (burnout, overqualification, poaching by competitors).

Build a 2D cross-tab: Department on rows, OverTime (Yes/No) on columns. Compute attrition rate in each cell. Paste the 2D table. Which Department-OverTime combination has the highest attrition rate? Is it more than 2x the company average? This interaction effect -- the combination of department and overtime that is particularly dangerous -- is the kind of finding that a VP of HR acts on.

Write the README for the new repo. State: the dataset source, the overall attrition rate, and the two specific high-risk combinations you found with their exact attrition rates. Example: "Sales Representatives working overtime have a 53% attrition rate, versus the 16% company average." Paste the README. A stranger who reads this should understand what the project found without opening any files.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the COUNTIFS formulas for the attrition rate table -- the two-criteria COUNTIFS (department + attrition = "Yes") is a common formula pattern and Claude writes it correctly. Verify the output against a manual filter for one department before applying the formula to all rows. Do NOT use Claude to generate hypotheses about why specific departments have high attrition. Those hypotheses must come from your reading of the data combined with domain knowledge, not from a model generating plausible-sounding HR narratives.
weeks.pre_flight: Download the IBM HR Analytics Employee Attrition dataset from Kaggle. Open it and compute the overall attrition rate manually: count the "Yes" values in the Attrition column, divide by the total row count. Write down that number. If it is not between 10% and 20%, something is wrong with your count. This overall rate is your benchmark -- every sub-group analysis should be interpreted relative to this baseline.
common_mistakes: Computing attrition rate as (total employees who left) / (total employees in company) instead of (employees in group who left) / (employees in group). The denominator must match the numerator. A Sales department with 100 employees, 20 of whom left, has a 20% rate -- not 20/1470.

Using a pivot table COUNT of Attrition to compute the rate without separating "Yes" from "No." A COUNT of the Attrition column counts all employees; you need a COUNTIFS for "Yes" only. Verify your pivot table by comparing the pivot total to the COUNTIFS total for one group.

Reporting attrition rates without confidence intervals or noting sample size. A 50% attrition rate in a group of 4 employees is very different from 50% in a group of 200. Always report the count alongside the rate.
Not sorting the Job Role table by attrition rate. A table in alphabetical order hides the ranking. Always sort by the metric of interest to make the most important finding immediately visible.

Missing the interaction effect by looking only at univariate tables. Attrition by Department tells one story. Attrition by Department and OverTime tells a more specific story. The interaction is almost always the most actionable finding.
weeks.debug_help: COUNTIFS with "Yes" and "No" criteria fails if the Attrition column has trailing spaces or different capitalisation in some rows. Run =TRIM(Attrition_cell) on a few cells and compare to the original -- any difference means there is whitespace. Fix: select the Attrition column and run Find & Replace for "Yes " (with space) to "Yes". Also run =LEN(A2) on a few Attrition cells; if the length is 4 instead of 3, there is a trailing space.
stretch: Compute the revenue impact of the highest-risk combination you found. Assume average salary of $60K and replacement cost of 150% of salary. If the Sales-Overtime group has 50 employees and a 53% attrition rate, the annual replacement cost is approximately 0.53 * 50 * $90K = $2.4M. This calculation converts an attrition rate into a business number that a VP of HR can bring to a budget conversation.

Visualise the two most important findings using charts rather than tables: a sorted bar chart for Job Role attrition, and a heat map for the Department × OverTime cross-tab. Charts communicate rate differences more immediately than tables.

Compute the statistical significance of the highest-attrition sub-group's rate versus the company average using a chi-squared test of proportions. =CHISQ.TEST() in Excel, or scipy.stats.chi2_contingency in Python. A group with a 40% attrition rate that contains only 10 employees may not be statistically different from the 16% company average.

weeks.title: HR Attrition v0.2: Tenure + cohorts
weeks.context:
Last week you identified which departments and roles have the highest attrition rates. This week you add the time dimension: when in an employee's tenure is the attrition risk highest?

The tenure analysis is the question that converts "who leaves" into "when do they leave" -- which is what HR needs to design interventions. If attrition is highest in the first 12 months, the intervention is better onboarding and 30-60-90 day check-ins. If it is highest at the 2-3 year mark, the intervention is promotion pipeline clarity and salary reviews at that tenure point. If it is highest after 10+ years, the pattern is usually retirement-age exits or long-tenured employees who were not promoted and eventually stopped expecting to be.

The IBM dataset has YearsAtCompany and YearsInCurrentRole. You will bucket YearsAtCompany into tenure bands (0-1 years, 2-3, 4-5, 6-10, 10+) and compute attrition rate per band. The shape of the curve tells you where risk is concentrated. In most datasets, it is highest in the first two years. But some roles are different -- high-tenure technical specialists may show a late-career spike.

The promotion gap variable is worth engineering. Employees who have been in the same role longer than their peers -- defined as YearsInCurrentRole minus the median YearsInCurrentRole for their job role -- are more likely to feel stalled and leave. This is a feature, not a raw column; you have to compute it. The feature engineering is the analysis.

The 2D interaction cross-tab between tenure band and salary band (from week 10) is the most actionable finding this week. An employee in the 2-3 year tenure band who is also in the lowest salary band has a compounding risk that neither factor alone captures.

By Sunday: tenure band attrition table, promotion gap analysis, and the tenure × salary cross-tab all committed, with a one-paragraph summary of the "danger zone" combination.

days.title: What tenure analysis is
days.summary: From WHO leaves to WHEN they leave. Concept, then sketch the hypothesis.

items.title: What tenure analysis is
items.body:
## What it is
Last week you found *who* leaves (which departments, roles, pay levels). This week adds the **time dimension**: *when* in an employee's tenure is the risk highest? Tenure is `YearsAtCompany`, and the question is whether attrition risk is flat over time or spikes at certain points.

## Why it matters
The intervention changes completely depending on the answer. If risk spikes in the **first 1-2 years**, the problem is onboarding and early experience — fix the first 90 days. If it spikes around **years 3-5**, it's career stagnation — fix promotion and growth paths. A flat curve would mean tenure isn't the lever at all. You can't design a retention program until you know *when* people are at risk, and most companies have never actually looked.

## The discipline (again)
Form the hypothesis first, before plotting: most attrition research finds an **early-tenure spike** — new hires who realise it's not a fit and leave within two years. Write that prediction down, then test it.

## What it is
Bin `YearsAtCompany` into tenure bands and compute attrition rate per band — the cut-then-groupby move again, now revealing the *shape* of risk over time.

## Why it matters
This single table tests your hypothesis and usually delivers the project's most strategic insight: the **early-tenure spike**. If years 0-2 show double the base rate, the company is losing people it just spent money hiring and training — the most expensive kind of attrition. Quantifying exactly how steep that early spike is tells HR how much to invest in onboarding and the first-year experience.
