days.title: Stagnation: years since promotion
days.summary: A second time driver. Concept, video, then the promotion-gap effect.

items.title: Stagnation: years since promotion
items.body:
## What it is
`YearsSinceLastPromotion` measures career *stagnation* — how long since the employee last moved up. Group attrition rate by it (binned) to test whether being stuck drives people out.

## Why it matters
Stagnation is a distinct lever from tenure and pay. Someone can be well-paid and long-tenured but feel *stuck* — no promotion in five years — and that resentment is a classic exit trigger. If the data shows attrition climbing with the promotion gap, the fix isn't money, it's a visible growth path. Separating "stuck" from "underpaid" matters because the company would otherwise treat a career problem with a salary solution that won't work.

## The pattern
Same cut-then-groupby. Watch whether the rate rises as the promotion gap widens — and remember this is correlational (a confounder could lurk), so phrase findings as 'associated with'.

items.title: Aggregation with groupby() & agg()
items.why: Grouping by a binned driver, reused. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate by years-since-promotion
```python
df["promo_gap"] = pd.cut(df["YearsSinceLastPromotion"],
    bins=[-1, 1, 3, 7, 16], labels=["0-1", "2-3", "4-7", "8+"])
print(df.groupby("promo_gap")["left"].mean().round(3))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
promo_gap
0-1      0.182
2-3      0.121
4-7      0.151
8+       0.196
Name: left, dtype: float64
```
The pattern here is U-shaped, not a clean climb: high for the just-promoted-or-not-yet (0-1) and again for the long-stuck (8+). That nuance is itself a finding — it warns you *not* to claim a simple "longer gap = more attrition" line the data doesn't support. Honest analysis reports the shape it sees, including the messy ones.

cards.whenWrong: No — report what the data shows, even when it's messy.

The most precise, most actionable insight is usually an *interaction*: not "Sales Reps are risky" and "early tenure is risky" separately, but "**early-tenure Sales Reps**" — a specific cell that might be at 60% attrition. items.title: Tenure x salary interaction
items.body:
## What it is
Another interaction: cross tenure band against salary band. The hypothesis is that **long-tenured but low-paid** employees — people who stayed loyal yet never got paid up — carry a distinct resentment risk.

## Why it matters
Interactions keep finding what single variables miss. Low pay alone is risky (Week 10); long tenure alone is *protective* (the curve falls). But the *combination* — someone who's been loyal for years and is still underpaid — can be uniquely toxic, because it signals being taken for granted. If the grid confirms it, the fix is targeted equity raises for that specific cell, not an across-the-board change. This is how analysis gets surgical instead of blunt.

## The pattern
`pivot_table(index=tenure_band, columns=income_band, values="left", aggfunc="mean")`, then look for cells that are *worse than either band alone would predict*.

days.title: Plot a survival curve
days.summary: Visualise retention over tenure. Concept, video, then the cumulative-leave chart.

items.title: Plot a survival curve
items.body:
## What it is
A **survival curve** plots how the workforce thins out over tenure — the cumulative share still employed (or, flipped, the cumulative share who've left) by each year. It turns your tenure table into one intuitive picture.

## Why it matters
A curve communicates retention to non-analysts instantly in a way a table can't: a steep early drop *is* the early-tenure spike, visible at a glance. It's also the standard tool of professional people-analytics and medical statistics (where it's literally about survival), so producing one signals fluency. For your dashboard next week, this single chart can carry the whole tenure story.

## The pattern
Compute attrition rate per tenure year (or band), then plot it as a line; or compute the cumulative leave rate and plot that. Either way it's a `groupby` feeding a `matplotlib` line plot — Week 2's plotting skill on an HR question.

items.title: Matplotlib in 15 minutes
items.why: Plotting a line chart, reused for the survival curve. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate by each tenure year, plotted
```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
by_year = df.groupby("YearsAtCompany")["left"].mean()

by_year.plot(kind="line", marker="o", figsize=(9,5))
plt.axhline(df["left"].mean(), color="red", ls="--", label="base rate 16.1%")
plt.title("Attrition rate by years at company")
plt.xlabel("Years at company"); plt.ylabel("Attrition rate")
plt.legend(); plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("attrition_by_tenure.png", dpi=150); plt.show()
```
The output is a line that starts **high on the left (year 0-1)** and falls toward and below the red base-rate line as tenure grows — the early-tenure spike, now a picture anyone can read. Describe it in your notebook: "risk is concentrated in the first two years, then drops below average." That sentence + this chart is dashboard-ready.

cards.whenRight: Right — a steep early drop shows the spike instantly, no table needed.
cards.whenWrong: It does — the curve makes the early-tenure risk visible immediately.

cards.whenWrong: It does — interaction findings are the more sophisticated, shippable result.
cards.sim: v0.1 single drivers -> v0.2 interactions + timing

items.title: Acceptance — v0.2 is done when
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Notebook has: tenure-band attrition, promotion-gap effect, tenure x role and tenure x salary pivots, and the survival curve PNG.
[CODE] Commit and tag:
```
git add .
git commit -m "HR Attrition v0.2: tenure, interactions, survival curve"
git tag hr-v0.2
git push --tags
```
[WRITE] Drop your repo link in the dashboard check-in.

weeks.project: HR Attrition v0.2 — tenure analysis. Specific finding: at what tenure HR should intervene. Cross-tabs identify danger combinations.

resources.label: Bucketing continuous variables in Excel - 6 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 6 min. Turn YearsAtCompany into 0-1, 2-5, 6-10, 11+ buckets. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Cross-tabulation in Excel - 5 min - Leila Gharani (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 5 min. Tenure × Role pivot is just a cross-tab. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Cumulative chart in Excel - 5 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 5 min. Show attrition piling up over years. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Survival Analysis intuition in 12 min - StatQuest
resources.note: 12 min. The math behind 'how many years until 50% leave'. Optional, beautiful.

exercises: Add interaction with OverTime — does overtime hurt new hires more?
Compare tenure curves by Department side-by-side
Find the single ROLE × TENURE combo with the highest attrition
questions: What's a survival curve?
Why does promotion gap predict attrition?
How would you validate that tenure×salary interaction is real and not noise?
mastery_questions: Bucket YearsAtCompany into five bands using VLOOKUP or nested IF: 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, 6-10, 10+. Compute attrition rate per band. Paste the table sorted by tenure band. At which tenure band is attrition highest? Write one sentence about the intervention that makes most sense at that stage -- the intervention depends on the diagnosis (new employee confusion versus stalled career versus burnout).

Engineer the promotion gap variable: for each employee, compute (YearsInCurrentRole - median YearsInCurrentRole for their Job Role). Use AVERAGEIFS to compute the median within role (or MEDIAN with CTRL+SHIFT+ENTER in an array formula). Paste the formula. Now bucket employees into "behind peers" (gap > 1 year), "on pace" (-1 to 1 year), and "ahead" (<-1 year). Compute attrition rate per bucket. Is being "behind peers" on promotion associated with higher attrition? Paste the rates.

Build the tenure band × salary band cross-tab. Rows: tenure bands. Columns: salary bands from week 10 ($0-3K, $3K-6K, $6K-9K, $9K+). Cells: attrition rate. Add conditional formatting: red for rates above 30%, yellow for 20-30%, green below 20%. Paste the table. Write one sentence identifying the single highest-risk cell and what it means for HR prioritisation.

Compute the "survival" curve visually: what percentage of employees who started at the company are still employed at each tenure milestone (1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10 years)? This is a simple cumulative-attrition calculation, not a Kaplan-Meier survival model. For each milestone, compute: (employees with YearsAtCompany >= milestone) / total employees. Paste the curve values. The steepest drop -- where the largest percentage of employees leave -- is the priority window.

Write a one-paragraph "danger zone" summary for the HR Director. State specifically: the tenure band with highest attrition, the salary band that amplifies it, the promotion gap pattern, and one specific actionable recommendation. Paste the paragraph. "Employees in the 2-3 year tenure band earning under $3K per month who are more than 1 year behind their peers on promotion have a 48% attrition rate versus the 16% company average. Recommend: targeted promotion reviews for this cohort at the 18-month mark." is the level of specificity needed.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the array formula for computing group median in Excel -- the syntax is non-obvious and Claude writes it correctly. Test it for two job roles manually. Do NOT use Claude to write the "danger zone" paragraph. That paragraph requires reading the specific numbers from your cross-tab and synthesising them into a recommendation, which requires understanding what those numbers mean in an HR context.
weeks.pre_flight: Before building the pivot tables, compute the median YearsAtCompany for all employees who left (Attrition = "Yes") versus all who stayed (Attrition = "No"). Paste both medians. If they are more than 1 year apart, tenure is a meaningful predictor. If they are within 0.5 years, tenure alone is not discriminating well and you will need the interaction terms to find signal.
common_mistakes: Using arithmetic mean instead of median for the promotion gap benchmark. Salary and tenure data are often skewed by a few extreme values. The median YearsInCurrentRole for a job role is a more robust benchmark than the mean.

Counting attrition as a proportion of total company headcount instead of headcount within each tenure × salary cell. The denominator in the cross-tab must be the number of employees in that specific cell, not the total 1,470.

Building the cross-tab before checking cell sizes. Some cells in the tenure × salary grid may have fewer than 10 employees. Attrition rates computed on 3 employees are not reliable. Highlight cells with n < 10 and note them as "insufficient data."

Interpreting the promotion gap variable as causal. Employees who are "behind peers" on promotion may leave because they are being passed over, or they may be "behind peers" because they are already planning to leave and have stopped performing. The variable is a predictor, not necessarily a cause.

Not checking whether tenure band is ordinal-consistent. "2-3 years" followed by "4-5 years" should show a declining or U-shaped attrition rate in most datasets. A non-monotonic pattern (rate goes up at 4-5, down at 6-10, up again at 10+) usually means there are within-band confounders worth investigating.
weeks.debug_help: Array formulas for MEDIAN by group in Excel require pressing CTRL+SHIFT+ENTER instead of just ENTER. The formula appears in curly braces {=MEDIAN(IF(JobRole_col=A2, YearsInCurrentRole_col))}. If you just press ENTER, the formula returns the median of the whole column instead of the group median. The sign that this happened is that all job roles have the same median value. In Python, the group median is df.groupby('JobRole')['YearsInCurrentRole'].median() -- much cleaner.
stretch: Add the Manager relationship as a predictor. Compute attrition rate by YearsWithCurrManager (bucket into 0-1, 2-4, 5+). Do employees who have been with their current manager for less than 1 year have higher attrition? In most datasets, manager transitions are a leading indicator of attrition.

Compute a simple "attrition risk score" per employee: the sum of three binary flags (tenure in danger zone, salary in bottom band, promotion gap above 1 year). An employee with all three flags is high risk; with none, low risk. Compute the attrition rate for each score level (0, 1, 2, 3). Does the risk score discriminate well?

Research the Glassdoor employee satisfaction data for a company in the HR dataset's industry. Does the sentiment on Glassdoor align with the attrition patterns you found? This connection between internal data and external signals is the kind of analysis a senior HR analyst or people analytics team does.

weeks.title: HR Attrition v0.3: Memo + dashboard
weeks.context:
Two weeks of HR attrition analysis is now ready to be packaged into deliverables. This week follows the same pattern as weeks 8 and 9 of the Superstore project, but the audience is different and the difference matters.

The Superstore analysis went to a retail executive who cares about revenue and margin. The HR attrition analysis goes to an HR Director who cares about retention, wellbeing, and culture -- and who is sensitive to how findings are framed. An analysis that says "the Sales department has a 35% attrition rate" lands differently than "35% of the Sales team left last year, costing approximately $2.1M in replacement costs." The second framing connects the attrition data to a business number the HR Director can bring to the CFO.

The dashboard for HR analysis has a different design pattern from a retail dashboard. The headline KPI is not revenue or margin -- it is the overall attrition rate, the number of at-risk employees, and the estimated annual cost. The filter-driven design is more important here because HR Directors typically need to slice by Department, Role, and Manager separately. A slicer that lets them click on "Sales" and see all the charts update is more useful than six charts for six departments.

The recommendations this week must be specific and paired with difficulty-and-impact ratings. "Increase salaries" is a recommendation but not a useful one because it conflicts with "reduce costs" that the CFO will bring to the same meeting. "Conduct mandatory 18-month tenure reviews for employees in the Sales role earning under $3K per month" is specific enough to schedule, budget, and evaluate.

By Sunday: a one-page filter-driven Excel dashboard, the HR Director memo (two pages, with the cost framing), and the five-slide deck with recommendations rated by difficulty and impact.

days.title: What HR actually needs
days.summary: Same packaging discipline, different audience. HR acts on people, privacy, and fairness.

items.title: What HR actually needs
items.body:
## What it is
You're packaging two weeks of attrition analysis into deliverables — like Superstore W8-9, but the audience is **HR leadership**, and that changes everything you emphasise.

## Why it matters
A sales director wants dollars; HR wants **actions on people**, framed around **retention, privacy, and fairness**. They don't care about your p-value; they care "which team do we help, and is this analysis fair to individuals?" Lead with the at-risk group and the intervention, not the methodology. Get the framing wrong and a technically perfect analysis gets ignored — or worse, raises legal/ethical flags (you must never single out *named* employees as flight risks).

## The rule for this audience
Talk about *groups and drivers* (overtime, early-tenure Sales Reps), never individuals. Recommend *policy* (cap overtime, fix onboarding), and acknowledge fairness (is the model just flagging a protected group?).

items.title: See it worked (audience framing)
items.body:
## Same finding, wrong vs right framing
```text
WRONG (for HR): "Our model flags these 12 employees as 87% likely to quit."
   -> targets individuals; privacy + fairness nightmare; HR can't use it.

RIGHT (for HR): "Attrition concentrates in first-year Sales Reps and anyone on
   chronic overtime (3x the base rate). Recommend an onboarding revamp for new
   Sales hires and an overtime cap policy."
   -> targets drivers + policy; actionable and fair.
```
The data is identical; the framing is the deliverable.

cards.prompt: An HR deliverable should target groups/drivers and policy, not flag named individuals as flight risks.
cards.whenRight: Right — individual targeting raises privacy and fairness problems; recommend policy.
cards.whenWrong: It should — talk drivers and policy, never single out employees.
cards.sim: 'first-year Sales Reps + overtime' not '12 named people'

cards.prompt: HR leadership most wants to see your statistical methodology up front.
cards.whenRight: Correct — they want the at-risk group and the action; methods are backup.
cards.whenWrong: Not quite — lead with the group and the intervention, not the stats.
cards.sim: lead: 'who's at risk + what to do', not 'p<0.05'

items.title: Your turn — frame for HR
items.body:
[WRITE] Name your audience (HR director) and the one decision they need to make.
[WRITE] Restate your top finding as a group+policy recommendation, with no individual targeting.

days.title: Build the dashboard
days.summary: A dashboard is a glanceable answer: a few KPIs + a few charts. Concept + the layout.

items.title: Build the dashboard
items.body:
## What it is
A **dashboard** is a single screen that answers the recurring questions at a glance — here, 4 KPI numbers (overall attrition, highest-risk department, overtime effect, first-year rate) plus 3 charts (by department, by tenure, by role).

## Why it matters
HR will check this monthly; they need the state of attrition in five seconds, not a notebook to run. A dashboard turns your one-off analysis into a *living instrument*. The discipline is restraint: a dashboard with 20 charts is as useless as none — pick the few numbers that drive decisions and make them unmissable.

## The layout
Top row: 4 big KPI numbers. Below: 3 charts (the department bar, the tenure survival curve, the role hotspot). One screen, no scrolling. Build it in Excel/Sheets or a notebook — the principle is the same.

items.title: See it worked (dashboard spec)
items.body:
## A 4-KPI + 3-chart layout
```text
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|  Attrition 16.1%  | Sales 20.6% | Overtime 3x | Yr-1 36%  |   <- 4 KPIs
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
|  [Bar: attrition by dept]   [Line: survival curve]        |
|  [Bar: attrition by role (top 5, sorted)]                 |   <- 3 charts
+-----------------------------------------------------------+
```
Every element answers a question HR asks every month. Nothing decorative.

cards.prompt: A good dashboard shows the few numbers that drive decisions, not every chart you made.
cards.whenRight: Right — restraint is the skill; one glanceable screen.
cards.whenWrong: It is — a few decision-driving KPIs beat a wall of charts.
cards.sim: 4 KPIs + 3 charts, one screen, no scroll

items.title: Your turn — build it
items.body: [PRODUCE] Build a dashboard with 4 KPIs (overall attrition, top department, overtime ratio, year-1 rate) and 3 charts (by department, survival curve, top roles).

days.title: Make it interactive (filters)
days.summary: A filter lets HR answer their own follow-ups. Concept + how.

items.title: Make it interactive (filters)
items.body:
## What it is
Add a **filter** (a slicer in Excel/Sheets, or a dropdown) so the viewer can slice the dashboard — e.g. show attrition for one department or one job level — without asking you.

## Why it matters
Static dashboards generate a flood of "can you also show me just Sales?" requests. A filter hands that power to HR, which makes the dashboard *self-serve* — the difference between a report you maintain forever and a tool they own. Self-serve dashboards are what get adopted; static ones get a glance and forgotten.

## The pattern
One or two filters max (department, job level). More than that and it's a control panel nobody understands. Wire the charts to respond to the filter so the whole screen updates together.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
## Before vs after a filter
```text
STATIC:  one view; HR emails you "now show only R&D" -> you redo it
FILTERED: a [Department v] dropdown; HR picks R&D themselves; all charts update
```
One dropdown turns a report into a tool. Keep it to 1-2 filters so it stays legible.

cards.prompt: A filter/slicer lets the viewer answer their own follow-up questions, making the dashboard self-serve.
cards.whenRight: Right — self-serve is what gets a dashboard actually adopted.
cards.whenWrong: It does — filters hand the slicing power to the viewer.

items.title: Your turn — add a filter
items.body: [PRODUCE] Add a department (and/or job-level) filter that updates all charts at once. Keep it to 1-2 filters.

days.title: Write the HR memo
days.summary: Headline -> evidence -> recommendation, tuned for HR. Concept + template.

items.title: Write the HR memo
items.body:
## What it is
A one-page memo, same structure as always — **headline -> evidence -> recommendation** — but the recommendation is an HR *program*, and you add a fairness/privacy note.

## Why it matters
The memo is what circulates to people who never open the dashboard. For HR it must lead with the at-risk groups and the proposed intervention, cite the drivers as evidence, and proactively address fairness — because an attrition analysis that ignores fairness will (rightly) be challenged. Naming the trade-off yourself builds trust; hiding it destroys it.

items.title: See it worked (HR memo template)
items.body:
```text
## Headline
Attrition (16.1%) concentrates in first-year Sales Reps and employees on
chronic overtime (~3x base). Two targeted programs could cut it materially.

## Evidence
- Overtime: 30.5% attrition vs 10.4% (2.9x).
- Tenure: 36% leave in year 1; risk falls steeply after.
- Role: Sales Representatives 39.8% (2.5x base).

## Recommendation
- Onboarding revamp for new Sales hires (target the year-1 spike).
- Overtime policy review for chronic-OT employees.
- Fairness note: drivers are role/workload, not protected attributes; flag at
  the GROUP level only, never individuals.
```

cards.prompt: An HR memo should proactively address fairness/privacy, not hide the trade-off.
cards.whenRight: Right — naming it builds trust; an unaddressed fairness gap gets the work rejected.
cards.whenWrong: It should — surface fairness yourself; it's a feature, not a weakness.

items.title: Your turn — the memo
items.body: [WRITE] Write `HR-Memo` with headline/evidence/recommendation, an HR program recommendation, and a fairness/privacy note. Real numbers.

days.title: Export as a polished PDF
days.summary: Format signals credibility. Concept + spec.

items.title: Export as a polished PDF
items.body:
## What it is
Turn the memo and a dashboard snapshot into one clean PDF — headings, embedded charts, page numbers — the artefact you actually send.

## Why it matters
HR forwards PDFs to executives and legal; a raw notebook or markdown file won't travel. A polished PDF reads as authoritative and is the format decisions get made from. Same content, far more credible wrapper — and it's the deliverable that ends up in someone's "approved" folder.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
PDF contents (1-2 pages):
  - Title + your name/date
  - The memo (headline / evidence / recommendation / fairness note)
  - A dashboard snapshot image
  - Page numbers
Export from Word/Docs or notebook -> PDF, commit it to the repo.
```

cards.prompt: A polished PDF travels and reads as more credible than a raw notebook to HR/execs.
cards.whenRight: Right — it's the format decisions are forwarded and made from.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a clean PDF is the shippable, forwardable deliverable.
cards.sim: memo + dashboard snapshot -> one clean PDF

items.title: Your turn — export
items.body: [PRODUCE] Export a clean PDF containing the memo and a dashboard snapshot, with page numbers; commit it.

days.title: Build a 4-slide exec deck
days.summary: Compress to 4 slides for leadership. Concept, video, structure.

items.title: Build a 4-slide exec deck
items.body:
## What it is
A 4-slide version for an HR exec meeting: headline, two findings, recommendation. Same BLUF discipline as the Superstore deck, tighter.

## Why it matters
Leadership gets minutes, not a dashboard tour. Four slides force you to pick the two findings that matter (overtime, year-1 spike) and lead with the recommendation. The deck is how the analysis turns into an approved program in the room.

items.title: Tips for presenting data at work
items.why: Data-presentation habits for the deck. Optional.

items.title: See it worked (4-slide spine)
items.body:
```text
Slide 1  "Two fixable drivers explain most of our attrition"  (+ the ask)
Slide 2  Overtime: 3x the attrition rate  [bar chart]
Slide 3  Year-1 Sales Reps: the hotspot   [survival curve / role bar]
Slide 4  Recommendation: onboarding revamp + overtime policy; pilot + measure
```
Titles alone tell the story.

cards.prompt: A 4-slide HR deck should lead with the recommendation and carry only the 2 findings that matter.
cards.whenRight: Right — BLUF + the two strongest findings; cut the rest.
cards.whenWrong: It should — lead with the ask, show only the decisive findings.

items.title: Your turn — the deck
items.body: [PRODUCE] Build a 4-slide deck (headline + 2 findings + recommendation), titles that tell the story alone.

days.title: Ship v0.3
days.summary: Commit dashboard + memo + deck, tag hr-v0.3.

items.title: Ship v0.3
items.body:
## What it is
Ship the deliverables layer: dashboard, PDF memo, 4-slide deck. Tag `hr-v0.3`.

## Why it matters
v0.1 found drivers, v0.2 added timing/interactions, v0.3 makes it *consumable* by non-analysts. A project only creates value once decision-makers can act on it — packaging is not optional polish, it's where analysis becomes impact.

cards.prompt: Packaging analysis into a dashboard/memo/deck is where it becomes usable impact, not optional polish.
cards.whenRight: Right — unconsumed analysis creates zero value.
cards.whenWrong: It is — deliverables are how the work reaches decisions.
cards.sim: v0.3 = the analysis HR can actually act on

items.title: Acceptance — v0.3 is done when
items.body:
[PRODUCE] Dashboard (4 KPI + 3 charts + filter), PDF memo with fairness note, and a 4-slide deck.
[CODE] `git commit -m "HR Attrition v0.3: dashboard + memo + deck"`; `git tag hr-v0.3`; push.
[WRITE] Drop your repo link in the dashboard check-in.

weeks.project: HR Attrition v0.3 — full deliverable set. Dashboard, memo PDF, deck PDF. Specific recommendations to the HR Director.

resources.label: Excel dashboard from scratch - 25 min - Leila Gharani
resources.note: 25 min. Build a complete dashboard with KPIs, slicers, charts. The single most useful Excel video for Week 12.

resources.label: Excel slicers in 5 minutes (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 5 min. Clickable filters on dashboards. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: 1-page memo structure - 6 min HBR (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 6 min. The HBR template every consultant uses. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Cost of employee turnover - 7 min SHRM (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 7 min. Industry numbers ($15k-$30k per replacement). Use this for your dollar impact. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

exercises: Add a 'manager' filter (column ManagerID isn't in the dataset but you could simulate it)
Add overtime hours estimate
Quantify dollar impact: cost of replacing one employee × attrition count = X
questions: What's 'cost of attrition' and how would you estimate it?
Why is 'overall attrition rate' a weak headline?
Where could your recommendations backfire?
mastery_questions: Build the KPI banner: three cells in the dashboard header, formatted as large numbers with labels. Overall attrition rate, count of employees in the danger zone, and annual replacement cost (danger zone count × attrition rate × 1.5 × median salary). Paste the three values. These three numbers are the "executive summary" of the dashboard -- a VP who sees only the KPI banner should understand whether this is an emergency or a manageable situation.

Add a Department slicer connected to all charts. When the HR Director selects "Sales," every chart updates to show Sales-only data. Confirm the slicer works by selecting one department and checking that the attrition rate shown matches the week-10 pivot table for that department. Paste the confirmed rate. A dashboard with a broken filter is a dashboard the HR Director will stop using after the second mistake.

Write the HR Director memo. Two pages. Page 1: the overall attrition picture and the most important finding (the danger zone combination with the estimated cost). Page 2: three specific recommendations, each with: Action (what HR should do), Timing (when), Cost (rough estimate), and Expected Impact (reduction in attrition rate for the target cohort, with basis). Paste the three recommendations in the Page 2 format. Each recommendation should be implementable with a budget conversation and a calendar invite.

Build the five-slide deck using the same Pyramid Principle structure as the Superstore deck. Slide 1: the situation (attrition rate, cost) and the recommendation summary. Slides 2-4: the three supporting findings (department/role finding, tenure finding, danger zone finding). Slide 5: the three recommendations with difficulty and impact ratings (High/Medium/Low on each axis). Paste the five headline sentences. If any headline does not contain a number, it is not specific enough.

Rate the three recommendations on a 2x2 difficulty-impact matrix (Low-Medium-High for each axis). Paste the matrix. The recommendations that are Low Difficulty / High Impact are the ones the HR Director should do first. If all three are High Difficulty / High Impact, you have identified the real problem (the interventions that would work are expensive) and that is itself a finding worth stating in the deck.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the speaker notes for the HR Director deck. Paste each slide headline and the supporting data point, and ask for two to three sentences of speaker notes pitched to an HR Director who has not seen the analysis. Review the notes for accuracy -- Claude will occasionally generate plausible HR context that does not match your specific data. Flag any note that makes a claim you cannot support with your analysis.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Your audience is the Head of People. They want the 3 things they can change next quarter to reduce attrition by 5pp. The data is just the case. Have a recommendation. Be ready to defend assumptions on dollar impact when challenged.
weeks.pre_flight: Before building the dashboard, write the three numbers that belong on the KPI banner at the top: overall attrition rate, number of employees currently in the "danger zone" combination, and estimated annual replacement cost for that cohort. You need these numbers to be exact, not estimated, before you build the dashboard. Compute them now from the pivot tables.
common_mistakes: Building the dashboard before agreeing on the three KPI banner numbers. If the KPI numbers are wrong, the rest of the dashboard is built on a wrong foundation. Always compute the key numbers first, validate them, then build the visual.

Writing recommendations that are not actionable by the HR Director alone. "Fix the company culture" is not a recommendation an HR Director can implement with a quarterly budget. "Add one skip-level meeting per quarter for employees in their first two years" is.

Making the deck longer than five slides because the analysis is complex. The analysis being complex is not a reason to make the deck longer. It is a reason to be more selective about what goes on each slide. The appendix handles complexity; the main deck handles clarity.

Rating all recommendations as "High Impact" without evidence. The impact estimate for each recommendation should be grounded in data: "Promotion reviews at 18 months should reduce 2-3 year attrition by approximately 8-12 pp, based on the observed attrition rate in employees who received promotion within this period versus those who did not."

Not testing the slicer on all departments before the deliverable. A slicer that works for Sales but breaks for R&D (because R&D has a different data structure or fewer rows) is a broken dashboard. Test every filter option.
weeks.debug_help: Excel slicers require that all charts and pivot tables using the slicer share the same data source (the same named table or PivotCache). If adding the slicer only affects some charts, right-click the slicer, select "Report Connections," and confirm all relevant pivot tables are checked. Charts built directly from ranges (not from pivot tables) cannot be connected to slicers -- they must be rebuilt as pivot charts connected to the pivot table.
stretch: Add a "manager risk report" tab to the dashboard: a list of managers whose direct reports have above-average attrition rates, sorted by the magnitude. The most useful version of an attrition analysis for an HR Director is not company-wide patterns but the specific managers and teams where intervention is most urgent.

Compute the total three-year cost of attrition if no action is taken: (danger zone employees × current attrition rate × replacement cost) summed over three years, assuming the population stays constant. This number, alongside the cost of the interventions, makes the business case for the recommended actions.

Read McKinsey's "The State of People Analytics" report (usually published annually, findable with a search). Note which attrition metrics the most advanced companies track and compare to what you built this week. The gap is the next analytical capability to develop.

weeks.title: HR Attrition v1.0: Ship + retro
weeks.context:
Three weeks of HR attrition analysis ends this week the same way the Superstore project ended: with a deliberate close, a retrospective, and a demo video that proves the project works.

The demo video is two to three minutes. Open the dashboard, click the Department slicer to show Sales, call out the attrition rate and the cost number, click to R&D and note the contrast. Switch to the deck and walk through the three recommendations. That is the demo. It is not a tutorial, not a presentation -- it is a record that the thing works, that you can speak intelligently about what it shows, and that a stranger watching can follow the logic without you in the room to explain.

The SQL version of the HR analysis is the second deliverable this week. Every pivot table and calculated metric from weeks 10 through 12 should be expressible as a SQL query. The attrition rate by department is a GROUP BY with a CASE-based COUNTIF equivalent. The tenure bucketing is a CASE statement. The cross-tabulation is a conditional aggregation. Adding these queries to queries.sql completes the pattern established in week 5 -- every analysis exists in both the spreadsheet and the SQL layer.

The retrospective this time should note what you did differently in Project 2 based on the week-9 retro from Project 1. If you wrote "I will write slide headlines before building charts" in the week-9 retro and you actually did that this time, note it. If you wrote it and reverted to the old habit, note that too -- the honest version is more useful than the flattering version.

By Sunday: demo video committed or linked, SQL version of all key metrics in queries.sql, RETRO.md written and committed, and the repo README updated to reflect the final Project 2 state.

days.title: List the rough edges
days.summary: Audit everything before the final ship. Concept + worked audit.

items.title: List the rough edges
items.body:
## What it is
Audit every HR artefact — notebook, dashboard, memo, deck — and write down every rough edge: errors, inconsistent numbers, unclear labels, anything half-done.

## Why it matters
"Shipping" means finishing. A written punch list converts "basically done" into completable tasks and catches the embarrassing inconsistency (a number that disagrees between memo and dashboard) before a stakeholder does. You can't fix what you haven't named.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
- notebook: cell 9 errors on Restart & Run All
- dashboard: overtime KPI says 2.9x, memo says 3x -> reconcile
- deck slide 3 chart unlabeled
- README missing 'how to run'
```
Specific, checkable items.

cards.prompt: A written rough-edge list before the final ship prevents shipping half-done work.
cards.whenRight: Right — it turns 'basically done' into finishable tasks.
cards.whenWrong: It does — listing gaps makes finishing concrete.

items.title: Your turn — audit
items.body: [WRITE] List every rough edge across the HR notebook, dashboard, memo, and deck. Specific; don't fix yet.

days.title: Fix them
days.summary: Work the list; polish compounds. Concept + checklist.

items.title: Fix them

## What it is

## Why it matters
Showing the *same* analysis in pandas and SQL across two projects proves durable tool-fluency. It also makes your portfolio searchable by the SQL keyword recruiters filter on. The attrition rate is just `AVG(CASE WHEN Attrition='Yes' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)`.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Attrition rate by department, in SQL
```sql
SELECT Department,
       AVG(CASE WHEN Attrition='Yes' THEN 1.0 ELSE 0 END) AS attrition_rate,
       COUNT(*) AS employees
FROM hr GROUP BY Department ORDER BY attrition_rate DESC;
```
```
Department              attrition_rate  employees
Sales                   0.206           446
Human Resources         0.190            63
Research & Development  0.138           961
```
Matches your pandas Week 10 result exactly — `AVG(CASE WHEN ...)` is the SQL of the 0/1 `left` mean.

weeks.title: Web scraping for business data
weeks.context:
Both projects so far used clean, pre-packaged datasets. Most real-world analyst work does not. Prices change on competitor websites. Product listings appear and disappear. Public datasets are updated irregularly. The skill of pulling structured data from unstructured web pages -- web scraping -- is not a developer skill, it is an analyst skill, and it is used constantly by anyone doing competitive intelligence, market research, or pricing analysis.

The context this week is competitor price tracking. You will choose a public website that lists prices -- a retailer's product page, a job board's salary listings, a real estate listing site, or a public government data portal -- and write a BeautifulSoup scraper that extracts the relevant fields, appends a row to a CSV with a timestamp, and can be run again tomorrow to capture the new prices.

The ethics of scraping matter and they are not complicated. Do not scrape sites that explicitly forbid it in their robots.txt. Do not scrape at a rate that burdens the server (add a 1-second delay between requests). Do not scrape personal data. Public product prices, public job listings, and public government data are generally acceptable. If you are unsure, read robots.txt before writing any code.

BeautifulSoup is the tool. It parses HTML and lets you find elements by tag, class, or ID. The workflow: requests.get(url) to fetch the page, BeautifulSoup(html, 'html.parser') to parse it, soup.find_all('div', class_='price') to extract the relevant elements. The elements change when the site redesigns -- your scraper is fragile by design, and knowing that it is fragile is part of the skill.

By Sunday: a competitor-price-tracker repo with a working scraper, an append-only history.csv that has at least 2 rows (two runs on different days), and a simple Google Sheets dashboard visualising the price history.

days.title: Why analysts scrape

items.title: Why analysts scrape
items.body:
## What it is
Both projects used clean, packaged datasets. Most real analyst work doesn't get that gift — the data you need (competitor prices, listings, public stats) lives on **web pages**, not in a tidy CSV. **Web scraping** is programmatically extracting that data into a table you can analyse.

## Why it matters
Scraping unlocks questions no packaged dataset can answer: "how did our competitor's prices move this month?" There's no CSV for that — but there's a web page, updated daily, that you can turn into one. The analyst who can build their own dataset isn't limited to questions someone already answered. It's the difference between consuming data and *sourcing* it.

## The shape of it
Three steps: fetch the page (HTML), parse it to pull the values you want, and write them to a DataFrame/CSV. This week: ethics first, then BeautifulSoup, then schedule it, then analyse the result.

```text
raw HTML         --BeautifulSoup-->  the values you want (price, title)

```
You're manufacturing a dataset that didn't exist before.

days.title: Scrape ethically (robots.txt)

items.title: Scrape ethically (robots.txt)
items.body:
## What it is
Before scraping, check the site's **robots.txt** (e.g. `example.com/robots.txt`) and Terms of Service. Respect what's disallowed, identify yourself, and don't hammer the server.

## Why it matters
Scraping carelessly can be rude (overloading a small site), against ToS, or in some cases legally risky. A professional scrapes *politely*: obeys robots.txt, rate-limits requests (a pause between them), scrapes only public data, and never republishes copyrighted content. This isn't just ethics — a scraper that gets your IP banned is also useless. Doing it right keeps the data flowing and keeps you out of trouble.

items.title: See it worked (the rules)
items.body:
```text
[ ] read example.com/robots.txt  -> respect Disallow paths
[ ] add a delay between requests (time.sleep(1-2s)) -> don't hammer
[ ] set a real User-Agent identifying you
[ ] scrape only PUBLIC data; don't log in and scrape private pages
[ ] don't republish copyrighted content; use it for analysis
```

cards.whenWrong: It is — robots.txt + a delay between requests is basic scraping etiquette.

items.title: BeautifulSoup hello world
items.body:
## What it is
`requests` fetches a page's HTML; **BeautifulSoup** parses it so you can pull out the elements you want by their tag/class. Together they're the standard beginner scraping toolkit.

## Why it matters
This is the core skill: turning a wall of HTML into the three values you actually care about. Once you can `find`/`find_all` the right elements, scraping any simple page is the same pattern — inspect the page to find the tag, then extract it. Start on a scraping-practice site (like books.toscrape.com), never a site that forbids it.

items.title: Easy web scraping with Python & BeautifulSoup
items.why: Fetch + parse a page live, then the code below is review. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Fetch a page and extract data
```python
import requests
from bs4 import BeautifulSoup

url = "https://books.toscrape.com/"        # a scraping-practice site
html = requests.get(url, headers={"User-Agent": "learn-scraper"}).text
soup = BeautifulSoup(html, "html.parser")

books = soup.find_all("article", class_="product_pod")
for b in books[:3]:
    title = b.h3.a["title"]
    price = b.find("p", class_="price_color").text
    print(title, "|", price)
```
Output:
```
A Light in the Attic | £51.77
Tipping the Velvet | £53.74
Soumission | £50.10
```
You just turned a web page into structured data. `find_all` got every book block; inside each, `find`/attribute access pulled the title and price.

days.title: Schedule the scraper
days.summary: Automate it to build a time series. Concept + how.

items.title: Schedule the scraper
items.body:
## What it is
Save your scraper as a `.py` script and run it automatically on a schedule (Windows Task Scheduler / cron) so it captures the data **over time** — appending each run's results with a date.

## Why it matters
A one-off scrape is a snapshot; a *scheduled* scrape is a **time series**, which is where the real insight lives ("prices rose 12% this month"). Automating it also means the dataset builds itself while you sleep — the analyst's leverage. The key habit: stamp each row with the scrape date and append, never overwrite.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```python
# scraper.py — append today's prices with a date stamp
import pandas as pd, datetime as dt
rows = scrape()                       # your Day-3 function -> list of dicts
df = pd.DataFrame(rows)
df["scraped_on"] = dt.date.today()
df.to_csv("prices.csv", mode="a", header=False, index=False)  # APPEND
```
```text
Schedule it: Windows Task Scheduler (daily) or cron `0 9 * * *`.
Each run adds today's rows -> a growing time series.
```

cards.prompt: Scheduling the scraper and appending date-stamped rows turns snapshots into a time series.
cards.whenRight: Right — the trend over time is where the insight is.
cards.whenWrong: It does — scheduled + appended = a growing time series.

cards.prompt: Each scheduled run should overwrite the previous file.
cards.whenRight: Correct — append with a date stamp; overwriting destroys the history you need.
cards.whenWrong: No — append; overwriting kills the time series.

items.title: Analyze price changes
items.body:
## What it is
Once the scraper has run a few times, your scraped CSV is an ordinary dataset — load it and use the pandas you already know to compute changes over time.

## Why it matters
This closes the loop: the scraping was only ever in service of a *question*. Now you answer it with groupby/sort/pct_change — the exact skills from Project 1, on data you sourced yourself. The point of the week wasn't scraping for its own sake; it was being able to answer a question that had no CSV.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Biggest movers between two scrape dates
```python
df = pd.read_csv("prices.csv", parse_dates=["scraped_on"])
pivot = df.pivot_table(index="title", columns="scraped_on", values="price")
pivot["change_%"] = (pivot.iloc[:, -1] / pivot.iloc[:, 0] - 1) * 100
print(pivot.sort_values("change_%", ascending=False).head(3).round(1))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
title            2026-06-01  2026-06-08  change_%
Widget A              19.99       24.99      25.0
Gadget B              50.10       55.10       10.0
Book C                51.77       50.77      -1.9
```
The scrape became a question answered: Widget A jumped 25% this week. Standard pandas — the data source was the only new part.

mastery_questions: Fetch the target page with requests.get and parse it with BeautifulSoup. Find the HTML element containing the price (use the browser Inspector to identify the tag and class). Paste the soup.find_all() call and the first element it returns. If the first element is not the price, the selector is wrong -- try a different class or ID. Write one sentence about how you identified the correct selector.

Extract the price, product name, and timestamp from the page. Write the extracted data to history.csv using pandas with mode='a', header=not os.path.exists(). Paste the CSV row. Run the script a second time and paste both rows -- the append-only pattern should produce two rows, not overwrite the first. If the file has only one row after two runs, the mode='a' logic is wrong.

Add a rate-limiting delay (time.sleep(1)) between requests if you are scraping multiple pages. Add a User-Agent header to the requests.get call that identifies your scraper honestly: headers={'User-Agent': 'price-tracker-bot/1.0 (contact: youremail)'}. Paste the requests.get call with headers. Explain in one sentence why a User-Agent matters -- it lets the site operator identify your traffic and contact you if you are causing issues.

Build a Google Sheets dashboard connected to the history.csv data. The dashboard has two elements: a chart showing price over time (x-axis: timestamp, y-axis: price) and a KPI showing the change from the first recorded price to the most recent. Paste the Sheets URL (set sharing to "anyone with link can view"). The chart proves the scraper is collecting data across time.

Write the README for the competitor-price-tracker repo. Include: what site is being tracked and why (one sentence), how to run the scraper (one command), what fields are collected, the robots.txt check result, and a note about rate limiting. Paste the README. A README that does not mention the ethical/legal context of web scraping is an incomplete README for a scraping project.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the BeautifulSoup selector for your specific target element. Paste the HTML snippet from the Inspector (right-click the element, copy outerHTML) and ask "write a BeautifulSoup expression to extract the price from this HTML." Test the generated selector on your fetched page and verify it returns the correct value. Do NOT use Claude to determine whether a site's scraping is ethically permissible -- that requires reading the actual robots.txt and terms of service, which Claude cannot access in real time.
weeks.pre_flight: Choose your target site before writing any code. Check robots.txt (add /robots.txt to the domain). Read the relevant Disallow rules. If the paths you want to scrape are disallowed, choose a different site. Write down the specific URL you will scrape and the three data fields you will extract. Opening the URL in the browser and finding the exact HTML element that contains the price (right-click > Inspect) takes 5 minutes and prevents an hour of confused Beautiful Soup debugging.
common_mistakes: Not reading robots.txt before scraping. Scraping a site that disallows it is a legal and ethical issue, not just a technical one. Some companies monitor for scrapers and send cease-and-desist letters. Read robots.txt first, always.

Not adding a delay between requests when scraping multiple pages. A scraper that hits 50 pages per second produces traffic indistinguishable from a DDoS attack. time.sleep(1) is the minimum; time.sleep(random.uniform(1, 3)) is better because it does not produce a metronomic traffic signature.

Using append mode without checking whether the CSV exists, resulting in the header row being written on every run. Use if not os.path.exists(filename) to write the header only on the first run. Or use pd.DataFrame.to_csv(mode='a', header=not os.path.exists(filename)).

Building the scraper around a specific class name that changes when the site updates its CSS. Scraper fragility is inherent -- document that the scraper targets a specific HTML structure and include the date it was written, so future debuggers know to re-inspect the page if it breaks.

Storing the scraped data only in memory and not persisting it. A scraper that prints the price but does not write to a file is not a price tracker -- it is a one-time lookup. Persistence (the append-only CSV) is the whole point.
weeks.debug_help: Two common BeautifulSoup failure modes. First: soup.find_all() returns an empty list. Either the class name is wrong (check the exact class in the Inspector -- classes often have multiple words separated by spaces, and BeautifulSoup requires a list or the exact string), or the content is loaded by JavaScript (BeautifulSoup only parses static HTML). For JavaScript-rendered pages, use playwright or selenium instead of requests. Second: the price text includes "$" and "," characters that prevent conversion to float. Use .text.strip().replace('$','').replace(',','') before float() conversion.
stretch: Add email alerting: if the price drops below a threshold you define, send yourself an email using smtplib. This converts the tracker from a data collection tool into an automated monitoring tool -- the kind of system a pricing analyst at an e-commerce company would build.
Schedule the scraper to run daily using cron or Task Scheduler. After one week, plot the 7-day price history. Seven days of actual price movement data is more interesting than two rows of test data.

Add a second competitor site to the tracker and compare prices side by side in the Sheets dashboard. Two-column price comparison over time is the actual output a purchasing manager or competitive intelligence analyst would use.

weeks.title: Project 3 — Marketing Funnel v0.1
weeks.context:
Project 3 uses real e-commerce data. The Olist dataset is a public Brazilian e-commerce dataset containing 100,000 orders from 2016 to 2018, with tables for orders, order items, payments, reviews, customers, sellers, and products. It is multi-table, which is meaningfully different from the single-table datasets you have worked with so far -- the analysis requires JOINs before it can answer most questions.

The marketing funnel question is: at each stage of the purchase journey, how many potential customers make it to the next stage, and where are the biggest drops? In a traditional e-commerce context the funnel is: visitor → product view → add to cart → checkout → purchase. The Olist data does not have visitor and view data, but it has order status (pending, processing, shipped, delivered, cancelled) and review data, which gives you a funnel from order placed to delivery to satisfaction.

The delivery-to-review connection is the most interesting question in this dataset. Olist is a marketplace -- sellers ship directly to customers, and delivery experience is entirely in the hands of third-party logistics. Review scores are the customer satisfaction signal. The question is whether delivery time (purchase date to delivery date) predicts review score. If it does, then late deliveries are not just an operational problem -- they are a reputation problem, and the analysis can quantify how much each day of delay costs in terms of review score.

This week is the exploration phase. You are not building the final dashboard yet -- you are understanding the schema, building the order status funnel, and computing the delivery-to-review correlation as a first signal. By the end of the week you will know whether there is a real story here, and you will have the building blocks for the deeper analysis in week 16.

By Sunday: schema diagram (a visual or written description of all seven tables and their join keys), the order status funnel computed, the delivery time distribution computed, and the delivery-review correlation with a scatter plot committed to a new olist-funnel-analysis repo.

days.title: What is a funnel?
days.summary: Project 3: e-commerce. Concept of a conversion funnel.

items.title: What is a funnel?
items.body:
## What it is
Project 3 uses **Olist** — a public Brazilian e-commerce dataset: ~100,000 orders (2016-2018) across multiple tables (orders, items, customers, reviews, payments). A **funnel** tracks how customers progress through stages (ordered -> shipped -> delivered -> reviewed), and where they drop off.

## Why it matters
Every drop-off is lost money, and the funnel shows *exactly where*. "We lose customers somewhere" is useless; "8% of orders never reach delivered" points at a fixable operations problem. Funnel thinking is the core of marketing and e-commerce analytics — and Olist's multi-table structure forces you to practise the `merge` skill on realistic, messy, relational data.

## What's new here
Unlike Superstore (one table), Olist is **relational** — answers require *joining* tables. That's this project's growth edge: real data is normalised across tables, and you'll live in `merge`.

items.title: See it worked (the funnel)
items.body:
```text
ORDERED ---> APPROVED ---> SHIPPED ---> DELIVERED ---> REVIEWED
 100%         98%           95%          92%            ~70% leave a review
              \ where do orders fall out? each gap = lost value
```
The whole project answers: where do customers drop, and why?

cards.prompt: A funnel tracks customers through stages and shows exactly where they drop off.
cards.whenRight: Right — each drop-off gap is a fixable loss.
cards.whenWrong: It does — the funnel localises where value leaks.

cards.prompt: Olist is a single flat table like Superstore.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it's relational (orders, items, customers, reviews); you must merge.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — Olist spans multiple tables; joining is the new skill.

items.body:

[WRITE] One question about where customers drop off that this project could answer.

items.title: Get the Olist data
items.body:
## What it is
Download the Olist dataset (Kaggle) — it's several CSVs (orders, order_items, customers, products, reviews). Load the ones you need into separate DataFrames.

## Why it matters
Working with multiple files is itself the realistic skill: you load each table, inspect it, and understand how they connect (via key columns like `order_id`, `customer_id`) before you can answer anything. Rushing to analysis before understanding the table relationships is how people produce wrong joins and wrong numbers.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Load the core tables
```python
import pandas as pd
orders   = pd.read_csv("olist_orders_dataset.csv")
reviews  = pd.read_csv("olist_order_reviews_dataset.csv")
customers= pd.read_csv("olist_customers_dataset.csv")
print(orders.shape, reviews.shape, customers.shape)
print(orders.columns.tolist()[:6])
```
Output (illustrative):
```
(99441, 8) (99224, 7) (99441, 5)
['order_id', 'customer_id', 'order_status', 'order_purchase_timestamp',
 'order_approved_at', 'order_delivered_customer_date']
```
~99k orders. Note the key columns (`order_id`, `customer_id`) — those are how you'll join the tables. The timestamp columns are how you'll measure each funnel stage.

cards.prompt: Olist comes as multiple CSVs that connect through key columns like order_id and customer_id.
cards.whenRight: Right — those keys are how you'll join the tables.
cards.whenWrong: It is — the keys link the separate tables for merging.

cards.prompt: You should start analysing before understanding how the tables relate.
cards.whenRight: Correct — map the keys/relationships first or you'll build wrong joins.
cards.whenWrong: No — understand the relationships first to avoid wrong merges.
cards.sim: know the keys before you join

days.title: Understand the schema (join tables)
days.summary: Relational data needs joins. Concept, video, code with output.

items.title: Understand the schema (join tables)
items.body:
## What it is
Map how the tables connect, then `merge` them on their keys to assemble the wide table you need (e.g. orders + their review scores + customer location).

## Why it matters
This is the project's core skill: real questions ("do late deliveries get worse reviews?") need columns from *different* tables, so you must join them correctly. Choosing the right join type (`how="left"` to keep all orders) and the right key is where accuracy is won or lost — a wrong join silently drops or duplicates rows and quietly corrupts every number downstream.

items.title: Merge and concat DataFrames — a quick guide
items.why: Joining tables on a key, applied to Olist. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Join orders to their reviews
```python
om = orders.merge(reviews[["order_id","review_score"]], on="order_id", how="left")
print(om.shape)
print(om[["order_id","order_status","review_score"]].head(3))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
(99992, 9)
        order_id        order_status  review_score
0  e481f51cbdc54...     delivered           4.0
1  53cdb2fc8bc7d...     delivered           4.0
2  47770eb9100c2...     delivered           5.0
```
Now each order carries its review score — a question that needed two tables, answered by one `merge`. `how="left"` kept every order, even those with no review (NaN score).

cards.prompt: Answering Olist questions usually requires merging columns from different tables on a key.
cards.whenRight: Right — relational data means join first, analyse second.
cards.whenWrong: It does — you assemble the wide table with merge before analysing.

cards.prompt: `how="left"` on a merge keeps all rows from the left table even if there's no match.
cards.whenRight: Right — left join preserves every order, NaN where no review.
cards.whenWrong: It does — left keeps all left rows; unmatched get NaN.

items.title: Funnel step: orders by status
items.body:
## What it is
The `order_status` column (delivered, shipped, canceled, unavailable…) is the funnel in one column. `value_counts` shows how many orders sit at each stage — and how many fell out.

## Why it matters
This is the funnel's headline: the share of orders that actually reach *delivered* vs those canceled/unavailable. A 3% cancellation rate might be fine; 15% is an operations fire. One `value_counts` quantifies the leak you'll spend the rest of the project explaining.

items.title: Aggregation with groupby() & agg()
items.why: Counting/grouping a category, applied to status. Optional.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Orders by status
```python
print(orders["order_status"].value_counts())
print((orders["order_status"]=="delivered").mean().round(3))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
delivered      96478
shipped         1107
canceled         625
unavailable      609
invoiced         314
processing       301
...
0.970
```
Read it: **97% of orders reach delivered** — a healthy funnel — but ~1,200 canceled/unavailable orders are the leak worth investigating. The base completion rate (97%) is the number every later cut compares against.

cards.prompt: order_status value_counts is the funnel: it shows how many orders reach each stage.
cards.whenRight: Right — the status column IS the funnel in one place.
cards.whenWrong: It is — value_counts on status quantifies each stage.

cards.prompt: A 97% delivered rate means there's nothing in the funnel worth investigating.
cards.whenRight: Correct — the ~1,200 canceled/unavailable orders are still a leak to explain.
cards.whenWrong: Not quite — even a small drop-off is lost value worth a look.

days.title: Time to delivery
days.summary: Compute a duration from timestamps. Concept + code with output.

items.title: Time to delivery
items.body:
## What it is
Subtract the purchase timestamp from the delivery timestamp to get **delivery time in days** for each order — a derived metric from two date columns.

## Why it matters
Delivery speed is a top driver of e-commerce satisfaction, and it sets up tomorrow's question (does slow delivery hurt reviews?). The skill is **datetime math**: parse the timestamp columns to real dates, subtract, and convert to days. Getting date handling right is a rite of passage — strings won't subtract; you must parse first.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Delivery time in days
```python
for col in ["order_purchase_timestamp","order_delivered_customer_date"]:
    orders[col] = pd.to_datetime(orders[col])

orders["delivery_days"] = (orders["order_delivered_customer_date"]
                           - orders["order_purchase_timestamp"]).dt.days
print(orders["delivery_days"].describe().round(1))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
count    96476.0
mean        12.1
std          9.5
min          0.0
50%         10.0
max        209.0
Name: delivery_days, dtype: float64
```
Read it: average delivery **~12 days**, median 10, but a long tail (max 209!). Those extreme deliveries are prime suspects for bad reviews — the link you test next. Note `pd.to_datetime` first: you can't subtract date *strings*.

cards.prompt: To compute delivery time you must parse the timestamp columns to datetimes first, then subtract.
cards.whenRight: Right — pd.to_datetime, then subtract, then .dt.days.
cards.whenWrong: It is — strings won't subtract; parse to datetime first.

cards.prompt: A long tail (max 209 days) of delivery times is worth flagging as a driver of bad reviews.
cards.whenRight: Right — extreme deliveries are prime suspects for low scores.
cards.whenWrong: It does — the slow tail is exactly what to test against reviews.
cards.sim: mean 12d but max 209d -> investigate the tail

items.title: Your turn — delivery time
items.body:
[CODE] Parse the timestamps and compute `delivery_days`; print describe().
[WRITE] One sentence: average delivery time and the worst case.

days.title: Do late deliveries hurt reviews?
days.summary: Link delivery time to review score. Concept + code with output.

items.title: Do late deliveries hurt reviews?
items.body:
## What it is
Combine the last two days: bin `delivery_days` and compute the average `review_score` per band. This tests the hypothesis that slow delivery -> worse reviews.

## Why it matters
This is the project's first real *finding* — a relationship across two derived/joined metrics, exactly the kind of cross-table insight Olist exists to teach. If reviews crater past a delivery-time threshold, that's an actionable operations target ("get every order under N days"). It's also a correlation, so phrase it carefully (slow delivery is *associated with* low scores).

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Review score by delivery-time band
```python
om = orders.merge(reviews[["order_id","review_score"]], on="order_id", how="left")
om["band"] = pd.cut(om["delivery_days"], bins=[-1,5,10,20,40,300],
                    labels=["0-5","6-10","11-20","21-40","40+"])
print(om.groupby("band")["review_score"].mean().round(2))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
band
0-5      4.31
6-10     4.18
11-20    3.79
21-40    3.951
40+      2.28
Name: review_score, dtype: float64
```
Clear signal: reviews fall from **4.3 (fast) to 2.3 (40+ days)**. Slow delivery is strongly associated with bad reviews — an actionable finding: cutting the long delivery tail would lift scores. (Association, not proof of cause — but a strong lead.)

cards.prompt: Binning delivery time and averaging review score per band tests the slow-delivery -> bad-review idea.
cards.whenRight: Right — cut + groupby on the joined table reveals the relationship.
cards.whenWrong: It does — band the duration, average the score per band.

cards.prompt: A clear band relationship proves slow delivery CAUSES bad reviews.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it's a strong association; phrase as 'associated with', not 'causes'.
cards.whenWrong: Careful — it's correlation; a confounder could contribute.
cards.sim: strong lead, not proof of cause

items.title: Your turn — the finding
items.body:
[CODE] Merge reviews, bin delivery_days, and average review_score per band.
[WRITE] One sentence: how do reviews change with delivery time?

mastery_questions: Load all seven CSVs into pandas. Run df.shape for each and paste a table: table name, rows, columns, join key. Confirm the join keys are consistent: every order_id in olist_order_items appears in olist_orders. Use set(items['order_id']).issubset(set(orders['order_id'])) to check. If it returns False, you have orphaned records. Write one sentence about whether orphaned records are a data quality issue or expected behaviour in this dataset.

Build the order status funnel. The olist_orders table has order_status values including "delivered," "shipped," "canceled," "unavailable," etc. Compute the count and percentage of orders in each status. Plot as a horizontal bar chart sorted by count. Paste the chart and the top-3 status values with their percentages. Write one sentence about what "unavailable" means in this context -- is it a cancelled order, a product that went out of stock, or something else?

Compute delivery time per order: (order_delivered_customer_date - order_purchase_timestamp) in days. Exclude orders where delivery date is null (undelivered). Paste the mean, median, P25, P75, and P95 delivery time. What does the P95 delivery time (the slowest 5% of orders) suggest about the worst-case customer experience in this marketplace?

Join orders to reviews on order_id. Compute the correlation between delivery time (days) and review_score. Paste the correlation coefficient and a scatter plot (delivery days on x, review score on y). Is the correlation negative (longer delivery → lower score)? Write one sentence about the magnitude: a correlation of -0.2 explains 4% of the variance in review scores, which means delivery time is a predictor but not the dominant one.

Write the schema diagram. For each table: table name, number of rows, key columns, and the join key to the central orders table. You can write this as a markdown table or as a text-based diagram. Paste it. A clear schema diagram is the deliverable that lets future-you (or a collaborator) understand the data structure without re-reading all seven CSVs.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to write the JOIN query that merges orders, order_items, and order_reviews into a single analysis-ready DataFrame. The join path is orders → order_items on order_id (to get product information), and orders → order_reviews on order_id (to get review scores). Paste the generated merge code and verify the resulting DataFrame has the expected number of rows and columns. Do NOT use Claude to interpret the delivery-review correlation -- that interpretation requires looking at the actual scatter plot and the domain context of a Brazilian e-commerce marketplace.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Your audience for the funnel work is a marketing director with a $200k budget. They want to know: 'Which 2 things should I spend this on to maximize repeat purchase?' Lead with that. Method second.
weeks.pre_flight: Download all seven Olist CSV files from Kaggle (search "Brazilian E-Commerce Public Dataset by Olist"). Before writing any code, draw the schema on paper: which tables have foreign keys to which other tables? The central table is olist_orders_dataset -- every other table joins to it on order_id or customer_id or seller_id. Write out the join path from orders to reviews (orders → reviews on order_id) and from orders to products (orders → order_items → products on order_id then product_id). Knowing the join path before querying saves an hour of confusion.
common_mistakes: Joining tables without checking for duplicate join keys. If a single order has multiple items (which it does in Olist), joining orders to order_items produces one row per item, not per order. After a join, run .shape to check whether the row count increased -- if it did, the join multiplied rows.

Treating null delivery dates as zero delivery time. Orders that have not been delivered yet have null delivery dates. Subtracting null from a date in pandas returns NaT. Filtering to delivered orders (order_status == 'delivered') before computing delivery time prevents this.

Computing the funnel as a percentage of the total before establishing whether the statuses are mutually exclusive. In Olist, each order has one status -- they are mutually exclusive. But in other funnel datasets, a customer might appear in multiple stages. Always check the uniqueness of the group column before computing funnel percentages.

Plotting a scatter plot of 100,000 points without any transparency. A dense scatter plot is an opaque black rectangle. Use plt.scatter(alpha=0.05) to make individual points visible even when overlapping. For very large datasets, a hexbin plot (plt.hexbin) or a 2D density plot is more informative than a scatter.

Interpreting the delivery-review correlation as causal without checking other explanations. Product quality, seller reputation, price expectations, and customer demographics all affect review scores. A -0.2 correlation with delivery time is a signal, not a complete explanation.
weeks.debug_help: Datetime subtraction in pandas requires both columns to be datetime type. If order_purchase_timestamp is object (string), df['order_purchase_timestamp'] = pd.to_datetime(df['order_purchase_timestamp']) converts it. After conversion, the subtraction produces a Timedelta, not an integer -- convert to days with .dt.days. If the result has negative values, one of the date columns has data quality issues (delivered before purchased) -- filter those out and note them in a comment.
stretch: Compute the delivery time distribution separately for each Brazilian state (customer_state column in the customers table). Do some states have significantly longer delivery times than others? The geographic distribution of delivery times is an operational finding that Olist's logistics team would act on.

Find the top 10 product categories by order volume. Do any categories have systematically lower review scores? A category where reviews are consistently low despite reasonable delivery times suggests a product quality or expectation-mismatch issue rather than a logistics issue.

Read Olist's publicly available blog posts about their platform (available on Medium). Compare what they say about their marketplace model and logistics partnerships to what the data shows. The combination of public narrative and internal data analysis is how business analysts build a complete picture.

weeks.title: Olist Funnel v0.2: Cohorts + repeat purchase
weeks.context:
Last week you found that delivery time correlates with review score. This week you move to a different marketing question: do Olist customers come back, and if so, what predicts whether they will?

Cohort analysis is the analyst's tool for measuring retention. A cohort is a group of customers who made their first purchase in the same time period -- the January 2017 cohort, the Q2 2017 cohort. By tracking each cohort through time, you can see whether customers acquired in different periods retained at different rates, and whether the business is getting better or worse at keeping customers over time.

The repeat purchase rate for Olist is surprisingly low. In most marketplaces, 30-40% of customers make a second purchase within 12 months. Olist is a B2C marketplace where many purchases are one-time (furniture, specific electronics, gifts) rather than recurring (groceries, consumables). The repeat rate you compute will probably be below 10%, and that is not necessarily a failure -- it is the nature of the product category mix. Knowing this matters for the marketing memo, because strategies optimised for repeat purchase (loyalty programmes, subscription offers) are less relevant for a low-repeat-purchase marketplace than strategies optimised for acquisition and first-purchase satisfaction.

The behavioral comparison between one-time and repeat buyers is where the interesting signal lives. Do repeat buyers rate deliveries higher? Do they come from different product categories? Do they have faster delivery times? These questions connect the delivery-review analysis from week 15 to the retention question.

By Sunday: a cohort retention matrix showing month-1 and month-3 retention by acquisition cohort, the overall repeat purchase rate computed correctly, the behavioral comparison table, and a one-paragraph write-up of the key finding for the marketing funnel memo.

days.title: What's a cohort?
days.summary: Group customers by when they joined. Concept, video, why it matters.

items.title: What's a cohort?
items.body:
## What it is
A **cohort** is a group of customers defined by a shared start — usually their **first-purchase month**. Cohort analysis tracks each group's behaviour over the months that follow, to see if and when customers come back.

## Why it matters
A single "repeat rate" hides whether retention is improving or decaying over time. Cohorts answer the sharper question: "of customers who first bought in January, how many bought again in month 2, month 3…?" — and whether newer cohorts retain better than older ones (is the business getting healthier?). It's the gold-standard retention tool in marketing and SaaS, and the reason VCs ask for "cohort curves".

## The shape
Rows = cohort (first-purchase month); columns = months since first purchase; cells = % of that cohort still active. A retention *matrix*.

items.title: Customer cohort analysis: retention & churn
items.why: What a cohort/retention matrix is. Optional.

items.title: See it worked (the matrix)
items.body:
```text
                months since first purchase
cohort        0     1     2     3
2017-01     100%   18%   12%    9%
2017-02     100%   21%   14%   10%
2017-03     100%   24%   15%  ...
            ^ everyone active at month 0; decay across the row;
              compare DOWN a column -> are newer cohorts retaining better?
```
Reading down a column tells you if retention is improving cohort over cohort.

cards.prompt: A cohort groups customers by a shared start (e.g. first-purchase month) to track them over time.
cards.whenRight: Right — same-start groups, followed across later months.
cards.whenWrong: It is — cohorts = customers grouped by when they began.

cards.prompt: A single overall repeat rate tells you everything a cohort matrix would.
cards.whenRight: Correct — only cohorts reveal the time-shape and whether retention is improving.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — one number hides the decay curve and cohort-over-cohort trend.
cards.sim: cohorts show decay + are newer cohorts better?

days.title: First-purchase month per customer
days.summary: Define each customer's cohort. Concept + code with output.

items.title: First-purchase month per customer
items.body:
## What it is
For each customer, find their **first** order's month — that label *is* their cohort. It's a groupby-min on the purchase date, formatted to year-month.

## Why it matters
Every later step depends on this label being right: assign the wrong cohort and the whole matrix is wrong. It's also a clean example of deriving a per-customer attribute (their start) and joining it back to every order — the same merge-the-label-back pattern from the CLV week.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Each customer's cohort month
```python
o = orders.merge(customers[["customer_id","customer_unique_id"]], on="customer_id")
o["order_month"] = o["order_purchase_timestamp"].dt.to_period("M")

first = o.groupby("customer_unique_id")["order_month"].min().rename("cohort")
o = o.merge(first, on="customer_unique_id")
print(o[["customer_unique_id","order_month","cohort"]].head(3))
```
Output (illustrative):
```
   customer_unique_id  order_month   cohort
0  0a1b...             2017-05      2017-05
1  0a1b...             2017-08      2017-05   <- same customer, cohort stays 2017-05
2  7c2d...             2017-06      2017-06
```
Note the second row: a customer's cohort is their *first* month and never changes, even on later orders. `to_period("M")` buckets dates to year-month; `groupby-min` finds the start; merge stamps it on every order.

cards.prompt: A customer's cohort is their FIRST purchase month and stays fixed on all later orders.
cards.whenRight: Right — groupby-min on date defines it once, merged onto every order.
cards.whenWrong: It is — the first month is the cohort, constant across later orders.
cards.sim: later orders keep the original cohort month

cards.prompt: Each order should get a cohort equal to that order's own month.
cards.whenRight: Correct — the cohort is the customer's FIRST month, not each order's month.
cards.whenWrong: No — cohort = the customer's first month, fixed for all their orders.
