mastery_questions: Create a dbt project (dbt init superstore_dbt). Configure the BigQuery connection in profiles.yml. Write the source definition in models/sources.yml: name the source "superstore_raw" and the table "superstore." Run dbt debug to confirm the connection works. Paste the last 5 lines of dbt debug output. A successful connection shows "Connection test: OK."

Write the staging model (stg_orders.sql): SELECT order_id, PARSE_DATE('%m/%d/%Y', order_date) as order_date, customer_id, customer_name, segment, country, region, category, sub_category, SAFE_CAST(sales AS FLOAT64) as sales, SAFE_CAST(profit AS FLOAT64) as profit, SAFE_CAST(discount AS FLOAT64) as discount FROM {{ source('superstore_raw', 'superstore') }}. Run dbt run --select stg_orders. Paste the row count from the BigQuery console. Confirm it matches the original CSV row count.

Write the intermediate model (int_customer_metrics.sql): aggregate from stg_orders to the customer level -- total sales, total profit, order count. Write the mart model (mart_category_margins.sql): compute Profit Margin by Category and Sub-Category. Run dbt run. Paste the results of SELECT * FROM mart_category_margins ORDER BY margin DESC LIMIT 5. Confirm it matches the week-1 Excel analysis.

Add two dbt tests in models/schema.yml: unique and not_null on order_id in stg_orders. Add at least one custom test: a range check that profit margin is between -1 and 1 (a margin outside that range indicates a data error). Run dbt test. Paste the test results. If a test fails, investigate -- do any orders have a profit margin outside the expected range?

Generate dbt docs (dbt docs generate) and start the documentation server (dbt docs serve). Navigate to the lineage graph in the browser. Paste a screenshot description or the URL if you have deployed it. The lineage graph shows stg_orders → int_customer_metrics and stg_orders → mart_category_margins, with the source node upstream. Write one sentence about what the lineage graph communicates that a plain SQL file does not.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the schema.yml file for your dbt models -- the structure of columns, tests, and descriptions is mechanical and Claude writes it correctly. Verify that the column names in schema.yml match the actual column names in your SQL models exactly (case-sensitive). Do NOT use Claude to write the mart model SQL. Writing the profit margin aggregation in BigQuery SQL yourself is the step that proves you can translate between the Excel, pandas, and SQL versions of the same analysis.
weeks.pre_flight: Create a Google Cloud account (free tier) and a BigQuery project before writing any code. Upload the Superstore CSV to a BigQuery dataset using the BigQuery console's import feature. Run SELECT * FROM your_dataset.superstore LIMIT 5 in the BigQuery console to confirm the data loaded correctly. Note any column names that changed during import (BigQuery may modify column names with spaces or special characters). Write down any name changes -- you will reference them in the dbt source configuration.
common_mistakes: Using direct BigQuery table references (project.dataset.table) inside dbt models instead of the {{ source() }} or {{ ref() }} Jinja macros. Hardcoded references bypass dbt's dependency resolution and break the lineage graph. Always use {{ source() }} for raw tables and {{ ref() }} for other dbt models.

Writing dbt models that include both transformation logic and business logic in the same file. The staging model should handle only type casting, column renaming, and basic filtering. Business logic (computing margins, aggregating to customer level) belongs in intermediate or mart models. This separation makes debugging much faster.

Running dbt run without first running dbt compile to check for syntax errors. dbt compile generates the SQL that will be executed without actually running it -- a fast way to catch Jinja or SQL syntax errors before they run against BigQuery.

Not setting the materialisation strategy. By default, dbt models are views, not tables. For the mart layer, set materialized='table' in the model config so downstream users query a pre-computed table rather than a view that re-runs the full query on every access.

Committing the profiles.yml file that contains BigQuery credentials. profiles.yml contains your service account credentials and must never be committed. Add it to .gitignore immediately after creation.
weeks.debug_help: The most common dbt BigQuery connection error is "google.auth.exceptions.DefaultCredentialsError." This means the BigQuery connection is not authenticated. Fix: run gcloud auth application-default login from the terminal (requires the gcloud CLI installed), then re-run dbt debug. The second most common error is "dbt.exceptions.CompilationException: Found a cycle." This means one of your {{ ref() }} calls creates a circular dependency between models. Draw the dependency graph on paper to find the cycle.
stretch: Add a dbt snapshot to track slowly-changing dimensions (e.g., if a customer's segment changes over time, the snapshot captures the history). Snapshots are an advanced dbt feature that appear in production data warehouses at companies like GitLab and Shopify.

Deploy the dbt docs to a static site (GitHub Pages or Netlify). The hosted documentation makes your data catalogue publicly browsable -- recruiters who see a link to a hosted dbt data catalogue in your README notice it.

Add a dbt package (from hub.getdbt.com): dbt_utils is the most useful first package, adding helper macros for surrogate keys, date spines, and safe division. Add it to packages.yml, run dbt deps, and use one macro from dbt_utils in a model.

weeks.title: Capstone v0.1: Multi-source dashboard scope
weeks.context:
The capstone is the fourth and final project in the data analysis roadmap. Unlike the previous three (Superstore, HR Attrition, Olist), this one uses data you find yourself -- ideally data from a domain you find genuinely interesting or that is relevant to a role you are targeting.

The specific deliverable this week is a scoped spec and a working data model. The capstone is a four-page Excel dashboard that tells a coherent story using data from at least three different sources. "At least three sources" means you need to merge tables you did not design -- the real-world analyst problem is that the data relevant to a business question is never conveniently in one table.

The multi-source merge is the analytical challenge. A retail capstone might merge: public store transaction data, publicly scraped competitor prices, and economic indicator data from the World Bank. A healthcare capstone might merge: hospital outcome data, publicly available demographic census data, and published insurance enrollment figures. A football (soccer) capstone might merge: match result data, player transfer fee data, and league attendance figures. The merge is where you build the star schema: one central "facts" table (orders, matches, outcomes) joined to multiple "dimension" tables (stores, players, hospitals).

The Power Pivot approach in Excel handles this without writing code. Power Pivot is Excel's in-memory analytics engine -- it lets you define relationships between tables (like SQL JOINs) and then use DAX formulas to create measures that span the relationships. For analysts who live in Excel, Power Pivot is the bridge to the same analytical capabilities that SQL offers without leaving the spreadsheet.

By Sunday: a scoped SPEC.md, all three data sources downloaded and inspected, the star schema drawn on paper and digitised, and the first KPI computed across at least two sources (proving the merge works).

days.title: What a capstone is
days.summary: Your own multi-source project, scoped by you. Concept + what makes it different.

items.title: What a capstone is
items.body:
## What it is
The capstone is the fourth and final DA project — and the first one **you** define. Unlike Superstore, HR, and Olist (handed to you), here you choose the question, combine **multiple data sources**, and build a polished multi-page dashboard end to end.

## Why it matters
A capstone is what a hiring manager actually looks for: proof you can take an *ambiguous* business problem, scope it, source and model the data, analyse it, and present a decision — without anyone holding your hand. The three guided projects taught the skills; the capstone proves you can apply them *unprompted*, which is the entire difference between someone who can follow a tutorial and someone who can do the job.

## What makes it harder (and better)
Multiple sources (you must join/relate them), self-defined scope (you decide what's worth answering), and a real deliverable (a 4-page dashboard a stakeholder could use). Ambiguity is the point — embrace it.

items.title: See it worked (capstone shape)
items.body:
```text
A good capstone:
  QUESTION: one clear business question you chose
  SOURCES:  2-3 datasets you combine (e.g. sales + weather + holidays)
  MODEL:    related tables joined on keys
  OUTPUT:   a 4-page interactive dashboard + a CEO memo + a demo
  PROOF:    "I scoped, sourced, modelled, analysed, and presented this myself."
```
The guided projects were practice; this is the performance.

cards.prompt: The capstone's value is proving you can scope and execute an ambiguous problem unprompted.
cards.whenRight: Right — that self-direction is what employers screen for.
cards.whenWrong: It is — handling ambiguity end to end is the capstone's whole point.
cards.sim: tutorials teach skills; the capstone proves judgement

cards.prompt: A capstone should use a single, pre-cleaned dataset like the earlier projects.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it should combine multiple sources you scope and model yourself.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — multi-source + self-defined scope is what makes it a capstone.

items.title: Your turn — pick the problem
items.body: [WRITE] Propose a capstone: one business question and 2-3 data sources you'd combine to answer it.

days.title: Write the SPEC
days.summary: A one-page plan before you build. Concept + template.

items.title: Write the SPEC
items.body:
## What it is
A one-page **spec**: the question, the audience, the data sources, the key metrics, and what 'done' looks like — written before you build anything.

## Why it matters
Scoping is where capstones live or die. Without a spec you'll wander, over-build, and never finish. The spec is a contract with yourself that defines the finish line and keeps you from scope-creep. Professionally, the analyst who writes a crisp spec before diving in is the one who delivers on time — it's a senior habit.

items.title: See it worked (spec template)
items.body:
```text
## Capstone SPEC
Question: "How do weather and holidays affect store sales, and which stores
           are most weather-sensitive?"
Audience: regional operations director.
Sources:  daily sales (synthetic), public weather API, public holiday calendar.
Metrics:  sales, weather-sensitivity index, holiday lift.
Done when: a 4-page dashboard + CEO memo answer the question with a recommendation.
```
One page. It defines the finish line.

items.title: Your turn — the spec
items.body: [WRITE] Write a one-page capstone spec: question, audience, sources, metrics, and 'done when'.

days.title: Build the dataset
days.summary: Source or synthesise realistic multi-source data. Concept + how.

items.title: Build the dataset
items.body:
## What it is
Assemble your data: combine real public datasets, or generate a realistic **synthetic** dataset (with pandas/`numpy`) when real data isn't available — covering the sources your spec named.

## Why it matters
Sourcing/creating data is a real skill (you practised it scraping). A good synthetic dataset must be *realistic* — sensible distributions, plausible relationships (sales actually dip in bad weather) — so the analysis has something true to find. Junk data makes for junk insight; building believable data is itself analytical thinking.

items.title: See it worked (synthetic data)
items.body:
```python
import pandas as pd, numpy as np
n = 2000
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "date": pd.date_range("2024-01-01", periods=n, freq="h"),
    "store": np.random.choice(["A","B","C"], n),
    "temp_c": np.random.normal(18, 8, n).round(1),
})
# build a REAL relationship: colder -> fewer sales
df["sales"] = (200 - 3*np.maximum(0, 10 - df["temp_c"]) + np.random.normal(0,20,n)).round(0)
print(df.head(3))
```
```
                 date store  temp_c  sales
0 2024-01-01 00:00:00     B    12.4  188.0
1 2024-01-01 01:00:00     A     6.1  168.0
2 2024-01-01 02:00:00     C    21.7  205.0
```
The baked-in relationship (cold -> lower sales) is what your analysis will 'discover'.

cards.prompt: A synthetic dataset must have realistic distributions and relationships for the analysis to find anything true.
cards.whenRight: Right — bake in real relationships, or there's nothing to discover.
cards.whenWrong: It must — believable data is what makes the analysis meaningful.
cards.sim: cold weather -> lower sales, built into the data

days.title: Diagram the schema
days.summary: Map how the sources relate. Concept + how.

items.title: Diagram the schema
items.body:
## What it is
Draw a simple **schema diagram**: each table, its key columns, and the relationships (which key joins to which). A box-and-line sketch is enough.

## Why it matters
With multiple sources, you must know how they connect *before* you join, or you'll produce wrong merges and silently wrong numbers. The diagram is your map — it forces you to identify the keys (date, store_id) that link the sources and to spot a missing link before it bites. Data modelling is a core, often-overlooked analyst skill.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
[ sales ]----store_id----[ stores ]
    | date
[ weather ]--date+location--/
[ holidays ]--date----------/
Keys: date links sales<->weather<->holidays; store_id links sales<->stores.
```
Now you know exactly which columns to merge on.

cards.prompt: A schema diagram identifies the keys that link your sources before you attempt joins.
cards.whenRight: Right — knowing the keys prevents wrong merges.
cards.whenWrong: It does — the diagram maps the join columns up front.

items.title: Your turn — the diagram
items.body: [PRODUCE] Sketch a schema diagram of your sources, marking the key columns that join them.

days.title: Build the data model
days.summary: Join the sources into one analysable model. Concept + code with output.

items.title: Build the data model
items.body:
## What it is
Execute the joins from your diagram to produce the unified, analysis-ready table(s) — `merge` the sources on their keys (the skill from the Olist week, now on your own data).

## Why it matters
This is where the multi-source nature pays off: a question like 'are cold-weather days worse for store B?' needs sales *and* weather joined. The model is the foundation everything downstream sits on, so getting the joins (and join types) right is critical — a wrong join here corrupts every KPI.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Join sales to weather on date
```python
model = sales.merge(weather, on="date", how="left")
print(model.shape)
print(model[["date","store","temp_c","sales"]].head(2))
print("nulls after join:", model["temp_c"].isna().sum())
```
```
(2000, 6)
                 date store  temp_c  sales
0 2024-01-01 00:00:00     B    12.4  188.0
1 2024-01-01 01:00:00     A     6.1  168.0
nulls after join: 0
```
Clean left join, no orphaned rows — the model is ready. Always check post-join nulls/row-count to confirm the join behaved.

cards.prompt: After joining sources, checking row count and post-join nulls confirms the merge behaved correctly.
cards.whenRight: Right — a bad join shows up as exploded rows or unexpected nulls.
cards.whenWrong: It does — verify the join didn't drop/duplicate/orphan rows.
cards.sim: check shape + isna() after every merge

items.body: [CODE] Merge your sources per the schema; print the shape and confirm post-join nulls are as expected.

days.title: First KPIs
days.summary: Define the headline metrics. Concept + code with output.

items.title: First KPIs
items.body:
## What it is
Compute the first version of your capstone's headline KPIs — the 3-4 numbers your dashboard will lead with, derived from the joined model.

## Why it matters
KPIs are the spine of the dashboard; defining them now (and confirming they compute) means the rest of the build is just presenting them well. Choosing the *right* few KPIs — the ones that actually answer your spec's question — is the judgement that separates a focused dashboard from a cluttered one.

items.title: See it in code (with output)
items.body:
## Headline KPIs from the model
```python
print("Total sales:", model["sales"].sum())
cold = model[model["temp_c"] < 10]["sales"].mean()
warm = model[model["temp_c"] >= 10]["sales"].mean()
print(f"Cold-day avg: {cold:.0f}  Warm-day avg: {warm:.0f}")
print(f"Weather sensitivity: {(warm-cold)/warm:.1%} drop on cold days")
```
```
Total sales: 392140.0
Cold-day avg: 171  Warm-day avg: 199
Weather sensitivity: 14.1% drop on cold days
```
There's your headline KPI and your spec's answer in one: sales drop ~14% on cold days. The dashboard will showcase this.

cards.prompt: Choosing the few KPIs that answer your spec's question keeps the dashboard focused, not cluttered.
cards.whenRight: Right — KPIs should map to the question, not show everything.
cards.whenWrong: It does — spec-aligned KPIs are the focused dashboard's spine.
cards.sim: weather sensitivity KPI answers the spec

mastery_questions: Download all three data sources. For each, run: row count, column names, key join column, and any data quality issues you notice immediately (nulls, format inconsistencies, date format mismatches). Paste a three-row table: source name, rows, key column, one data quality note. The data quality note prevents the surprise that arrives in week 23 when the merge fails because the join key is formatted differently across sources.

Draw the star schema: one central facts table, connected to dimension tables via foreign keys. Digitise it as a markdown table or an image. For each relationship, specify: which column in the facts table joins to which column in the dimension table, and whether it is a one-to-many relationship (one store, many transactions) or a many-to-one. Paste the schema.

Load all three sources into Excel and define the relationships in Power Pivot (Data > Manage Data Model > Create Relationship). Paste the relationship definitions. Now write one DAX measure that uses values from two different tables: for example, SUM([sales]) / RELATED(target[monthly_target]) for a sales-vs-target KPI. Run the measure in a pivot table. Paste the output.

Compute the first headline KPI that requires the multi-source merge. This should be the KPI that could not be computed from any single source alone. Paste the computation and the value. Write one sentence about why this KPI requires the merge -- what does each source contribute that the other does not have?

Write SPEC.md. Required: the central question, the three data sources with URLs, the star schema description, four dashboard page titles (one per page you will build in weeks 23 and 24), the headline KPI for each page, and the out-of-scope list. Paste the file. A complete spec prevents the scope creep that derails most capstone projects.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the DAX measure syntax for your first headline KPI. DAX is a language with enough quirks (context transitions, CALCULATE vs FILTER, ALL vs ALLEXCEPT) that the first few measures are faster to write with Claude's help. Read the generated measure and understand what each function does before using it. Do NOT use Claude to design the star schema -- the schema design requires understanding what questions you are trying to answer, which requires domain knowledge of your chosen capstone domain.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Before writing one line of code for the capstone: who is the audience for the final deliverable, and what decision will they make differently after seeing it? If you can't answer both in one sentence each, the scope is wrong.
weeks.pre_flight: Choose the capstone domain before opening Excel. Write three candidate domains and for each: the central question, the three data sources (with URLs confirming the data is publicly downloadable), and the KPI you will compute on the first page of the dashboard. The domain where you can name all three data sources with specific URLs is the one to build. The domain where you say "I think there is data for this" is not ready.
common_mistakes: Choosing data sources that cannot be merged because they have no common join key. A public sales dataset and a weather dataset can be merged on date. A sales dataset and a demographic dataset can be merged on geographic code. Before finalising the domain choice, confirm the join key exists in all sources.

Using a many-to-many relationship in the star schema without an intermediate bridge table. Power Pivot handles one-to-many and many-to-one relationships cleanly but requires a bridge table for many-to-many. If your schema has a many-to-many relationship, add a bridge table before building the data model.

Downloading data but not checking its licence. Some public datasets are licensed for research use only, not for commercial publication. Check the licence before committing the data to a public GitHub repo. Link to the source rather than committing the file if the licence is unclear.

Setting up the star schema in Power Pivot before confirming the join key values match between tables. If the customer_id in the facts table uses a different format than in the customers dimension table (integer vs string, upper vs lower case), the relationship will be silently inactive and measures will return unexpected values.

Treating the capstone scope as fixed once the spec is written. The spec is a living document until week 24. If week 23 reveals that one of the data sources is unusable, update the spec and note the change. An honest updated spec is better than continuing to build against a known-broken assumption.
weeks.debug_help: Power Pivot relationships fail silently when the join key has duplicates on both sides (many-to-many). The symptom is a pivot table that shows the same value for every row or that returns BLANK for measures. Fix: check whether the dimension table's key column is unique (one row per key value). If it is not, aggregate the dimension table to the correct grain before defining the relationship. Also check that both columns are the same data type -- a text customer_id on one side and an integer customer_id on the other side will not match.
stretch: Import the data model from Excel Power Pivot into Power BI Desktop. Power BI reads the Excel data model directly. Note whether the relationships you defined in Power Pivot transfer correctly, and whether the DAX measures produce the same values. This cross-tool compatibility is useful to document because many employers use both Excel and Power BI.

Add a date dimension table to the data model: a table with one row per day, with columns for year, quarter, month, week, and day-of-week. Join it to the facts table on the date column. A proper date dimension enables time intelligence DAX functions (YTD, MTD, same-period-last-year) that require a contiguous date spine.

Write a one-paragraph "data sourcing" section for the SPEC.md that explains how the data was obtained, any transformations applied before loading, and the data quality limitations of each source. Transparency about data quality is what separates a credible analysis from an unexamined one.

weeks.title: Capstone v0.2: Pages 1 + 2
weeks.context:
The data model is built. This week you build the first two pages of the capstone dashboard and confirm that the cross-page filter architecture works before building pages 3 and 4.

Multi-page dashboards in Excel have a specific design pattern that is different from single-page dashboards. Each page answers a different level of question: page 1 is the executive summary (the three KPIs a CEO would check every Monday morning), page 2 is the operational detail for one department or function, page 3 is a deeper dive on the most important finding from page 2, and page 4 is the cohort or trend analysis that gives the time dimension. Every page connects to the others through shared slicers.

The KPI band design is the visual pattern for the executive summary page. A KPI band has three elements: the current value (large, prominent), the change from a reference period (green up-arrow or red down-arrow with a percentage), and a small sparkline showing the trend. Three KPI bands, arranged horizontally across the top of page 1, give a CEO everything they need to know in 10 seconds: is the business up or down on the three metrics that matter, and are the trends consistent with the numbers?

Cross-page slicer architecture means that when the user clicks "Q3 2024" on the slicer, every chart on every page updates. This requires all pivot tables to share the same PivotCache in Excel. Setting this up before building any charts saves the frustration of rebuilding them later.

By Sunday: pages 1 and 2 built, cross-page slicers working for at least one slicer, and the visual style consistent (same font, same colour palette, same border style on every chart) across both pages.

days.title: Page 1 layout
days.summary: Design the overview page first. Concept + layout.

items.title: Page 1 layout
items.body:
## What it is
Page 1 is the **overview** — the executive summary of your capstone: KPI band on top, then the 2-3 charts that answer the headline question, designed before you build anything.

## Why it matters
Designing the layout first (on paper or in your head) prevents the common mistake of building charts and cramming them in afterwards. Page 1 must answer the spec's question at a glance; everything else is detail pages. A deliberate layout is what makes a dashboard feel designed, not assembled.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
PAGE 1 — OVERVIEW
+-----------------------------------------------------+
| KPI: Total Sales | Cold-day drop 14% | Top store    |   <- KPI band
+-----------------------------------------------------+
| [trend: sales over time]  [bar: sales by store]     |
| [the headline chart: sales vs temperature]          |
+-----------------------------------------------------+
```
The headline question answered on one screen.

The row of big-number KPI tiles at the top of page 1 — your headline metrics, formatted large and clear.

## Why it matters
The KPI band is the first thing anyone reads; it must communicate the state of the business in seconds. Clean formatting (rounded numbers, clear labels, maybe a trend arrow) is what makes it glanceable. This is the same KPI skill from the dashboard weeks, now leading your capstone.

```text
Big, rounded, labelled. Optional: a small up/down arrow vs last period.
```

items.title: Trend chart
items.body:
## What it is
A line chart of your key metric over time — the standard 'is it going up or down?' visual on page 1.

## Why it matters
Time trends answer the question every stakeholder asks first. A clean trend (labelled axes, maybe a reference line for average or target) instantly shows direction and seasonality — and seasonality might itself be a finding (sales dip every cold month).

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
sales
  |      /\      /\
  |   /\/  \  /\/  \      <- monthly sales, with cold-month dips visible
  | /        \/        \
  +------------------------> time
Add a dashed average line so 'above/below normal' is obvious.
```

cards.prompt: A trend chart answers 'is the metric going up or down?' and can reveal seasonality.
cards.whenRight: Right — direction + seasonality at a glance.

days.title: Segment breakdown
days.summary: Break the metric by a key dimension. Concept + how.

items.title: Segment breakdown
items.body:
## What it is
A bar chart breaking your metric by a key dimension (store, region, product) — showing *where* the totals come from.

## Why it matters
A total hides the distribution; the breakdown shows which segment drives or drags it. It's the chart that turns 'sales are $392k' into 'Store C drives 40% of it' — the actionable detail. This is groupby-then-bar, the most common analytical visual.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
Store C ############## 40%
Store A #########      28%
Store B ########       24%  ...
Sorted descending so the biggest contributor is obvious.
```

cards.prompt: A segment breakdown shows which part of the business drives the total a single KPI hides.
cards.whenRight: Right — it turns a total into 'where it comes from'.
cards.whenWrong: It does — the breakdown localises what drives the KPI.

days.title: Page 2: the detail view
days.summary: A drill-down page. Concept + layout.

items.title: Page 2: the detail view
items.body:
## What it is
Page 2 is the **detail** page — a deeper, filterable table/charts for someone who wants to dig past the overview (e.g. sales detail by store and day).

## Why it matters
Two-page structure separates the *summary* (page 1, for executives) from the *detail* (page 2, for analysts who want specifics). This layering is what makes a dashboard serve multiple audiences without cluttering the front page. The overview answers 'what'; the detail answers 'show me'.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
PAGE 2 — SALES DETAIL
+-----------------------------------------------------+
| [filterable table: date, store, temp, sales]        |
| [small multiples: sales by store, one mini-chart each]|
+-----------------------------------------------------+
For the analyst who wants the specifics behind page 1.
```

cards.prompt: A detail page lets users dig past the overview without cluttering page 1.
cards.whenRight: Right — summary up front, detail behind it.
cards.whenWrong: It does — layering serves execs and analysts separately.
cards.sim: page 1 = what; page 2 = show me the detail

days.title: Link the filters
days.summary: One filter controls both pages. Concept + how.

items.title: Link the filters
items.body:
## What it is
Wire a shared filter (e.g. store, date range) so selecting it updates *both* pages consistently — the cross-page filter architecture.

## Why it matters
Inconsistent filters are confusing and erode trust ('why does page 2 show different numbers?'). Linked filters make the whole dashboard feel like one coherent tool, and let a user 'follow' a selection across the overview and detail. Getting this architecture right early prevents painful rework later.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
[ Store: C v ] [ Date: 2024 v ]   <- one filter panel
   -> Page 1 KPIs + charts update
   -> Page 2 table + charts update to the SAME selection
Consistency across pages = trust.
```

cards.prompt: Linked cross-page filters keep numbers consistent and make the dashboard feel like one tool.
cards.whenRight: Right — inconsistent filters erode trust; linking fixes it.
cards.whenWrong: It does — shared filters give a coherent, trustworthy dashboard.

mastery_questions: Build the KPI band for the first headline metric. Three cells formatted in a wide rectangle: the large current-period value, the change arrow and percentage (using an IF formula for the arrow character and conditional formatting for the colour), and the sparkline. Paste the formulas for the change cell and the threshold formatting rule. Confirm the arrow changes direction and colour when you change the reference period.

Build the second KPI band and confirm the three KPI bands are visually consistent: same font size, same border, same colour for the change arrows. Add a "as of" date label below each band so a reader knows which period is current. Paste the layout description. Consistency is the property that makes a dashboard look professional rather than assembled.

Build the first chart on page 2 (the operational detail page). It should show a breakdown of the headline metric from page 1 by one dimension (product category, department, geography). Paste the chart type and the finding it reveals. The finding on page 2 should add information beyond the page 1 KPI -- not "sales are up" (that is on page 1) but "sales are up in the North, down in the South" (that is the page 2 value add).

Connect the slicer to all charts on both pages. In Excel: right-click the slicer, select Report Connections, and check all pivot tables that the slicer should control. Test by clicking a filter value and confirming both page 1 KPI bands and the page 2 chart update simultaneously. If any chart does not update, its pivot table is not connected to the slicer -- fix before proceeding to pages 3 and 4.

Apply the visual style guide to both pages. Define: the primary colour (hex code), the secondary colour, the font (name and sizes for titles, axis labels, and body text), and the chart border style. Paste the style guide as a bulleted list. Apply it consistently to every element on pages 1 and 2. A dashboard where every chart looks like it was built by a different person is a dashboard that feels unreliable, regardless of the quality of the analysis.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the sparkline formula for the KPI trend line -- Excel sparklines are configured through the chart wizard, not formulas, so Claude's help is less useful here. For the KPI change formula (the arrow and percentage), Claude can write the IF formula that displays up-arrow, down-arrow, or neutral based on the direction and magnitude of the change. Verify the formula logic with three test cases: positive change, negative change, and zero change.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Page 1 = the CEO's page. 4-6 numbers max, each tied to a business question. Page 2 = the Sales VP's page. Drill into what THEY care about (rep performance, regional trends, pipeline). Different audiences need different pages, not the same page filtered.
weeks.pre_flight: Before building anything, define the three KPIs for page 1 with exact formulas. For each KPI: the current-period value formula, the reference-period value formula, the change calculation, and the threshold that turns it red (below X%) or green (above Y%). Write these down. Building KPI bands without pre-defined thresholds produces KPI bands that are always green (optimistic but uninformative) or always red (alarming but useless).
common_mistakes: Building page 2 before confirming the page 1 KPIs are correct. Page 2 is the drill-down of page 1 -- if page 1 has a wrong number, page 2 amplifies the error. Always validate the KPI band values against the raw data before adding detail pages.

Using more than three KPI bands on page 1. The CEO summary page should have three metrics, not seven. More than three means "we could not decide what matters most," which is an editorial failure. Choose the three that the relevant executive checks first.

Not testing the cross-page slicer until page 4 is built. If the slicer architecture is wrong, you will discover it on page 4 and have to rebuild the connection for all charts. Test after page 1 is done, before starting page 2.

Using absolute cell references in KPI band formulas that break when the page is moved or the reference period is changed. Use named ranges (Insert > Name Manager) for the current period and reference period dates. Named ranges make the formulas readable and resilient to layout changes.

Forgetting to hide the gridlines, row/column headers, and formula bar on the dashboard sheets. A dashboard should look like a dashboard, not like a spreadsheet. View > Uncheck Gridlines, Headings, and Formula Bar converts a spreadsheet into a dashboard in 30 seconds.
weeks.debug_help: Cross-page slicers fail when one of the pivot tables uses a different data source connection than the others. In Excel, all pivot tables connected to the same slicer must share the same PivotCache (the same underlying data connection). Check this: right-click any pivot table, select PivotTable Options, and look at the "Data" tab -- the "Save source data with file" option indicates the cache is embedded. All connected pivot tables must reference the same cache. If one pivot table was created from a different data range, rebuild it from the same data source as the others.
stretch: Add a "period selector" user control: a data validation dropdown that lets the user switch between "This Quarter," "This Year," and "Last 12 Months" without using the slicer. The dropdown drives a CHOOSE or SWITCH formula that changes the reference period for all KPI band calculations simultaneously.

Add a KPI "threshold editor" -- a small table on a hidden "settings" sheet where the green/red thresholds are defined. Reference those cells in the conditional formatting rules. This way, the KPI thresholds can be updated without editing the conditional formatting formulas on the dashboard page.

Write a short "user guide" tab in the workbook explaining what each page shows, what the slicers do, and what the alert colours mean. A dashboard without documentation assumes the reader understands your design choices, which is rarely true for someone who did not build it.

weeks.title: Capstone v0.3: Pages 3 + 4
weeks.context:
Pages 1 and 2 are built and the slicer architecture works. This week you complete pages 3 and 4 and confirm that the full four-page dashboard is visually consistent and alert-driven.

Page 3 is the deep-dive page. The chart on page 2 identified the dimension that most influences the headline KPI -- the region, product, or department with the biggest gap. Page 3 goes one level deeper into that dimension: what is driving the gap? If page 2 shows "North region is outperforming," page 3 shows which product categories within the North are driving the outperformance, and whether any categories in the North are underperforming within the overall positive picture.

Page 4 is the trend and cohort page. It answers the time-dimension question: is this getting better or worse, and how does the current cohort compare to previous cohorts? For a retail capstone, this is the monthly revenue trend with year-over-year overlay. For an HR capstone, this is the quarterly attrition rate by cohort. The cohort matrix from week 16 is the model -- rows are cohorts, columns are periods since cohort start, cells are the metric of interest.

The alert-driven design is what separates an operational dashboard from an informational one. An informational dashboard shows numbers. An operational dashboard flags numbers that require action. The alert is usually an IF formula with conditional formatting: if the metric falls below a threshold, highlight the cell red and add a text indicator. The threshold is defined by the business context (a gross margin below 20% is a warning; a gross margin below 10% requires immediate attention) and must be specified before building the dashboard.

By Sunday: all four pages complete, the alert rules defined and documented in the README, the visual style consistent across all four pages, and the dashboard reviewed by one person who has not seen it.

days.title: Page 3 — Customer view
days.summary: A customer-focused page. Concept + layout.

items.title: Page 3 — Customer view
items.body:
## What it is
Page 3 focuses on **customers/segments** — who they are, their value, their behaviour — reusing your CLV/cohort skills on the capstone data.

## Why it matters
A complete dashboard answers more than 'what happened' (pages 1-2); it answers 'who' (customers) and 'how well are we running' (operations, page 4). The customer page is where retention/value insights live, and it shows you can carry a customer lens into any project.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
PAGE 3 — CUSTOMER
KPIs: customers | repeat rate | avg value
[segment value bar]  [cohort retention mini-matrix]
The 'who' behind the sales.
```

## Why it matters
Cohort retention is a senior signal, and embedding it in the capstone proves you can deploy advanced analysis inside a polished product, not just in a notebook. Even a small retention heatmap tells a stakeholder whether the business keeps its customers.

```text
Jan     100%  22%  14%
```

items.title: Page 4 — Operations
items.body:
## What it is
Page 4 covers **operations** — efficiency, fulfilment, quality metrics (delivery time, error rates, capacity) relevant to your capstone's domain.

## Why it matters
Operations is the 'how well are we running' view that completes the picture. Including it shows you understand a business has multiple stakeholders (finance, customer, ops) and can build for all of them — the mark of a mature analyst, not a one-dimensional one.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
PAGE 4 — OPERATIONS
KPIs: avg fulfilment time | on-time % | issue rate
[trend: fulfilment time]  [bar: issues by type]
The 'how well are we running' view.
```

items.title: Add an Alerts section
items.body:
## What it is
An **Alerts** block on page 1 that flags metrics breaching a threshold (e.g. 'Store B sales down 20% this month') — turning the dashboard from passive display into active guidance.

## Why it matters
A dashboard that just shows numbers makes the viewer hunt for problems; one that *flags* them does the thinking. Alerts (conditional text/colour driven by rules) are a high-value feature — they're the difference between a report and a decision-support tool. This is conditional logic applied to KPIs.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
ALERTS (page 1)
  ! Store B sales -20% vs last month
  ! Cold-week fulfilment time +30%
  (only shows when a rule is breached; green/quiet otherwise)
```

cards.prompt: An alerts section that flags threshold breaches turns a dashboard from passive display into guidance.
cards.whenRight: Right — it does the problem-hunting for the viewer.
cards.whenWrong: It does — alerts make the dashboard a decision tool, not a report.

items.title: Your turn — alerts

days.title: Unified filter panel

items.title: Unified filter panel
items.body:
## What it is
Consolidate filters into one consistent panel that controls all four pages — the same selection (store, date) applied everywhere.

## Why it matters
Across four pages, inconsistent or scattered filters are confusing and break trust. A single, persistent filter panel makes the whole thing feel like one coherent application a user can navigate confidently. This is the polish that distinguishes a professional dashboard from a stack of charts.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
[ Store v ][ Date v ][ Segment v ]   <- one panel, every page obeys it
Navigate page 1->4 with Store C selected: all four stay on Store C.
```

cards.prompt: A single filter panel controlling all pages makes a multi-page dashboard feel like one coherent app.
cards.whenRight: Right — consistency across pages is what builds user trust.
cards.whenWrong: It does — one persistent panel = a coherent application.

items.title: Polish + branding
items.body:
## What it is
A consistency + branding pass over all four pages: unified colours/fonts, a title and logo, aligned elements, removed clutter — so it reads as one designed product.

## Why it matters
Branding and consistency are what make a portfolio dashboard look *professional* rather than student-made. Recruiters judge polish in seconds; a consistent colour scheme and clean layout borrow credibility for the analysis. This is the design pass from the deck weeks, applied across the whole app.

```text
[ ] one colour palette across all 4 pages
[ ] consistent title style + a simple logo/header
[ ] every chart labelled, aligned, decluttered
[ ] consistent fonts and spacing
```

resources.label: Drill-through dashboards in 10 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 10 min. Click a customer name, jump to their detail page. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Alerts on dashboard KPIs in 8 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 8 min. Flag below-target KPIs in red automatically. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Print-ready dashboards in 7 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 7 min. Export-to-PDF layout. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

exercises: Add a 5th page: 'Drill into one customer' for the customer success team
Add a printable export-ready layout view
Add scenario comparison (this quarter vs target)
questions: What's the trade-off of having 4 pages vs 1?
Why is a unified filter panel better than per-page filters?
What's an alert-rule and where would you misuse it?
mastery_questions: Build page 3 (deep-dive page). The main chart should be a breakdown of the page-2 finding by a second dimension. If page 2 shows "North region underperforms," page 3 might show "within the North, Furniture underperforms by the widest margin" using a bar chart sorted by the gap versus the company average. Paste the chart type and the specific finding it reveals. The finding on page 3 must be more specific than the finding on page 2 -- if it is not, page 3 is redundant.

Build the cohort retention matrix on page 4. Use the conditional formatting pattern from week 11: green for above-threshold retention, yellow for moderate, red for below-threshold. Add a trend line or sparkline showing whether each cohort's month-3 retention is improving over time. Paste the matrix data (the values, not the formatting). Write one sentence about whether the most recent cohorts are better or worse than the first cohorts.

Add the alert rules to page 1. For each KPI band: if the current value falls below the warning threshold, the large number cell turns yellow. If it falls below the critical threshold, it turns red. Paste the conditional formatting rule for one KPI. Test it by temporarily changing the value to below each threshold and confirming the colour changes correctly.

Review the full four-page dashboard for visual consistency. Open each page and check: same font, same colour palette, same chart border style, same spacing. Write down any inconsistencies you find. Fix them. Paste the updated consistency checklist: font name (confirmed), primary colour hex (confirmed), chart border (confirmed), slicer position (consistent across pages).

Share the dashboard with one person who has not seen it. Ask them: "Without my explanation, which page would you go to first? What does that page tell you? What question does it leave unanswered?" Write down their answers. The first question reveals your dashboard's natural entry point. The unanswered question is what goes in the appendix or becomes a next-version feature.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate the conditional formatting rule formula for a complex alert condition -- for example, an alert that fires when both the current metric is below threshold AND the YoY change is negative (double trigger). The syntax for nested conditions in Excel conditional formatting is non-obvious and Claude writes it correctly. Test the rule with four cases: below threshold + declining, below threshold + improving, above threshold + declining, above threshold + improving.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Page 3 = Customer/Marketing team. Page 4 = Operations team. Each page must answer their specific job-to-be-done in 10 seconds. Run a mental test: 'If I were them, would I act on this?'
weeks.pre_flight: Define the alert rules before building page 3. For each metric that has an alert: the metric name, the warning threshold, the critical threshold, and the visual treatment (yellow for warning, red for critical). Write them as a bulleted list. If you cannot define the thresholds before building, you do not understand the business context well enough yet -- research what "normal" looks like for your domain and set the thresholds accordingly.
common_mistakes: Building page 3 as a repetition of page 2 at slightly more granularity. Pages 3 should answer a different question, not the same question with more detail. If page 2 answers "which region?", page 3 answers "why that region?" or "what within that region?" -- the causal or compositional question behind the page-2 finding.

Using too many alert colours. Two alert colours (warning and critical) are enough. Three or more (info, warning, watch, critical) produce alert fatigue -- the viewer learns to ignore them because there are too many. Keep the colour vocabulary small.

Not testing the alerts on boundary conditions. The warning threshold is the boundary. Test that a value of exactly the threshold value triggers the alert (some conditional formatting rules use > versus >= differently). The business user who sees a value at exactly the threshold needs to know whether it is in or out of the warning zone.

Building a cohort matrix where the cohorts are labelled ambiguously. "2017 Q1" could mean customers who acquired in Q1 2017, or it could mean Q1 2017 performance for all customers. The label must be unambiguous. Add "(acquisition cohort)" or "(performance period)" to the axis label if there is any risk of confusion.

Calling the dashboard "done" without the outside reader review. The outside reader feedback is the quality gate. A dashboard that makes sense to the person who built it but confuses the first reader is not ready to ship.
weeks.debug_help: Cohort matrix conditional formatting in Excel applies incorrectly when the cells contain formulas that return text (e.g., a cell that says "N/A" for cohorts without enough follow-up data). Conditional formatting rules that reference numeric thresholds will not apply to text cells -- they appear unformatted, which can be confused with a "passing" result. Fix: use a separate column for the display value ("N/A" as text) and a separate hidden column for the numeric value (used for conditional formatting). Apply the formatting rules to the hidden numeric column and display the text column to the user.
stretch: Add a "print view" for each page: a hidden button that temporarily increases chart sizes and removes slicers, optimised for PDF export. The print view allows the dashboard to be exported as a multi-page PDF for stakeholders who will read it offline.

Build a fifth "appendix" page with the full underlying data tables, the source links, and the methodology notes. The appendix handles the "where did this number come from?" question without cluttering the main dashboard pages.

Apply the "squint test" to each dashboard page: squint at the page so that text becomes unreadable. Does the most important number still stand out visually? If the squint test fails (the most important element is not visually dominant), adjust size, colour, or position until it passes.

weeks.title: Storytelling masterclass
weeks.context:
The capstone dashboard is built. This week you make it tell a story instead of displaying data.

There is a meaningful difference between a dashboard that contains correct numbers and a dashboard that communicates a finding. Both are common in analyst portfolios. Only one gets a second look from a hiring manager or a department head. The difference is usually not the analysis -- it is the presentation layer: the headline, the visual hierarchy, and the spoken narrative.

The Pyramid Principle is the analytical equivalent of "conclusion first." Every consultant, investment banker, and senior analyst learns it in their first year. The idea: lead with the answer, support it with three or four arguments, and use evidence only to support arguments that need proof. Applied to a dashboard presentation: the first sentence you say is the finding, not the methodology. "Furniture is our biggest profitability problem" comes before "I looked at profit margin by category."

Killing unnecessary charts is the hardest editorial decision in the process. Every chart you built felt necessary when you built it. Some of them are not necessary for the story -- they support the analysis but not the narrative. The test is simple: if you removed this chart, would the audience miss any information needed to understand or act on the recommendation? If no, remove it. A five-chart presentation with a clear narrative beats an eight-chart presentation where the audience stops following at chart 4.

The recorded practice is the quality gate. Most analysts can explain a dashboard clearly on the fourth try. Rarely on the first. Recording yourself forces you to hear what the audience hears: the filler words ("um," "so," "basically"), the moments where you lost the thread, and the places where you assumed the audience knew something they do not. Two recordings and two revisions is the minimum.

By Sunday: the capstone deck reduced to the minimum number of slides that tell the complete story (probably three to five), each slide with a one-sentence headline, the spoken narrative practiced and recorded at least twice, and the recording committed or linked.

days.title: Why storytelling beats analysis
days.summary: A dashboard displays; a story persuades. Concept, video.

items.title: Why storytelling beats analysis
items.body:
## What it is
There's a real gap between a dashboard that *displays data* and a presentation that *tells a story* — a narrative with a point, a tension, and a recommendation. This week you turn your capstone into a story.

## Why it matters
Decisions are made by people, and people act on stories, not spreadsheets. Two analysts can have the identical numbers; the one who frames them as "here's the problem, here's the evidence, here's what we should do" gets the budget. Storytelling is the highest-leverage, least-taught analyst skill — it's what turns correct analysis into actual influence. Your analysis is already done; this week multiplies its impact.

items.title: Tips for presenting data at work
items.why: Data-storytelling habits. Optional.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
DISPLAY:  "Here are 12 charts about our sales."  (audience: so...?)
STORY:    "We're losing 14% of sales on cold days, concentrated in Store B.
           Here's why, and a $X fix."  (audience: tell me more)
Same data; the story has a point, tension, and an ask.
```

cards.prompt: People make decisions from stories with a point and an ask, not from raw dashboards.
cards.whenRight: Right — narrative is what turns analysis into influence.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a story with a point persuades; a chart dump doesn't.

items.title: Your turn — find the story
items.body: [WRITE] In 2-3 sentences, what's the story your capstone tells (the problem, the insight, the recommendation)?

days.title: Distil it to ONE sentence
days.summary: The single takeaway. Concept + how.

items.title: Distil it to ONE sentence
items.body:
## What it is
Compress your entire capstone into **one sentence** — the single thing the audience must remember if they forget everything else.

## Why it matters
If you can't say it in one sentence, you don't yet know your own point — and your audience certainly won't find it. The one-sentence takeaway becomes your title slide, your memo headline, and the spine every other slide supports. This forced compression is the hardest and most clarifying step in the whole presentation.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
RAMBLING: "We looked at sales, weather, holidays, stores, and customers and
           found several interesting patterns across the dataset."
ONE SENTENCE: "Cold weather costs us 14% of sales, and Store B is twice as
               exposed as the rest — a $X annual fix."
The second one is a presentation's spine.
```

cards.prompt: If you can't compress the capstone to one sentence, you haven't found your point yet.
cards.whenRight: Right — the one-sentence takeaway is the spine of the whole talk.
cards.whenWrong: It is — forced compression reveals (and sharpens) your point.
cards.sim: one sentence = title slide + memo headline

items.title: Your turn — one sentence
items.body: [WRITE] Write the single sentence your audience must remember; reject anything vague or multi-part.

days.title: Slide as visual hierarchy
days.summary: Guide the eye to the point. Concept + how.

items.title: Slide as visual hierarchy
items.body:
## What it is
Design each slide so the eye lands on **the point first** — the biggest, boldest element is the takeaway, with supporting detail smaller and secondary.

## Why it matters
Viewers don't read slides, they *scan* them — and they look at the biggest thing first. If your slide's largest element is a busy chart instead of the conclusion, you've buried the lede. Deliberate visual hierarchy (size, colour, position) makes the audience absorb your point before they even read the details. It's how a slide communicates in the 3 seconds before someone tunes out.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
WEAK slide: a big chart, tiny title -> eye hits the chart, point unclear.
STRONG slide: BIG bold takeaway sentence at top, the chart below as evidence,
              the one number that matters highlighted in colour.
Eye path: takeaway -> supporting chart -> highlighted number.
```

cards.prompt: Viewers scan to the biggest element first, so the takeaway (not a busy chart) should dominate the slide.
cards.whenRight: Right — make the conclusion the visual focal point.
cards.whenWrong: It does — size/colour/position should lead the eye to the point.
cards.sim: big bold takeaway > big busy chart

items.title: Your turn — hierarchy
items.body: [PRODUCE] Redesign one slide so the takeaway is the dominant element and the chart is clearly supporting.

days.title: Show only the numbers that matter
days.summary: Cut to the decisive figures. Concept + how.

items.title: Show only the numbers that matter
items.body:
## What it is
Ruthlessly cut the numbers on each slide down to the few that *support the story* — delete every figure that's merely true but not decisive.

## Why it matters
More numbers feel rigorous but actually dilute the message — the audience can't tell which figure matters. One highlighted number ('14% sales loss') lands; a table of twenty drowns it. Choosing what to *leave out* is as important as the analysis itself, and it's a discipline that signals you understand what your audience needs versus what you happen to know.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
WEAK: a 6x8 table of every metric by store and month.
STRONG: "14%" in huge type, with "(Store B: 28%)" beside it. One chart.
Every number on the slide must earn its place by supporting the point.
```

cards.prompt: Cutting to the few decisive numbers makes the message land; a table of everything drowns it.
cards.whenRight: Right — choosing what to leave out is part of the skill.
cards.whenWrong: It does — one decisive number beats twenty true ones.

items.title: Your turn — cut numbers
items.body: [PRODUCE] Strip each story slide to only the numbers that support the point; highlight the single most important one.

days.title: Speaker notes that work
days.summary: Write what you'll say, not what's on screen. Concept + how.

items.title: Speaker notes that work
items.body:
## What it is
Write **speaker notes** — what you'll *say* aloud — that add context and narrative beyond what's on the slide, rather than just reading the slide text.

## Why it matters
Reading your slides aloud is the cardinal presentation sin (the audience can read faster than you talk). Good notes carry the *story between* the slides — the 'why this matters', the transition, the anecdote. The slide is the evidence; your voice is the narrative. Prepared notes are also what let you present confidently instead of improvising.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
SLIDE shows: "Cold days: -14% sales"
BAD notes:   "On cold days, sales drop 14 percent."   (just reading it)
GOOD notes:  "This surprised us. We assumed weather was noise, but it's our
              single biggest controllable driver - and Store B is twice exposed,
              which points to a roofing/heating issue we can actually fix."
```

cards.prompt: Speaker notes should add narrative beyond the slide, not just read the slide text aloud.
cards.whenRight: Right — your voice carries the story between the evidence.
cards.whenWrong: It does — notes add the 'why it matters', not a re-read.

items.title: Your turn — speaker notes
items.body: [PRODUCE] Write speaker notes for your 4-5 key slides that add story/context beyond the on-screen text.

days.title: Record and practice
days.summary: Rehearse the full story. Concept + rubric.

items.title: Record and practice
items.body:
## What it is
Record yourself delivering the full capstone story (5-7 minutes) and watch it back against a rubric.

## Why it matters
The story only works if delivered well. Recording surfaces the pacing problems, the filler, the slide you can't explain, and whether your one-sentence takeaway actually opens the talk. Two practice rounds turn a shaky walkthrough into a confident narrative — and confidence is itself persuasive.

items.title: See it worked (rubric)
items.body:
```text
[ ] Did I open with the one-sentence takeaway?
[ ] Pacing: 5-7 min, no rushing?
[ ] Filler count (um/like) trending down?
[ ] Every slide: could I explain it without reading it?
[ ] Did I end on the recommendation/ask?
```

cards.prompt: Recording and reviewing your delivery turns a shaky walkthrough into a confident narrative.
cards.whenRight: Right — practice surfaces pacing/filler before the real room.
cards.whenWrong: It does — review-and-redo builds the confidence that persuades.

items.title: Your turn — rehearse
items.body: [PRODUCE] Record a 5-7 min delivery of the capstone story; score it on the rubric; note two fixes.

days.title: Ship: storyteller
days.summary: Commit the story deck + notes, tag storyteller.

items.title: Ship: storyteller
items.body:
## What it is
Ship the storytelling layer: the narrative deck, speaker notes, and your practice recording. Tag `storyteller`.

## Why it matters
You can now do the thing most analysts can't — turn correct analysis into a persuasive story that drives a decision. Combined with the dashboard, your capstone now has both the *substance* and the *delivery*, which is the complete package employers rarely see in a junior.

cards.prompt: Pairing strong analysis with storytelling is the complete package most junior analysts lack.
cards.whenRight: Right — substance + persuasive delivery is rare and hireable.
cards.whenWrong: It is — analysis plus storytelling is the full skill set.

items.title: Acceptance — storyteller is done when
items.body:
[PRODUCE] A narrative deck with a one-sentence spine, decisive numbers, speaker notes, and a practiced delivery.
[CODE] `git tag storyteller`; push. Drop your repo link.

resources.note: 6 min. 30-second beats per slide. What to say, what to skip. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Self-tape your presentation - 5 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 5 min. Camera angle, lighting, voice. Pro look in 10 minutes of setup. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

exercises: Try the deck in front of an actual person — get feedback
Replace one chart with a single big number
Find an example of 'bad' chart design and remake it
questions: What's the difference between a chart that's pretty and a chart that's persuasive?
Why do executives skim slides not read them?
What kills credibility fastest in a presentation?
mastery_questions: Apply the editorial cut. Look at the current deck and mark each chart as: "load-bearing" (the recommendation falls apart without this chart) or "supporting" (the chart helps but the main point survives without it). Cut all non-load-bearing charts to the appendix. Paste the new slide count (before and after) and the one finding that was hardest to cut because you thought it was important but it is not load-bearing.

Write the one-sentence headline for each slide. The headline must be a complete sentence with a specific number or comparison. Example: "Furniture's 7.2 pp margin gap from Technology explains 63% of the overall company profit shortfall." If any headline is a question ("Why is Furniture struggling?") or a vague description ("Profitability Analysis"), rewrite it as a finding. Paste all headlines.

Practice the five-minute walkthrough out loud. Record it (phone, Loom, any tool). Do not prepare a script -- narrate from the headlines. Time it. If it runs over six minutes, you have too many charts or too much explanation per chart. If it runs under three minutes, you are skipping something important. Paste the recording URL or file path.

Watch the recording. Identify: one moment where you lost the thread and had to recover, one chart you spent more than 60 seconds on (which means either the chart is too complex or the finding needs more setup), and one place where you used jargon that a non-analyst would not understand. Fix all three before recording a second take.

Record the second take. Paste the URL. Write one sentence comparing the two takes: what specifically improved between take 1 and take 2. The improvement should be nameable -- "I led with the finding on slide 2 instead of the methodology" or "I cut the explanation of the cohort matrix to 30 seconds instead of 90." Vague improvements ("it flowed better") are not improvements you can systematically replicate.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to critique your five slide headlines as a set. Paste all five and ask: "Do these headlines tell a coherent story with a clear finding and a logical progression? What is missing or inconsistent?" The critique will surface the slide that is doing too much (combining two arguments) or too little (restating a previous finding). Do NOT ask Claude to write the headlines -- they must reflect your specific findings from your specific analysis.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: The headline IS the insight. The chart is just proof. Cole Knaflic's rule: if you take the chart away, does the slide still convey the point? If yes, the chart is decoration. Cut it.
weeks.pre_flight: Write the full narrative arc of the capstone in four sentences: the situation (what is true today), the complication (what problem that creates), the question (what the business needs to know), and the answer (your recommendation). This is the Barbara Minto Pyramid Principle structure at its shortest. If you cannot write all four sentences clearly, the story is not clear enough yet to present.
common_mistakes: Keeping charts that you like because you found them interesting, not because they are necessary for the recommendation. Interesting to the analyst is not the same as load-bearing for the audience. Apply the load-bearing test ruthlessly.

Writing slide headlines that contain the word "analysis." "Profitability Analysis" is a section title, not a headline. Headlines contain findings. "Technology's 15.4% margin is 7.2 pp above Furniture's 8.2%" is a headline.

Practicing the deck by reading it silently. Reading and speaking are different cognitive tasks. A deck that reads clearly may have sentences that are hard to say aloud -- subject-verb separation too long, dependent clauses that require the audience to remember context. You only discover these problems by speaking.
Not cutting the intro slides. Most decks start with an agenda ("Today I will cover X, Y, Z") and a data source slide. These are overhead. Lead with the first finding. The audience will follow.
Recording one take and calling it done. The first take always has something to fix. The second take fixes it. Record at least twice.
weeks.debug_help: The most common narrative breakdown happens between the second and third supporting point. The first supporting argument is fresh. The third is the one the audience is still tracking when they should be focused on the recommendation. If the transition from your second to third supporting point is where you lose the thread, try: "The third reason this matters is..." as a explicit verbal transition, or cut the third point and make it an appendix reference. The recommendation is the destination -- every slide should visibly advance toward it.
stretch: Read "The Pyramid Principle: Logic in Writing and Thinking" by Barbara Minto, Chapter 1. The Pyramid Principle was developed for McKinsey consultants but applies to every analyst presentation. Chapter 1 explains the top-down structure in 30 pages -- the fastest ROI in analytical communication skills.

Show the recording to someone who does not work in data (a family member, a friend in a different field). Ask them: "What is the one thing this business should do?" If they cannot answer correctly, the recommendation is not clear enough for a mixed-technical audience. Iterate until they can answer.

Write the speaker notes for each slide: two to three sentences that you would say aloud while the slide is showing, in plain language. The speaker notes should add information not visible on the slide, not repeat it.

weeks.title: Capstone v1.0: Ship + roadmap retro
weeks.context:
The capstone ships this week. The pattern is the same as weeks 9, 13, and 19 -- demo video, polished deliverables, retrospective -- but this close is different from the previous three in two ways. It is the last project on the roadmap, and it is the most ambitious project you built. Both facts warrant more deliberate reflection.

The CEO memo is a deliverable this week that is different from the analyst memos you have written before. The previous memos went to a VP of Sales, an HR Director, and a Marketing Director -- functional leaders who understand their domain well and need data to make a specific decision. A CEO memo is different. The CEO does not know the specific details of your analytical choices. The memo must give them the situation, the finding, the recommendation, and the business case without requiring them to understand what a cohort retention matrix is. One page. No charts -- charts are for the appendix or the deck. Words and numbers only.

The board deck is another deliverable that appears here and almost nowhere else in an analyst portfolio. A board deck is typically 10-15 slides, presented quarterly to board members who see the company once every three months and need a complete picture in 45 minutes. The analytical standards are high (every number must be defensible), the density is controlled (never more than one finding per slide), and the tone is different from an internal management deck -- boards see patterns across many companies and will ask whether your numbers compare favourably to public benchmarks.

The roadmap-level retrospective answers the question that the weekly retros cannot: across 28 weeks, across four projects, what changed? The analyst who started week 1 and the analyst at week 26 are measurably different -- in speed, in the sharpness of findings, in how they structure a memo. Name what specifically changed. That named change is the evidence of learning.

By Sunday: capstone fully shipped with demo video and public URL, CEO memo committed as a PDF, board deck committed as a PDF, and the roadmap-level RETRO.md reflecting honestly on all 28 weeks.

days.title: Write the CEO memo
days.summary: The one-page executive memo. Concept + template.

items.title: Write the CEO memo
items.body:
## What it is
A one-page memo addressed to a CEO: the capstone's headline, the evidence, and the recommendation with its business impact — the polished written companion to your story.

## Why it matters
The CEO memo is the artefact that survives the meeting and circulates to people who weren't there. For the highest audience it must be exceptionally tight: the recommendation and its dollar impact in the first two lines, evidence curated to the essential, and a clear ask. This is the memo discipline from every project, at its most demanding.

items.title: See it worked (CEO memo)
items.body:
```text
## To: CEO   Re: Weather exposure in retail sales
Cold weather costs ~14% of daily sales ($X/yr), concentrated in Store B
(twice the exposure of other sites). A targeted fix pays back in N months.

Evidence: sales vs temperature (14% cold-day drop); Store B 28% vs 14% network.
Recommendation: weatherproofing + dynamic cold-day promotions at Store B;
   pilot one quarter, measure sales lift vs control.
```

cards.prompt: A CEO memo must put the recommendation and its dollar impact in the first two lines.
cards.whenRight: Right — the highest audience needs the answer instantly.
cards.whenWrong: It does — lead with the rec + impact; curate the rest.

items.body: [WRITE] Write a one-page CEO memo: headline + impact, curated evidence, recommendation with payback.

items.title: Build the board deck
items.body:
## What it is
A 5-slide deck for a board/executive audience — your storytelling work, formalised: title takeaway, problem, evidence, recommendation, ask.

## Why it matters
The board deck is the formal version of your story — the highest-stakes presentation format. It must be flawless: BLUF title, one idea per slide, decisive numbers, a clear ask. Producing a board-grade deck from your own capstone is a portfolio flex that signals you can operate at the level decisions are made.

items.title: Tips for presenting data at work
items.why: Presentation habits for the board deck. Optional.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
S1  "Weather costs us 14% of sales — a $X fix" (the takeaway IS the title)
S2  The problem: cold-day sales drop, network-wide
S3  The evidence: sales vs temp + Store B exposure
S4  Recommendation: weatherproofing + cold-day promos
S5  The ask: approve a one-quarter pilot at Store B
```

cards.prompt: A board deck should be the formalised story: BLUF title, one idea per slide, a clear ask.
cards.whenRight: Right — highest stakes, maximum discipline.
cards.whenWrong: It is — the board deck is the story at its most polished.

items.title: Record a demo video
items.body:
## What it is
A 2-3 minute demo of the capstone dashboard and its story — the most shareable proof the project works. Link it (Drive/YouTube) per the video policy.

## Why it matters
The capstone demo is the single best item in your portfolio: it shows a complete, interactive, self-built product *and* you presenting it persuasively. It's what you link at the top of your CV and LinkedIn — recruiters who won't run code will watch three minutes.

items.title: See it worked (script)
items.body:
```text
0:00 "I built this dashboard to answer: how does weather affect our sales?"
0:30 "The headline: cold days cost 14% of sales." [page 1]
1:10 "Store B is twice as exposed." [drill via filter]
1:50 "So I recommend weatherproofing + cold-day promos at Store B."
2:20 "Built from 3 sources, 4 pages. Repo + memo linked." (stop)
```

cards.whenRight: Right — a self-built interactive product + persuasive delivery.
cards.whenWrong: It is — the demo is the headline of your portfolio.

items.title: SQL version of all KPIs
items.body:
## What it is
Write `capstone_queries.sql` reproducing every dashboard KPI in SQL — the joins and aggregations behind the visuals.

## Why it matters
It proves the dashboard isn't magic — every number traces to a verifiable query — and it gives recruiters the SQL artefact they filter for. Across four projects you've now shown the same analyses in pandas, SQL, dbt, Tableau, and Power BI: undeniable, demonstrated tool-fluency.

items.title: SQL aggregate functions, GROUP BY & HAVING
items.why: GROUP BY for the KPI queries. Optional.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```sql
-- Weather-sensitivity KPI in SQL
SELECT
  AVG(CASE WHEN temp_c < 10 THEN sales END) AS cold_avg,
  AVG(CASE WHEN temp_c >= 10 THEN sales END) AS warm_avg
FROM capstone_model;
-- -> cold 171, warm 199 -> matches the dashboard's 14% drop
```

cards.prompt: Backing every dashboard KPI with a SQL query proves the numbers are verifiable, not magic.
cards.whenRight: Right — traceable numbers + a SQL artefact recruiters want.
cards.whenWrong: It does — SQL behind each KPI makes the dashboard auditable.
cards.sim: each KPI -> a query that reproduces it

items.title: Final polish + branding
items.body:
## What it is
A final pass across all deliverables — dashboard, memo, deck, demo, repo — for consistent branding, reconciled numbers, working links, and a clean README.

## Why it matters
This is the public face of your entire roadmap; recruiters judge it in seconds. One inconsistent number or broken link undercuts everything. The final polish is what makes four projects read as the work of a careful professional, ready to share widely.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
[ ] one brand/palette across dashboard, memo, deck
[ ] every number reconciled to one value everywhere
[ ] all links (repo, demo, dashboard) click through
[ ] README: overview, links, how-to-run, your name
[ ] repo public + secret-free
```

cards.prompt: The final polish across all deliverables is the public face recruiters judge in seconds.
cards.whenRight: Right — one broken link or stray number undercuts it all.
cards.whenWrong: It does — consistency across everything signals professionalism.
