days.title: Get three readers
days.summary: Wider feedback before shipping. Concept + the test.

items.title: Get three readers
items.body:
## What it is
Show the capstone to **three** different people and gather where each gets confused — a wider review than the single reader of earlier projects.

## Why it matters
Three readers reveal patterns one can't: if all three stumble on the same slide, it's definitely broken; if only one does, it might be them. For your flagship project, this broader feedback is worth it — it catches the issues that would otherwise surface in an interview, where the stakes are highest.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
Reader A: confused by the cohort tile        }
Reader B: also confused by the cohort tile   } -> definitely fix (pattern)
Reader C: got it -> single confusions are lower priority
Ask each: "one sentence - what am I recommending?"
```

cards.prompt: Multiple readers reveal patterns (all stumble on X = definitely broken) a single reader can't.
cards.whenRight: Right — repeated confusion is a clear signal to fix.
cards.whenWrong: It does — patterns across readers separate real issues from one-offs.
cards.sim: 2-3 readers hit the same slide -> fix it

items.title: Your turn — three readers
items.body: [PRODUCE] Get three people to review it; note which confusions repeat; fix the patterns.

days.title: Ship v1.0 + ROADMAP RETRO
days.summary: Tag v1.0 and reflect on the whole journey. Concept + template.

items.title: Ship v1.0 + ROADMAP RETRO
items.body:
## What it is
Tag the capstone `capstone-v1.0` — then write a **roadmap retro** reflecting on the entire Data Analysis journey: four shipped projects, the skills built (Excel, pandas, SQL, stats, Tableau, Power BI, dbt, storytelling), and where you go next.

## Why it matters
This is the end of the Data Analysis track. You have a portfolio of four complete, shipped, reader-tested projects across retail, HR, e-commerce, and a self-defined capstone — built with the full modern analyst toolkit and presented like a professional. The roadmap retro cements the transformation: you began unable to load a CSV and end able to scope, analyse, model, visualise, and *persuade*. That's a job-ready analyst.

items.title: See it worked (roadmap retro)
items.body:
```text
## Data Analysis — Roadmap Retro
Shipped: Superstore, HR Attrition, Olist, Capstone (4 projects, all v1.0).
Skills:  Excel -> pandas -> SQL -> stats -> Tableau/Power BI -> dbt -> storytelling.
Proudest: the capstone - scoped and built entirely myself.
Hardest:  multi-source modelling and ruthless storytelling compression.
Next:     specialise (BI engineer? analytics engineer?) and apply to roles.
```

cards.prompt: Finishing the track means a portfolio of four shipped projects and the full modern analyst toolkit.
cards.whenRight: Right — that's a job-ready analyst, demonstrated not claimed.
cards.whenWrong: It is — four projects + the toolkit = ready to be hired.
cards.sim: Superstore + HR + Olist + Capstone, all shipped

resources.label: CEO memo writing in 6 min - HBR
resources.note: 6 min. Re-watch. Apply to your capstone.

resources.label: Loom demo best practices in 4 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 4 min. Re-watch. Script first, record in one take. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

resources.label: Getting 3 readers - 6 min (top YouTube result)
resources.note: 6 min. The DMs that get responses. (Click the FIRST video in the search results - it is the intended one.)

exercises: Apply to one analyst job using the portfolio
Post the capstone on /r/dataanalysis
Schedule a 30-min portfolio review with a working analyst
questions: Of the 4 projects, which one defends best in an interview?
Which week stretched you most?
If you started over, what would you change?
mastery_questions: Ship the capstone. Confirm all four pages of the dashboard work with the cross-page slicer. Export the dashboard as a PDF (this requires Print Area configuration for each page). Link the public dashboard, the CEO memo PDF, the board deck PDF, and the demo video in the README. Paste the README links section. Every link should open in under 5 seconds.

Write the CEO memo. One page. Structure: situation (two sentences describing the business context and why this analysis was needed), finding (two sentences with the most important finding and the specific numbers), recommendation (three bullets, each with an action and an expected impact), and next step (one sentence describing what the CEO should do in the next 30 days). Paste the memo. A CEO memo that requires the reader to know what "cohort retention" means is not written for a CEO.

Build the board deck. 10-12 slides. Slide 1: executive summary (the finding and recommendation in two sentences). Slides 2-9: supporting evidence, one finding per slide, with context that a board member who sees the company once per quarter can follow. Slide 10-12: appendix with the detailed tables and methodology. Paste the 10 slide headlines. If any headline is longer than one sentence, it is two findings and needs to be split or simplified.

Record the demo video. Three to four minutes. Open the dashboard, demonstrate all four pages and the cross-page slicer, call out the two most important findings with specific numbers, and close with the top recommendation. Paste the URL. Watch it back and write one sentence about the single improvement you would make if you recorded it again.

Write the roadmap-level RETRO.md. Required sections: most improved skill across all four projects (specific, with evidence -- "my memos went from 3 pages with no specific recommendations to 2 pages with 3 specific recommendations each"), biggest surprise across the roadmap (what was harder than expected? what was easier?), the repeatable analytical process you now have (the three-step or four-step framework), and what you would do in weeks 29 and 30 if the roadmap continued. Paste the file.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to review the CEO memo for language that assumes analytical background knowledge. Paste the memo and ask "identify any sentence that requires the reader to know what a specific analytical technique or data term means." Replace each identified term with plain language or a parenthetical definition. The CEO memo should be readable by a board member with an MBA and no data background.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Get 3 real people to read your CEO memo before shipping. Pick 1 person from the actual audience (an exec or senior person), 1 senior technical person, 1 layperson. Their critiques tell you exactly what to fix.
weeks.pre_flight: Before writing anything, open the README from week 1's Superstore project and read it. Then read your most recent project's README. The gap between the two -- in clarity, in specificity of findings, in the quality of the out-of-scope decisions -- is the evidence of 25 weeks of deliberate practice. Write down two specific things that are better in the current README. Those are your week 1-to-26 improvements.
common_mistakes: Writing a CEO memo that starts with methodology ("We analysed the dataset using Excel and SQL..."). The CEO does not care about the tools. Start with the situation and the finding.

Building a board deck that is 20 slides because "there is a lot to cover." A board deck that is 20 slides suggests the presenter could not decide what was important. Cut to 12 slides maximum. If 12 slides does not fit the content, the content needs to be simplified.

Recording the demo video before the dashboard is polished. A demo where you say "ignore that formatting issue" or "this number is a bit off" is worse than no demo -- it draws attention to the problems you hoped the viewer would overlook.

Writing a roadmap retro that only covers what went well. The roadmap retro is the most important retro you will write because it covers the longest period. The honest version -- what was genuinely hard, what you would change about the roadmap design itself -- is the version that helps you plan the next 6 months of learning.

Not submitting a job application this week. The capstone is the last project. The application is overdue. Apply to at least one role this week -- any role where the four projects are relevant to at least 60% of the job description.
weeks.debug_help: PDF export from Excel dashboard pages is the most common final-week blocker. The issue is usually that charts or shapes extend beyond the print area boundary. Fix: for each dashboard page, set the print area (Page Layout > Print Area > Set Print Area) to exactly the dashboard range, then File > Export as PDF. If the PDF shows only part of the dashboard, the print area is too narrow. If it shows blank pages, the print area includes blank rows below the dashboard. Adjust and re-export until the PDF matches what you see on screen.
stretch: Submit the capstone project to a relevant Kaggle discussion or a relevant LinkedIn group. Getting external feedback on a finished project from practitioners in the domain is the fastest way to identify gaps in the analysis that you cannot see from the inside.

Create a 3-minute "case study" version of the capstone project: the business problem, the analytical approach, the key finding, and the recommendation, without the dashboard. This is the version you use in interviews when the interviewer says "tell me about a project you've done." Write it down and practise it until it is 3 minutes.

Read the most recent annual report of a public company in your capstone's domain. Compare the KPIs they report publicly to the KPIs you built in your dashboard. The comparison reveals which metrics the company considers most important and whether your dashboard would be relevant to their actual management reporting.

weeks.title: Portfolio + interview prep
weeks.context:
The roadmap is complete. Four projects are shipped. The analytical process is repeatable. This week the work shifts entirely to making the evidence visible and converting it into interviews.

The portfolio site is the central URL. It does not need to be beautiful -- it needs to load, link to all four projects with one sentence each, and have a contact method. A GitHub Pages site built from a template takes two hours. Spending a week on the portfolio site instead of applying is the wrong trade-off. Ship the minimum viable portfolio and start applying.

LinkedIn matters more for data analysts than for most roles because business stakeholders (not just technical recruiters) search LinkedIn for analysts. A VP of Finance looking for a business analyst will often search LinkedIn before posting a job. A profile that is specific ("Data Analyst with 4 completed projects in retail, HR, e-commerce, and BI") is findable; a profile that says "Data Analysis | Excel | SQL | Python" is not.

The specific interview preparation this week is for the three types of questions data analyst interviews include: technical SQL questions, business case questions ("how would you analyse X?"), and behavioural questions about past projects. SQL questions require practice, not knowledge -- the patterns (GROUP BY, CTEs, window functions, self-joins) are in your queries.sql files from four projects. Business case questions require the three-step framework from week 26's retro. Project questions require the 90-second pitch for each of your four projects.

One application is the minimum this week. Not a stretch application -- a real one, for a role where you meet at least 70% of the listed requirements.

days.title: Audit what you have
days.summary: Inventory your four projects as evidence. Concept + the audit.

items.title: Audit what you have
items.body:
## What it is
The analytical work is done — four shipped projects. This week shifts entirely to making that work **visible** to employers. Step one: audit everything you've built into a single inventory.

## Why it matters
You almost certainly underestimate what you've produced. Four end-to-end projects (Superstore, HR, Olist, Capstone) across retail, HR, and e-commerce — with notebooks, dashboards, memos, SQL, dbt, Tableau/Power BI, and demo videos — is a *stronger* portfolio than most working analysts have. But a recruiter can't see it unless you collect and frame it. The audit turns scattered repos into a presentable body of work, and reminds you how far you've come.

PROJECT       ARTEFACTS                                 SKILLS SHOWN
Superstore    notebook, memo, deck, SQL, Tableau        Excel->pandas->SQL, viz
HR Attrition  notebook, dashboard, memo, SQL, demo      rates, interactions, HR
Olist         notebook, cohort matrix, SQL, demo        relational joins, cohorts
Capstone      4-page dashboard, board deck, demo        scoping, modelling, story

Four projects, every modern analyst skill, demonstrated — not claimed.

days.title: Claim your home base (domain)
days.summary: A simple web presence. Concept + how.

items.title: Claim your home base (domain)
items.body:
## What it is
Optionally buy a cheap domain (yourname.com) and set up a simple landing page — a single professional home that links to your projects, GitHub, and LinkedIn.

## Why it matters
A personal domain signals seriousness and is memorable on a CV ('see yourname.com') versus a long GitHub URL. It's not required — a GitHub Pages site or a good LinkedIn works — but a clean home base where everything links together makes you look like a professional, not a hobbyist. Even a one-page site beats scattered links.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
Options (cheapest -> nicest):
  - GitHub repo README as your hub (free)
  - GitHub Pages 1-page site (free, yourname.github.io)
  - Custom domain -> simple site (~$12/yr, yourname.com)
All do the same job: ONE link that leads to everything.
```

cards.prompt: A single home base (even a free one) that links to all your work looks more professional than scattered links.
cards.whenRight: Right — one memorable link beats a pile of URLs.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a hub page reads as professional and is easy to share.

items.title: Your turn — home base
items.body: [PRODUCE] Set up a home base (GitHub Pages or a domain) — a one-page site linking your four projects, GitHub, and LinkedIn.

days.title: Build a 1-page portfolio site
days.summary: The page recruiters actually read. Concept + structure.

items.title: Build a 1-page portfolio site
items.body:
## What it is
A single, skimmable page: a one-line intro, then your four projects each as a card (title, one-sentence problem, the result/finding, links to the demo + repo).

## Why it matters
Recruiters spend seconds per portfolio. A one-page site with project cards, each leading with the *result* ('found discounts cost $62k; recommended a cap'), is far more effective than a wall of repos they have to decode. Leading with outcomes, not tech lists, is what makes them click into your work. Skimmability is the whole game.

items.title: See it worked (project card)
items.body:
```text
[ Superstore Analytics ]
"Found that discounts above 30% turn orders unprofitable; recommended a cap
 worth ~$62k/yr."
Excel · pandas · SQL · Tableau     [ Demo ]  [ Repo ]
---
(repeat for HR, Olist, Capstone — result first, links right there)
```

cards.prompt: Portfolio project cards should lead with the RESULT/finding, not a list of technologies.
cards.whenRight: Right — outcomes make recruiters click; tech lists don't.
cards.whenWrong: It does — lead with what you found, then the tools.

items.title: Your turn — portfolio page
items.body: [PRODUCE] Build a one-page site with four project cards, each leading with the result and linking to demo + repo.

days.title: Write 3 LinkedIn posts
days.summary: Turn projects into reach. Concept + template.

items.title: Write 3 LinkedIn posts
items.body:
## What it is
Write three short LinkedIn posts, one per project (use your strongest three), each telling the mini-story: the question, the finding, what you learned — with a link.

## Why it matters
Recruiters and hiring managers are on LinkedIn, and a post about a real project you built demonstrates skill *and* communication in a way a resume bullet can't. Posting also surfaces you in feeds and shows you can explain analysis to a general audience — itself a hireable signal. Three good posts can generate more inbound interest than dozens of applications.

items.title: See it worked (post template)
items.body:
```text
"I analysed 1,470 employees to find why people quit. The biggest driver
 wasn't pay - it was overtime: those on OT left at 3x the rate.

 Here's how I found it (pandas + a simple rate-by-group analysis) and what
 I'd recommend HR do about it. [link]

 #dataanalytics #python #peopleanalytics"
```
Story + finding + link + tags. Repeat for two more projects.

cards.prompt: A LinkedIn post about a real project demonstrates skill AND communication better than a resume bullet.
cards.whenRight: Right — it shows the work and that you can explain it.
cards.whenWrong: It does — a project post proves skill + communication + reach.

items.title: Your turn — 3 posts
items.body: [WRITE] Draft three LinkedIn posts (one per project): question, finding, what you learned, a link, and tags.

days.title: Update LinkedIn + GitHub

items.title: Update LinkedIn + GitHub
items.body:
## What it is
Update both profiles to reflect the analyst you now are: a clear headline, a summary naming your skills and projects, pinned repos, and clean READMEs on every project.

## Why it matters
Your profiles are what recruiters find first. A headline that says "Data Analyst | Python, SQL, Power BI | 4 shipped projects" plus pinned, well-documented repos converts a profile visit into an interview. Inconsistent or empty profiles waste the strong work behind them — the profile is the storefront for everything you built.

items.title: See it worked (checklist)
items.body:
```text
LinkedIn: headline (role + tools), summary (skills + linked projects), open-to-work
GitHub:   profile README, 4 projects PINNED, each with a clean README + demo link
Both:     same name/photo, links to your portfolio site
```

cards.prompt: Recruiters often see your LinkedIn/GitHub before your application, so they must reflect your real level.
cards.whenRight: Right — the profile is the storefront; make it match the work.
cards.whenWrong: It does — strong profiles convert visits into interviews.

items.title: Your turn — update profiles
items.body: [PRODUCE] Update your LinkedIn headline/summary and pin your 4 GitHub repos with clean READMEs + demo links.

days.title: Practice 3 interview questions
days.summary: Rehearse talking about your work. Concept + the questions.

items.title: Practice 3 interview questions
items.body:
## What it is
Rehearse answering the three questions every analyst interview asks: "walk me through a project", "a time you found something surprising", and a basic technical one ("how would you find the top customers?").

## Why it matters
You did the work, but interviews test whether you can *talk* about it clearly under pressure. Practising out loud turns "um, I did some analysis" into a crisp, structured story (situation -> what you did -> the finding -> the impact). Your four projects are perfect material — rehearsing how to narrate them is what converts the portfolio into an offer.

items.title: See it worked (STAR-ish)
items.body:
```text
"Walk me through a project":
  Situation: "Superstore had loss-making sub-categories."
  Task:      "I tested whether discounting was the cause."
  Action:    "Binned discounts, found profit turns negative above 30%."
  Result:    "Recommended a cap addressing 24% of orders (~$62k)."
Practice each of the 3 questions out loud until it's smooth.
```

cards.prompt: Interviews test whether you can clearly TALK about your work, not just whether you did it.
cards.whenRight: Right — rehearsing the narration converts the portfolio to an offer.
cards.whenWrong: It does — clear, structured answers are what win interviews.
cards.sim: situation -> action -> finding -> impact, out loud

items.title: Your turn — rehearse
items.body: [PRODUCE] Practise out loud: (1) walk through a project, (2) a surprising finding, (3) 'how would you find top customers?'. Record one if you can.

days.title: Ship + apply
days.summary: Publish everything and start applying. Concept + the close.

items.title: Ship + apply
items.body:
## What it is
Publish the portfolio, profiles, and posts — then **start applying**. The roadmap's core is complete; this is the bridge to the job.

## Why it matters
A portfolio that no one sees changes nothing. Shipping it and applying is the action that turns months of work into interviews and offers. You're now genuinely job-ready: four shipped projects, the full modern analyst toolkit (Excel, pandas, SQL, stats, Tableau, dbt, and — next week — Power BI), and the ability to present and defend your work. Apply with evidence, not hope.

cards.prompt: A portfolio only creates opportunity once it's public and you're actively applying.
cards.whenRight: Right — visible work + applications = interviews; hidden work = nothing.
cards.whenWrong: It does — shipping and applying is what converts work into a job.

mastery_questions: Build and deploy the portfolio site. Required content: name, one-sentence summary of what you do, links to all four projects with one-sentence descriptions, and a contact method. Paste the URL. Open it in an incognito tab on a phone. If it loads in under 5 seconds and the four projects are visible without scrolling, it passes the minimum bar.

Update the LinkedIn profile. Summary: four sentences covering what you do, what you have built, the tools you use fluently (Excel, SQL, Python, Tableau, Power BI, dbt), and what you are looking for. Featured section: link to portfolio site. Projects section: all four projects with one bullet each and the specific finding. Skills section: ranked skills backed by the project evidence. Paste your profile URL.

Write the SQL practice answer for this question: "Given a table of monthly customer orders, write a query that returns each customer's total orders, total revenue, average order value, and whether they are in the top 10% of customers by revenue." This combines GROUP BY, window functions, and a CASE or NTILE. Paste the query. Time yourself -- if it takes more than 15 minutes, do 30 minutes of SQL practice daily before interviews.

Write the spoken answer to the business case question: "Our e-commerce company has seen a drop in checkout conversion rate over the last quarter. How would you analyse this?" Use the three-step framework: clarify the metric and the context (what counts as conversion? which part of the funnel?), describe the data you would pull and the analysis you would run (funnel breakdown by device, browser, user segment, time of day), and state what findings would change your recommendation. Time the answer -- aim for 90 seconds. Paste the written version.

Submit one job application. Paste the company name and role title. In the cover letter or application notes, reference one specific project that is directly relevant to the role. A referenced project with a live URL is the single most effective thing you can add to a data analyst application -- it proves you can do the work, not just that you know the tools.
weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to generate 10 SQL practice questions at increasing difficulty (GROUP BY, CASE WHEN, window functions, CTEs, self-joins). Solve each one yourself before reading Claude's solution. After solving, ask Claude to critique your solution for readability and efficiency. The critique often catches an unnecessary subquery that could be a CTE, or a GROUP BY on too many columns that could be simplified.
weeks.pre_flight: Before building the portfolio site, write the one-sentence description for each of the four projects. The sentence should state: the dataset, the main finding, and the specific recommendation that came out of the analysis. If you cannot write the sentence without looking at the project README, the project is not ready to be in a portfolio -- you need to be able to describe it from memory.
common_mistakes: Spending the week building a beautiful portfolio site instead of applying. The portfolio site is done when it is live and links to the projects. The application is the action that produces interviews.

LinkedIn profiles that list tools without projects. "Excel, SQL, Python, Tableau, Power BI" as skills without any linked projects makes you look identical to thousands of other candidates who list the same tools. The four projects are what differentiate you.

Practising SQL by reading solutions instead of writing them. SQL interview preparation requires solving problems yourself, timing yourself, and checking your solution. Reading solutions without attempting the problem is not practice.

Business case answers that describe a generic analysis without referencing your actual experience. "I would build a funnel analysis" is generic. "I built a funnel analysis on the Olist e-commerce dataset -- the biggest drop was between order shipped and delivered, and a 3-day delivery delay reduced review scores by 0.8 points. I would approach your checkout analysis similarly, starting with the biggest conversion drop by segment" is specific and credible.

Not submitting the application because "I am not ready." The moment of maximum readiness is now -- you have four projects, a working portfolio, and 28 weeks of analytical practice. Applications submitted now produce interviews. Applications deferred to "when I am more ready" produce nothing.
weeks.debug_help: The SQL business case question that most analysts struggle with in interviews is not the syntax -- it is the framing. Interviewers do not want a query. They want to hear you think. Structure your answer: first state what data you need (name the tables and columns), then describe the analytical question the query answers (the GROUP BY logic), then state what you would do with the result (the interpretation and recommendation). The query itself comes last and is almost secondary to the thinking.
stretch: Apply to three more roles this week. Track them in a spreadsheet: company, role, date applied, response date (update as it arrives). Ten applications is the minimum useful sample for calibrating response rate. Under five is too few to learn anything.

Do one mock technical interview with a friend who is also in the job market. Ask them to give you one SQL problem and one business case question. Do the reverse for them. The peer review surfaces the explanations that make sense in your head but not to someone who hears it for the first time.

Research the data analyst hiring process at two companies you want to work for. Check Glassdoor interview reviews (filter by "data analyst" and last 12 months). What SQL topics appear? What case study frameworks do they use? Knowing the specific format before you see it is a preparation advantage.

weeks.title: Power BI Mastery - DAX, modeling, deployment
weeks.context:
You learned Tableau in week 20. This week you learn Power BI -- the other half of the market, and the tool that dominates in Microsoft-stack companies (which is to say, most large enterprises). Having fluency in both is the difference between being the analyst who can only work in the organisation's preferred tool and being the analyst who can evaluate which tool is right for the problem and use either.

Power BI's advantage over Tableau is the Microsoft ecosystem integration. Power BI pulls directly from Azure, SQL Server, SharePoint, and Excel with native connectors. If your company runs on Microsoft, the data is already where Power BI can reach it. Power BI also has a more developed enterprise governance layer -- row-level security, workspace permissions, certified datasets, and deployment pipelines are all more mature in Power BI than in Tableau.

Power BI's distinctive feature is DAX (Data Analysis Expressions). DAX is a formula language for writing measures and calculated columns. If you have used SUMIFS and AVERAGEIFS in Excel, DAX will feel familiar at first -- and then you will encounter context transitions and CALCULATE and everything will stop being familiar. Context is the thing that makes DAX hard and powerful: a DAX measure's result depends on the filter context imposed by whatever slicer, filter, or row context is currently active, and CALCULATE is the function that lets you modify that context deliberately.

The time intelligence DAX functions are the most directly useful for business analysis: TOTALYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, and DATESINPERIOD compute the year-to-date sum, the same-period-last-year value, and any rolling window. These calculations require a properly constructed date dimension table -- which is why you spent time on the date dimension in week 22.

By Sunday: the Superstore analysis rebuilt in Power BI Desktop with four pages, proper data modeling, DAX measures for YTD and YoY growth, drill-through pages, and published to Power BI Service at a shared workspace URL.
topics: Power BI Desktop interface and Power Query (M language basics)
Star schema vs flat tables in Power BI
DAX measures vs calculated columns (when to use which)
Time intelligence DAX (YTD, YoY, rolling averages)
Publishing to Power BI Service + workspaces
Power BI vs Tableau - when to recommend each

items.title: Install Power BI + first dashboard
items.body:
## What it is
**Power BI** is Microsoft's BI tool — the other half of the market with Tableau (Week 20). You'll rebuild your Superstore dashboard in it, so the focus is the tool. Power BI Desktop is free on Windows.

## Why it matters
Power BI dominates Microsoft-stack companies (a huge share of the corporate world), so knowing both it and Tableau makes you eligible for nearly every BI role. Because you already know the analysis and Tableau's concepts, Power BI's similar drag-and-drop model will come fast — the second BI tool is always quicker than the first. Rebuilding a known dashboard lets you judge the tool, not relearn the data.

Same dashboard as Week 20's Tableau -> you compare the TOOLS directly.

days.title: Data modeling and relationships
days.summary: Connect tables in the model view. Concept + how.

items.title: Data modeling and relationships
items.body:
## What it is
Power BI's **Model view** lets you define **relationships** between tables (e.g. orders to a date table) by dragging key to key — a visual version of SQL joins that powers everything downstream.

## Why it matters
Power BI's real strength is the data model: once tables are related, a measure automatically works across all of them (sales by region by month, no manual joins). Getting relationships and their direction right is *the* foundation — a wrong relationship gives wrong totals everywhere. This is data modelling (your capstone schema skill) inside a BI tool.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
Model view:
  [ orders ]---order_date--->[ Calendar ]
       |---region (or a regions table)
Drag a key from one table to the matching key in another -> a relationship line.
A star schema (one fact table + dimension tables) is the goal.
```

cards.prompt: Power BI relationships let a measure work across tables automatically, like pre-defined joins.
cards.whenRight: Right — model once, then measures span all related tables.
cards.whenWrong: It does — relationships are reusable joins the whole model uses.
cards.sim: relate orders<->Calendar -> sales by month just works

items.title: Your turn — model it
items.body: [PRODUCE] In Model view, add a date/Calendar table and relate it to orders; confirm a relationship line connects them.

days.title: DAX measures
days.summary: Power BI's formula language. Concept + code with output.

items.title: DAX measures
items.body:
## What it is
**DAX** (Data Analysis Expressions) is Power BI's formula language for **measures** — reusable calculations like Total Sales, Profit Margin, or Average Order Value that recompute correctly under any filter.

## Why it matters
DAX is the skill that separates Power BI button-pushers from real analysts. A measure like `Profit Margin = DIVIDE(SUM(Profit), SUM(Sales))` automatically respects whatever the user filters (region, month) — that filter-awareness is DAX's superpower and the thing interviews probe. It's the Power BI equivalent of a calculated field, but more powerful.

items.title: See it worked (with result)
items.body:
## Define measures in DAX
```dax
Total Sales = SUM('orders'[Sales])
Total Profit = SUM('orders'[Profit])
Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales])
```
Drop `Profit Margin` into a card and a table by Region:
```
Region    Profit Margin
Central        3.0%
East          13.0%
South         11.9%
West          14.9%
```
The *same* measure recomputed per region automatically — that's DAX's filter-awareness. `DIVIDE` safely handles divide-by-zero (returns blank, not an error).

cards.prompt: A DAX measure recomputes correctly under whatever filter the user applies (e.g. per region).
cards.whenRight: Right — filter-awareness is DAX's defining superpower.
cards.whenWrong: It does — one measure adapts to every filter context.
cards.sim: one Profit Margin measure -> correct per region

cards.prompt: `DIVIDE(a, b)` is safer than `a / b` in DAX because it handles divide-by-zero.
cards.whenRight: Right — DIVIDE returns blank instead of erroring on zero.
cards.whenWrong: It is — DIVIDE guards against divide-by-zero cleanly.
cards.sim: DIVIDE(profit, sales) -> blank, not error, if sales=0

items.title: Your turn — write measures
items.body: [PRODUCE] Create DAX measures for Total Sales, Total Profit, and Profit Margin (using DIVIDE); show Profit Margin by Region and verify the numbers.

days.title: Time intelligence
days.summary: Compare across time with DAX. Concept + code with output.

items.title: Time intelligence
items.body:
## What it is
DAX **time-intelligence** functions compute period comparisons — year-over-year, year-to-date, prior period — using your related Calendar table (`SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR`, `TOTALYTD`, etc.).

## Why it matters
'How are we doing vs last year?' is the most-asked business question, and time intelligence answers it in one measure instead of manual date math. It's a flagship Power BI capability and a frequent interview topic — and it only works because you built the Calendar relationship on Day 2 (which is *why* the model matters).

items.title: See it worked (with result)
items.body:
## Year-over-year sales in DAX
```dax
Sales LY = CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Calendar'[Date]))
Sales YoY % = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - [Sales LY], [Sales LY])
```
By year:
```
Year   Total Sales   Sales LY   YoY %
2015     470,533     484,247    -2.8%
2016     609,206     470,533   +29.5%
2017     733,215     609,206   +20.4%
```
One measure gives every year's comparison to the prior year — powered by the Calendar relationship. This is the payoff of proper modelling.

cards.prompt: DAX time-intelligence (e.g. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR) computes period-over-period comparisons in one measure.
cards.whenRight: Right — YoY/YTD in a single measure, no manual date math.
cards.whenWrong: It does — time-intelligence functions handle period comparisons.

cards.prompt: Time intelligence works even without a proper related date/Calendar table.
cards.whenRight: Correct — it depends on the Calendar relationship you built on Day 2.
cards.whenWrong: Not so — it requires the Calendar table relationship to work.
cards.sim: no Calendar relationship -> time intelligence breaks

items.title: Your turn — time intelligence
items.body: [PRODUCE] Create a YoY sales measure with SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR; show Total Sales, Sales LY, and YoY % by year.

items.title: Multi-page report
items.body:
## What it is
Assemble a multi-page Power BI report — overview, detail, and a customer or operations page — using your measures, with charts and KPI cards on each.

## Why it matters
A single chart isn't a deliverable; a structured multi-page report is. This mirrors your capstone structure in Power BI and shows you can build a real BI product in the Microsoft stack. Reusing your DAX measures across pages demonstrates the efficiency of a good model — define once, use everywhere.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
PAGE 1 Overview: KPI cards (Total Sales, Margin, YoY) + trend + region bar
PAGE 2 Detail:   sales table by sub-category, sortable
PAGE 3 Customer/Ops: top customers / fulfilment metrics
All pages reuse the SAME DAX measures -> consistent numbers everywhere.
```

cards.prompt: Reusing the same DAX measures across report pages keeps numbers consistent and saves work.
cards.whenRight: Right — define a measure once, use it on every page.
cards.whenWrong: It does — shared measures = consistency + efficiency.
cards.sim: one Profit Margin measure used on all pages

items.title: Your turn — multi-page report
items.body: [PRODUCE] Build a 2-3 page report (overview + detail + one more) reusing your DAX measures, with KPI cards and charts.

days.title: Drill-through and bookmarks
days.summary: Power BI's interactivity. Concept + how.

items.title: Drill-through and bookmarks
items.body:
## What it is
**Drill-through** lets a user right-click a data point (a region) and jump to a detail page filtered to it; **bookmarks** save specific views/states you can switch between (e.g. a 'reset' button or a guided tour).

## Why it matters
These are Power BI's standout interactivity features — they turn a static report into an explorable app. Drill-through gives users a natural 'show me more about this' path, and bookmarks enable polished, guided experiences. Knowing them signals you can build *professional* Power BI, not just basic charts — exactly what employers test for beyond the basics.

items.title: See it worked
items.body:
```text
Drill-through: set up a 'Region Detail' page with a drill-through filter on Region.
   -> user right-clicks 'West' on page 1 -> jumps to that page, filtered to West.
Bookmarks: capture a view (e.g. all filters cleared) -> assign to a 'Reset' button.
```

cards.prompt: Drill-through and bookmarks turn a static Power BI report into an explorable, app-like experience.
cards.whenRight: Right — they're the interactivity that signals professional Power BI.
cards.whenWrong: It does — drill-through + bookmarks make the report explorable.

items.title: Your turn — add interactivity
items.body: [PRODUCE] Add a drill-through detail page (filtered by region) and one bookmark (e.g. a reset-filters button).

items.title: Publish + compare to Tableau
items.body:
## What it is
Publish your report to the Power BI Service (free with a Microsoft account) for a shareable link, then write a short comparison of Power BI vs Tableau from your hands-on experience with both.

## Why it matters
A published Power BI report plus your Tableau Public dashboard means you can *show* both tools — covering essentially the entire BI job market. The comparison note proves genuine, hands-on judgement ("Power BI's DAX + modelling is more powerful; Tableau's viz is faster/prettier"), which is exactly the kind of informed opinion interviewers love. You now finish the track fluent in both dominant BI platforms.

cards.prompt: Having published work in BOTH Power BI and Tableau covers essentially the whole BI job market.
cards.whenRight: Right — the two tools split the market; you can show both.
cards.whenWrong: It does — both platforms demonstrated = maximum job eligibility.
cards.sim: Power BI + Tableau published = full BI coverage

items.body:
[PRODUCE] Report published to Power BI Service (data model + DAX measures + time intelligence + drill-through/bookmarks).
[WRITE] A short Power BI vs Tableau comparison from your experience, in your portfolio.
[CODE] Commit the .pbix + notes; tag `powerbi-ready`; push. Add the published link to your portfolio. Data Analysis track COMPLETE.

weeks.ai_assist: Use Claude to explain the difference between row context and filter context in DAX, with a specific example using your Superstore data. Row context is the current row being iterated (in a calculated column or SUMX). Filter context is the set of filters imposed by slicers, visual filters, and CALCULATE. Understanding the difference is what makes DAX measures predictable rather than mysterious. Do NOT use Claude to write the time intelligence measures -- writing TOTALYTD and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR yourself, understanding each function's arguments, is the skill.
weeks.stakeholder_moment: Power BI is the de facto tool inside Microsoft-stack companies (60% of mid-large enterprises). Your audience is often a manager who already uses Power BI in their day job - they'll ask 'why didn't you use Tableau?' Be ready to defend the tool choice based on the company's existing stack, not personal preference.
mastery_questions: Create the date dimension table in Power BI using a DAX calculated table: DateTable = CALENDAR(DATE(2014,1,1), DATE(2018,12,31)). Add columns for Year, Quarter, Month, and MonthNumber using YEAR(), QUARTER(), FORMAT(), and MONTH() DAX functions. Mark it as a Date Table (Table Tools > Mark as date table, select the Date column). Create the relationship from DateTable[Date] to Orders[Order Date]. Paste the DAX for the DateTable creation. Confirm the relationship appears as active (solid line) in Model view.

Write four DAX measures: Total Sales = SUM(Orders[Sales]), Total Profit = SUM(Orders[Profit]), Profit Margin = DIVIDE([Total Profit], [Total Sales], 0), YTD Sales = TOTALYTD([Total Sales], DateTable[Date]). Paste all four. Add them to a card visual and confirm they show the same values as the week-1 Excel analysis. Write one sentence explaining what DIVIDE(..., 0) handles that a simple division operator does not.

Write a YoY Sales Growth measure: YoY Sales Growth = DIVIDE([Total Sales] - CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DateTable[Date])), CALCULATE([Total Sales], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR(DateTable[Date])), 0). common_mistakes: Not marking the date table as a Date Table before using time intelligence functions. TOTALYTD and SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR require the Date Table to be marked, and they fail silently (returning blank or incorrect results) if it is not.

Using calculated columns for metrics that should be measures. A calculated column computes a value for every row in the table and is stored in memory. A measure computes a value based on the current filter context without storing per-row values. Profit Margin should be a measure (it changes with every filter), not a calculated column.

Creating a many-to-many relationship between Orders and the Date Table. Orders has one date per row; the Date Table has one row per date. The relationship should be one-to-many (one date, many orders). If Power BI shows a many-to-many warning, the Order Date column in Orders has dates that are not in the Date Table range -- extend the CALENDAR function range.

Publishing to Power BI Service without setting the correct workspace permissions. A report published to "My Workspace" is not shareable without Power BI Pro. For a portfolio, publish to a shared workspace (free tier) and copy the URL from the workspace, not from "My Workspace."

Writing DAX measures without testing them at multiple filter contexts. A measure that is correct at the total level may be wrong at the Category level or at the individual order level. Always test measures in a table visual with at least two levels of granularity before relying on them.
weeks.debug_help: Two specific DAX debugging patterns. First: a measure returns BLANK instead of a value. Usually means either the filter context has filtered out all data (check if all slicers and filters are compatible with the data), or a DIVIDE function is returning BLANK because the denominator is 0 (change the alternate result parameter: DIVIDE(numerator, denominator, 0) returns 0 instead of BLANK). Second: SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR returns the same year instead of the previous year. The Date Table is not marked as a Date Table, or the relationship between the Date Table and the Orders table is not active. Check both in the Model view.
